9.1|In conservative thought, why is sudden, radical political change viewed with skepticism?|Because human beings are infallible and always make optimal choices|Because existing institutions embody the accumulated wisdom of past generations and abrupt change invites chaos|Because rapid reform always leads directly to absolute economic equality|Because the state must never adapt to changing technological conditions|Option B|Conservatives value continuity and tradition, arguing that established social fabrics contain tested wisdom that radical revolutions destroy.
9.1|Which of the following pairs correctly matches an ideology with its primary institutional objective?|Anarchism and the establishment of a powerful centralized bureaucracy|Communism and the preservation of inherited class privileges|Fascism and the promotion of decentralized autonomous regional soviets|Liberalism and the protection of individual rights through a constitutional limited government|Option D|Liberalism seeks to safeguard personal freedoms by restricting government power through constitutional frameworks.
7.1|Which of the following best distinguishes power from authority in political science?|Power relies strictly on economic incentives while authority relies on physical violence|Power is the probability of imposing one's will despite resistance through sanctions whereas authority involves recognized legitimacy|Power requires constitutional frameworks to function whereas authority is inherently informal and illegal|Power is a voluntary psychological state whereas authority is a temporary economic arrangement|Option B|Power involves coercion and imposing will regardless of resistance, whereas authority is defined by the recognized right to command obedience.
7.1|An absolute monarch ruling strictly by virtue of long-standing hereditary customs and ancient traditions exemplifies which of Max Weber's types of authority?|Charismatic authority|Legal-rational authority|Traditional authority|Technocratic authority|Option C|Traditional authority derives its legitimacy from established customs, social hierarchies, and long-standing historical practices.
7.1|When a revolutionary leader inspires widespread mass obedience through exceptional personal heroism and extraordinary character traits, they are exercising which form of domination?|Traditional authority|Charismatic authority|Legal-rational authority|Coercive power|Option B|Charismatic authority is founded on devotion to the exceptional sanctity, heroism, or exemplary character of an individual leader.
7.1|Modern bureaucratic governance grounded in written constitutions, explicit legal statutes, and impersonal offices is characteristic of which Weberian category?|Traditional authority|Charismatic authority|Legal-rational authority|Normative power|Option C|Legal-rational authority derives its legitimacy from a system of explicit rules, laws, and institutional procedures applied impartially.
7.1|If a government successfully compels citizens to comply with tax laws primarily by threatening them with criminal prosecution and imprisonment, what mechanism is predominantly at play?|Authority|Power through coercive sanctions|Charismatic leadership|Traditional legitimacy|Option B|Compelling compliance through threatened punishment or negative sanctions is a hallmark of coercive power rather than legitimate authority.
7.1|Why is legitimacy considered a crucial element that separates authority from naked power?|It eliminates the need for any form of government administration|It ensures that obedience is given voluntarily because the command is viewed as right and proper|It guarantees that a state will experience perpetual economic growth|It transforms traditional leaders into legal-rational bureaucrats instantly|Option B|Legitimacy transforms raw power into authority by establishing a moral or normative right to command that subordinates recognize and accept.
7.1|Which of the following scenarios best illustrates legal-rational authority in action?|Citizens following a tribal chief because their family has ruled for centuries|Citizens obeying a police officer because they are enforcing established constitutional traffic laws|Citizens supporting a populist speaker due to their mesmerizing public speaking skills|Workers striking against an employer to demand higher wages|Option B|A police officer enforcing written statutory laws represents the impersonal, rules-based nature of legal-rational authority.
7.1|What happens when a charismatic leader's movement institutionalizes and establishes permanent administrative offices and written rules?|The authority transforms entirely into pure coercion|The authority typically routinizes into traditional or legal-rational forms|The system immediately collapses due to a lack of power|The leader retains pure charismatic status indefinitely without rules|Option B|Weber noted that charismatic authority is unstable and tends to routinize into traditional or legal-rational authority over time.
7.1|Which dimension is fundamentally absent in pure authority that distinguishes it from coercion-based power?|The necessity of physical force or immediate sanctions to secure compliance|The existence of a recognized command structure|The presence of subordinate actors|The transmission of directives from a superior|Option A|Authority relies on voluntary recognition and legitimacy, meaning it does not inherently depend on the constant application of physical force or sanctions.
7.1|In the context of Max Weber's typology, how is obedience secured under traditional authority?|Through belief in the sanctity of age-old rules and hereditary status|Through adherence to rationally enacted legal codes and statutes|Through emotional devotion to a revolutionary leader's extraordinary qualities|Through the calculated exchange of economic goods and services|Option A|Traditional authority secures obedience because subordinates accept the sanctity and permanence of historic customs and hereditary titles.
8.1|How is political legitimacy primarily defined in the study of political science?|The physical capacity of a state to enforce laws through military police power|The psychological conviction among citizens that rulers possess the moral right to govern|The legalistic framework established solely by international treaties and foreign recognition|The total economic output and resource distribution managed by a centralized government|Option B|Legitimacy refers to the psychological acceptance and conviction by the public that those in power have a moral right to exercise authority over them.
8.1|Which of the following is considered a primary source or foundation of political legitimacy?|Arbitrary royal decree without popular consent|Routine performance in delivering public goods and upholding the rule of law|Strict suppression of dissenting political factions through censorship|Unilateral military occupation by foreign allied forces|Option C|Performance in delivering public goods and maintaining the rule of law builds public trust, which reinforces the moral right of rulers to govern.
8.1|What distinguishes political influence from other forms of power in a political system?|It relies exclusively on physical coercion and institutionalized violence|It relies on shaping decisions through persuasion prestige rational argument and lobbying without coercive force|It requires absolute control over the national budget and financial institutions|It operates only within totalitarian regimes where opposition is illegal|Option B|Political influence is characterized by shaping political outcomes through non-coercive means such as persuasion and argument rather than force.
8.1|If a government successfully convinces citizens to adopt a new environmental policy by presenting scientific data and logical arguments without threats what mechanism is being utilized?|Coercion|Political influence|Authoritarian mandate|Structural domination|Option B|Using rational argument and persuasion to shape decisions without utilizing coercive force is the core definition of political influence.
8.1|Which of the following actions best exemplifies political influence rather than direct coercion?|Imposing heavy fines or prison sentences for violating new tax codes|Deploying the national guard to disperse an unauthorized public gathering|Lobbying lawmakers and using reasoned persuasion to alter a pending bill|Dissolving the legislature by executive decree during an emergency|Option C|Lobbying and persuasion rely on non-coercive arguments to shape political decisions, which fits the definition of political influence.
8.1|Why is psychological conviction a critical component of legitimacy rather than mere compliance?|Compliance can be achieved through fear of punishment whereas legitimacy implies a voluntary moral acceptance of authority|Psychological conviction prevents citizens from ever questioning government policies or economic strategies|It ensures that the state never has to collect taxes or maintain a formal police force|Conviction eliminates all forms of political conflict and ideological diversity in society|Option A|Legitimacy differs from bare obedience because it involves a belief in the moral rightness of authority, whereas compliance can be forced through fear.
8.1|How do regular and credible elections contribute to the political legitimacy of a government?|By guaranteeing that economic inflation will remain at zero percent indefinitely|By reinforcing the psychological conviction that leaders hold office through a moral and procedurally fair mandate|By completely eliminating the need for public administration or policy implementation|By granting absolute immunity from judicial review to all elected officials|Option B|Elections provide a procedural mechanism that fosters the psychological conviction among citizens that their leaders have a moral and valid right to rule.
8.1|Which scenario best illustrates a deficit in political legitimacy?|Citizens willingly paying taxes and participating in civic institutions because they trust the system|Rulers maintaining power solely through fear and severe repression because public trust has collapsed|A high voter turnout during a deeply contested national election|The peaceful transition of power following a constitutional judicial ruling|Option B|When a government loses legitimacy, it often has to rely entirely on coercion and fear to maintain control because the psychological conviction of its right to rule is gone.
8.1|In the context of political science tools what role does prestige play in political influence?|It serves as a coercive financial penalty for political opponents|It enhances a political actor's ability to persuade and shape decisions without using force|It legally invalidates opposition parties through constitutional amendments|It dictates the military budget and allocation of defense resources|Option B|Prestige is a non-coercive asset that enhances a political actor's standing, making it easier to persuade others and exercise political influence.
8.1|What is the relationship between the rule of law and political legitimacy?|The rule of law undermines legitimacy by restricting executive power too severely|Upholding the rule of law strengthens legitimacy by demonstrating fair and predictable governance|The rule of law is completely irrelevant to how citizens perceive the moral authority of leaders|Legitimacy exists only in states that completely reject the rule of law in favor of absolute monarchy|Option B|When rulers adhere to the rule of law, it builds trust and reinforces the psychological conviction that the government exercises authority morally and fairly.

14.1|What is the purpose of impersonality in the execution of official duties within a bureaucracy according to Max Weber?|To alienate citizens and discourage public participation in state affairs|To ensure that official business is conducted without bias, favoritism, or emotional influence|To protect corrupt officials from individual criminal accountability|To eliminate all forms of human communication within the workplace|Option C|Impersonality ensures that bureaucrats apply laws and regulations uniformly and rationally to all citizens without letting personal feelings or favoritism affect their decisions.
14.1|Which principle governs career tenure and personnel advancement in a classic Weberian bureaucracy?|Appointment and promotion based strictly on objective merit and professional qualifications|Selection based on familial lineage and aristocratic inheritance|Frequent political rotation determined by whichever party wins the election|Random assignment through a lottery system open to all citizens|Option A|Weber argued that modern bureaucratic efficiency requires a merit-based system where tenure and promotions depend on demonstrated competence and qualifications.

14.1|Which of the following sets of characteristics exclusively represents Max Webers ideal model of bureaucracy?|Charismatic leadership, divine right, hereditary office, and informal norms|Fixed jurisdictions, hierarchical command, written records, and merit tenure|Decentralized chaos, emotional decision-making, flexible rules, and political patronage|Voluntary participation, temporary contracts, public voting, and rotating leadership|Option B|Weber explicitly identified fixed jurisdictions, a hierarchy of authority, written files, impersonality, and merit-based careers as the core pillars of his ideal bureaucracy.

4.1|Which of the following is explicitly listed as a core tenet of the behavioural credo?|Value-free inquiry|Revolutionary political action|Moral absolutism|Historical idealism|Option A|Value-free inquiry is a central tenet of the behavioural credo, aiming to separate personal biases from scientific observation.

3.1|Which key political actor or entity would an institutionalist scholar primarily study when analyzing a government decision?|A grassroots protest movement marching outside parliament|The formal legislative voting procedure inside the parliament assembly|The unspoken economic leverage held by corporate monopolies|The psychological motivations of individual voters at the polls|Option B|Institutionalists prioritize formal state structures, such as legislative bodies and their official operating rules, rather than external informal actors.
3.1|Why might the legalistic approach fall short when analyzing a politically unstable developing nation?|It overemphasizes the role of illegal revolutionary factions|It accounts for too many informal variables at once|It overlooks powerful informal forces like corruption and military influence that bypass constitutional rules|It relies too much on statistical polling data rather than historical texts|Option C|Developing nations often experience a wide gap between formal constitutional texts and real political practice, which legalistic frameworks fail to capture.
3.1|How does the institutional approach typically view the role of pressure groups and interest groups?|As the core engine driving all constitutional change|As a vital institutional branch of the judiciary|As elements often ignored or understated due to a strict focus on official government machinery|As the primary formal actors recognized within constitutional texts|Option C|Because the traditional legalistic approach concentrates strictly on official state organs, it largely overlooks the informal influence of pressure groups.
3.1|Which of the following research questions best reflects the institutional approach to political science?|How do informal ethnic alliances shape legislative voting behavior behind closed doors?|What are the exact constitutional powers granted to the executive branch by article two of the constitution?|How do socioeconomic class divisions dictate voter turnout rates?|Why do citizens feel alienated from modern political parties?|Option B|This question directly examines formal constitutional text and official jurisdictional limits, which is the hallmark of institutional analysis.
3.1|What distinguishes the institutional approach from behavioral or sociological approaches to political science?|Its primary focus on written laws and formal institutions rather than human behavior and social forces|Its heavy reliance on psychological profiling of political leaders|Its use of radical economic theory to critique state structures|Its emphasis on predicting future revolutions through mathematical modeling|Option A|Unlike behavioralism which studies human behavior, the institutional approach focuses tightly on structural rules, laws, and formal institutions.
3.1|In the context of institutional analysis, what is the significance of examining courts and legislatures?|They represent the unorganized masses in civil society|They are the primary formal arenas where legal rules are interpreted and enforced|They serve as the main channels for underground political resistance|They embody the informal cultural norms of a society|Option B|Courts and legislatures are core official institutions tasked with creating, interpreting, and applying formal legal rules in a state.
3.1|Why is the legalistic approach sometimes criticized as being overly descriptive?|It spends too much time building complex predictive mathematical models|It tends to describe what the constitution or laws say without critically analyzing why or how power actually functions|It relies exclusively on experimental laboratory data rather than historical documents|It focuses entirely on futuristic technological impacts on governance|Option B|Being descriptive means the approach catalogs formal structures accurately without probing deeply into the messy, unwritten realities of power politics.
6.1|Which political theorist defined sovereignty as supreme power over citizens and subjects that is unrestrained by law?|Thomas Hobbes|Jean Bodin|John Austin|Max Weber|Option B|Jean Bodin introduced the classical concept of sovereignty as absolute and permanent power that is not bound by positive laws.
6.1|In Thomas Hobbes' political theory, what mechanism justifies the creation of an absolute sovereign Leviathan?|A divine right mandate inherited from ancient monarchs|A social contract forged out of a mutual fear of the chaotic state of nature|An economic treaty established to regulate international trade routes|A democratic election conducted among all adult citizens within a territory|Option B|Hobbes argued that individuals escape the violent state of nature by surrendering their rights to a powerful sovereign through a social contract.
6.1|How does John Austin conceptualize sovereignty within his legal positivist framework?|As a moral consensus shared universally among all global communities|As the habitual obedience given to a determinate human superior who is not in the habit of obedience to a like superior|As a revolutionary force led by the working class to dismantle capitalist states|As an elastic constitutional arrangement subject to daily public referendum|Option B|Austin defined sovereignty command-wise through the habitual obedience rendered to a supreme, determinate political superior.
6.1|Which characteristic of sovereignty asserts that supreme power cannot be legally transferred, granted, or partitioned away to another entity?|Permanence|Universality|Inalienability|Absoluteness|Option C|Inalienability dictates that sovereignty is an intrinsic attribute that cannot be surrendered or transferred without destroying the state itself.
6.1|What distinguishes a de jure sovereign from a de facto sovereign in political science?|De jure refers to physical military control while de facto refers strictly to moral authority|De jure denotes rightful legal constitutional authority whereas de facto denotes actual physical and coercive control|De jure describes transient emergency powers while de facto describes permanent legislative acts|De jure applies exclusively to democratic nations while de facto applies to monarchies|Option B|De jure sovereignty represents lawful authority granted by law, whereas de facto sovereignty represents actual power backed by coercion regardless of formal legality.
6.1|If a sovereign state experiences a temporary civil war that changes its government leadership, which core attribute ensures that sovereignty itself endures?|Indivisibility|Permanence|Legal pluralism|Popular consent|Option B|Permanence ensures that sovereignty persists continuously across shifts in government regimes or temporary internal upheavals.
6.1|Where does political or popular sovereignty primarily reside in a modern representative democracy?|Within the permanent bureaucracy of civil servants|Within the supreme court judiciary|Within the electorate or the body of citizens|Within the standing military forces|Option C|Political or popular sovereignty locates ultimate supreme power and legitimacy within the hands of the voting citizenry or electorate.
6.1|What does the characteristic of indivisibility imply regarding supreme political power within a state?|Power can be endlessly fragmented among regional councils without a final authority|Power cannot be legally split or shared among rival co-equal bodies without risking systemic breakdown|Power must alternate annually between competing political parties|Power is shared equally between citizens and foreign entities|Option B|Indivisibility maintains that supreme authority must ultimately rest in a single final center of decision-making rather than being perpetually split.
6.1|Which theorist's conceptualization of sovereignty aligns most closely with strict legal positivism and the command theory of law?|Jean Bodin|Thomas Hobbes|John Austin|Aristotle|Option C|John Austin pioneered legal positivism by defining law as the command of a sovereign backed by sanctions.

8.1|How does political influence fundamentally differ from coercion?|Influence relies on persuasion, prestige, and rational argument rather than physical force or threats|Influence can only be exercised by elected heads of state while coercion is used by citizens|Influence is always illegal whereas coercion is sanctioned by international treaties|Influence requires absolute military superiority to change citizens' political opinions|Option A|Political influence is distinct because it shapes decisions and behaviors through voluntary means like persuasion and prestige, completely avoiding coercive force.

3.1|Which of the following is considered a major merit of the legalistic institutional approach?|It effectively maps out hidden corruption networks within a regime|It accurately predicts revolutionary upheavals based on economic class friction|It clearly clarifies constitutional rights and jurisdictional limits of state organs|It thoroughly explains the political influence of non-governmental pressure groups|Option C|A primary merit of this approach is its ability to provide precise clarity regarding formal constitutional rights and the jurisdictional boundaries of political institutions.
3.1|What is a central limitation associated with the institutional approach to political science?|It is overly dynamic and changes too rapidly to establish stable theories|It is largely static and descriptive ignoring informal power dynamics|It places too much emphasis on revolutionary socio-economic forces|It completely disregards the written text of a nation constitution|Option B|The legalistic institutional approach is often criticized for being static and overly descriptive while failing to account for informal power dynamics that shape politics.
3.1|How does the legalistic institutional approach view the role of pressure groups and informal actors?|As the primary driving force behind all modern state constitutions|As essential components that must be formally integrated into lawmaking|As largely ignored or treated as secondary to formal legal structures|As illegal entities that undermine the legitimacy of any democratic system|Option C|Because it focuses narrowly on official bodies like courts and legislatures the institutional approach tends to ignore or minimize the impact of informal actors and pressure groups.
3.1|Which specific institutions are central to the analysis of the legalistic institutional framework?|Trade unions and underground resistance cells|Legislatures courts and executive bodies established by law|Multi-national corporations and global financial institutions|Revolutionary vanguards and social media activist networks|Option B|The approach prioritizes official institutional machinery such as formal legislatures courts and executive organs defined by constitutional law.
3.1|Which factor is most likely to be overlooked by a strict adherent of the legalistic institutional approach?|The amendment procedure outlined in a nation written constitution|The official legal jurisdiction assigned to a supreme court|Socio-economic inequalities and how they affect political access|The statutory duties mandated for an elected head of state|Option C|Socio-economic forces and underlying economic inequalities fall outside the narrow formal focus of traditional legalistic institutional analysis.
3.1|Why is the institutional approach sometimes criticized as being static?|It relies entirely on real-time computer simulations of voting behavior|It assumes political systems change constantly without any rules|It emphasizes formal legal structures while missing evolving behavioral realities|It rejects the study of historical documents in favor of future predictions|Option C|The approach is considered static because legal frameworks change slowly and studying only formal texts misses the dynamic, everyday realities of political behavior.
3.1|What role do formal constitutional texts play within the legalistic institutional approach?|They are treated as secondary background material with little analytical value|They serve as the core foundational object of study and evaluation|They are viewed merely as propaganda tools masking economic exploitation|They are analyzed exclusively for their hidden psychological impacts|Option B|Constitutional texts form the cornerstone of the legalistic approach, providing the primary rules and parameters for government organization.
3.1|Which critique best highlights the blind spot of the legalistic institutional approach regarding corruption?|It assumes all politicians strictly follow written legal mandates without deviation|It focuses too heavily on underground criminal syndicates rather than elections|It claims that corruption is legally mandated in modern constitutions|It measures corruption using complex mathematical formulas instead of laws|Option A|Because the approach assumes official institutions operate strictly by the book, it often overlooks real-world phenomena like corruption that bypass formal rules.
3.1|What distinguishes the legalistic institutional approach from approaches that study socio-economic forces?|Institutionalists study wealth distribution whereas socio-economic theorists study laws|Institutionalists focus on formal rules whereas socio-economic theorists focus on material conditions and class|Institutionalists reject the state entirely whereas socio-economic theorists worship the state|Institutionalists rely on experimental psychology whereas socio-economic theorists use anthropology|Option B|The key distinction lies in the institutional focus on formal legal rules versus the socio-economic focus on material conditions, class structures, and distribution of wealth.
4.1|Which school of thought primarily drove the emergence of the behavioural approach to political science during the 1950s?|The Chicago school|The Oxford analytical school|The Frankfurt critical school|The Paris structuralist school|Option A|Behaviouralism emerged primarily from the Chicago school in the 1950s through scholars like David Easton and Harold Lasswell focusing on empirical study.|
4.1|What core methodological focus distinguishes the behavioural approach in political science from traditional institutionalism?|Empirical and quantitative study of human political behavior|Historical evolution of legal constitutions|Philosophical analysis of normative justice|Ethical evaluation of state sovereignty|Option A|Behaviouralism shifts focus toward the empirical, scientific, and quantitative measurement of actual human behavior in politics.|
4.1|According to the credo of behaviouralism as outlined by David Easton, what does the principle of verification entail?|Testing and validating empirical statements against observable data|Accepting normative claims based on tradition and authority|Prioritizing philosophical deduction over factual induction|Relying exclusively on historical case studies without data|Option A|Verification requires that political claims and hypotheses be tested and validated against observable, empirical data rather than accepted dogmatically.|
4.1|Which tenet of the behavioural credo emphasizes keeping political inquiry neutral and distinct from ethical evaluations?|Value-free inquiry|Systematization|Quantification|Regularities|Option A|Value-free inquiry asserts that scientific political research should focus on what is rather than what ought to be, avoiding subjective moral judgments.|
4.1|What is the primary critique that post-behaviouralism raised against classical behaviouralism?|Overlooking urgent social crises and societal relevance in pursuit of pure quantification|Failing to use statistical data and rigorous mathematical modeling|Rejecting the use of empirical observation in political studies|Emphasizing historical context too heavily over contemporary data|Option A|Post-behaviouralism emerged because critics felt behaviouralism was too obsessed with pure technique and quantification while ignoring real-world crises like war and poverty.|
4.1|Which key theorist is most closely associated with the formulation of the behavioural approach and its intellectual credo?|David Easton|Max Weber|Karl Marx|Thomas Hobbes|Option A|David Easton is widely recognized as a central figure who systematized the behavioural approach and outlined its defining intellectual tenets.|
4.1|What role does quantification play within the traditional behavioural credo?|Providing precise measurement and analysis of political phenomena|Replacing theoretical frameworks with historical anecdotes|Dictating the moral objectives of public policy legislation|Eliminating the need for any qualitative context in research|Option A|Quantification allows researchers to measure variables precisely, facilitating rigorous statistical analysis of political behavior.|
4.1|How does post-behaviouralism view the relationship between political science research and societal action?|Research must be socially relevant and actively address human problems|Research must remain strictly isolated from public policy debates|Action should be completely divorced from empirical findings|Scholars should focus solely on theoretical abstraction|Option A|Post-behaviouralism insists that political science must remain socially relevant and actively apply its tools to solve human crises like inequality and war.|
4.1|In the context of the behavioural approach, what is the purpose of searching for regularities in political behavior?|To discover uniformities that can be generalized and expressed in scientific theories|To establish rigid moral laws that dictate how citizens should vote|To prove that political choices are entirely random and unpredictable|To eliminate the study of institutions altogether|Option A|The search for regularities aims to uncover recurring patterns in human political behavior that allow for theoretical generalization and prediction.|
4.1|Which characteristic best defines the systematization tenet of behaviouralism?|Interrelating data and theory closely into an ordered body of knowledge|Accumulating isolated facts without any overarching framework|Relying purely on intuitive judgments and unstructured interviews|Treating every political event as a completely isolated phenomenon|Option A|Systematization involves closely linking theory and research so that empirical findings contribute to an integrated, coherent body of scientific knowledge.|

4.1|What is the primary methodological focus of the behavioural approach to politics?|Empirical and quantitative study of human political behaviour|Qualitative analysis of historical legal texts|Normative evaluation of ideal state constitutions|Philosophical inquiry into moral justice|Option A|Behaviouralism prioritizes the empirical and quantitative investigation of observable human actions within political systems.

4.1|How does behaviouralism view the relationship between political science and values?|It advocates for value-free inquiry to maintain objective scientific standards|It demands that political science actively prescribe moral standards|It believes political science should serve a specific religious ideology|It argues that values are the only proper subject of study|Option A|Behaviouralism promotes value-free inquiry to keep scientific research free from personal, ideological, or moral bias.

4.1|Why did post-behaviouralists criticize strict behaviouralism?|For focusing too narrowly on techniques while neglecting urgent social problems and moral crises|For being insufficiently quantitative in its data collection methods|For relying too heavily on historical case studies instead of experiments|For rejecting the use of empirical observation altogether|Option A|Post-behaviouralism emerged as a reaction against the overly detached, technique-driven nature of behaviouralism, arguing it ignored pressing societal crises like war and inequality.

6.1|Which characteristic of sovereignty implies that supreme power cannot be transferred, alienated, or granted away without destroying the state itself?|Permanence|Indivisibility|Universality|Inalienability|Option D|Inalienability dictates that a sovereign cannot cede its fundamental supreme authority to another entity without forfeiting its nature.
6.1|When a government holds absolute legal authority under the constitution, but a powerful military junta exercises actual physical coercive control over the territory, what type of power does the junta possess?|De Jure sovereignty|De Facto sovereignty|Popular sovereignty|Legal sovereignty|Option B|De facto sovereignty describes the actual physical control and coercive power wielded by an entity, regardless of formal constitutional status.
6.1|What distinguishes legal sovereignty from political or popular sovereignty?|Legal sovereignty resides with the electorate while political sovereignty resides with parliament|Legal sovereignty refers to the supreme law-making authority whereas political or popular sovereignty rests with the ultimate power of the electorate|Legal sovereignty is temporary while political sovereignty is permanent|Legal sovereignty applies only to federal states while political sovereignty applies only to confederations|Option B|Legal sovereignty is the supreme legal power to make laws (such as Parliament), whereas political or popular sovereignty resides with the underlying electorate or political forces.
6.1|Which core attribute of sovereignty asserts that supreme power applies universally across all persons and associations within the territorial jurisdiction?|Permanence|Universality|Indivisibility|De jure status|Option B|Universality means that the sovereign authority extends over all individuals and groups within the geographical boundaries of the state without exception.
6.1|If a constitutional monarch reigns according to the established laws of the land, possessing the formal constitutional right to govern, what type of sovereignty do they hold?|De Facto sovereignty|Popular sovereignty|De Jure sovereignty|Absolute sovereignty|Option C|De jure sovereignty means having the legal and constitutional right to exercise supreme power, even if day-to-day enforcement varies.
6.1|Which theorist's view of sovereignty aligns most closely with the command theory of law where laws are orders backed by threats from a supreme authority?|Jean Bodin|Thomas Hobbes|John Austin|Aristotle|Option C|John Austin pioneered the command theory of law, viewing law as the explicit command of a sovereign political superior backed by sanctions.
6.1|What does the characteristic of indivisibility mean in the context of classical sovereignty?|Supreme power cannot be legally fragmented or shared among rival co-equal branches without causing conflict|Sovereignty must change hands every generation|Supreme power must be geographically shared among municipal bodies|Sovereignty can be revoked at any time by citizens|Option A|Classical theorists like Bodin and Hobbes maintained that sovereignty is indivisible, meaning supreme authority cannot be split without destroying the unity of the state.

4.1|Which historical development is most closely associated with the emergence of the behavioural approach in political science during the 1950s?|The establishment of the Chicago school focusing on empirical and quantitative methods|The sudden abandonment of institutional frameworks in favor of normative philosophical debates|The strict rejection of all statistical modeling in favor of historical narrative analysis|The immediate global consensus to address poverty and war through political action|Option A|Behaviouralism emerged during the 1950s primarily through the Chicago school emphasizing empirical and quantitative study of human political behavior.
4.1|Which of the following best captures the primary methodological emphasis of the behavioural approach in political science?|Purely normative philosophical speculation about the ideal state|Empirical observation and quantitative measurement of political behavior|Historical analysis of legal texts and institutional charters|Intuitive interpretation of political rhetoric and ideological texts|Option B|Behaviouralism prioritizes empirical data collection, systematic observation, and quantitative analysis rather than purely normative or historical methods.
4.1|David Easton and Harold Lasswell are foundational figures most prominently linked to which political science paradigm?|Classical political philosophy|Institutionalism|Behaviouralism|Marxist political economy|Option C|David Easton and Harold Lasswell are key architects of the 1950s Chicago school who shaped the behavioural revolution in political science.
4.1|What is the core meaning of the verification tenet within the credos of behaviouralism?|Propositions and empirical claims must be testable and subject to empirical proof|Political theories are inherently subjective and impossible to validate scientifically|Moral values should guide the final evaluation of any political system regardless of data|Qualitative case studies hold higher scientific validity than statistical metrics|Option A|The verification tenet dictates that scientific claims in political science must be empirically testable and subject to proof.
4.1|How does the behavioural approach view the role of value-free inquiry in political research?|Values should dominate the formulation of all scientific hypotheses and data interpretation|The researcher must separate personal value judgments from empirical observation and analysis|Value neutrality is entirely impossible and therefore behaviouralism abandons all objectivity|Values should be imposed directly onto citizens to ensure systematic political order|Option B|Behaviouralism stresses value-free inquiry, meaning researchers strive to keep personal values separate from empirical analysis.
4.1|What does the systematization tenet in the behavioural credo primarily emphasize?|Gathering random political facts without any overarching theoretical framework|Interrelating data collection and theory building into an organized body of knowledge|Relying exclusively on unstructured interviews to capture raw human emotions|Discarding old theoretical models every fiscal year to maintain novelty|Option B|Systematization involves organizing research so that data collection and theoretical frameworks are tightly integrated into a coherent body of knowledge.
4.1|What was a primary critique raised by post-behaviouralism against traditional behaviouralism?|Behaviouralism focused too heavily on solving immediate human crises like poverty and war|Behaviouralism was overly obsessed with empirical data collection while ignoring urgent social relevance and human crises|Behaviouralism rejected the use of quantitative techniques and statistical software entirely|Behaviouralism relied exclusively on normative philosophy rather than scientific observation|Option B|Post-behaviouralism emerged because critics argued behaviouralism neglected pressing real-world crises like war, poverty, and inequality in its pursuit of pure value-free science.
4.1|Which concept is central to the post-behavioural movement pioneered in response to behaviouralism?|Hyper-quantification and total detachment from social issues|Social relevance and the application of political science to solve human crises|Strict adherence to traditional legal-institutional description|The total elimination of empirical methods in favor of subjective intuition|Option B|Post-behaviouralism insists that political science must remain socially relevant and actively address real-world human crises.
4.1|Which of the following attributes is part of the core credo of behaviouralism as outlined by political scientists?|Regularities and quantification|Normative idealism and moral instruction|Historical determinism and teleology|Philosophical intuition and introspection|Option A|The core credos of behaviouralism include regularities, verification, techniques, quantification, value-free inquiry, and systematization.
4.1|If a political researcher uses advanced statistical modeling to find patterns in voter turnout without letting personal political opinions skew the results, which two behavioural credos are primarily being demonstrated?|Regularities and moral philosophy|Quantification and value-free inquiry|Systematization and historical narrative|Verification and normative judgment|Option B|Using statistical modeling reflects quantification, while ensuring personal opinions do not skew results demonstrates value-free inquiry.
6.1|Which political theorist defined sovereignty as supreme power over citizens and subjects that is unrestrained by law|Thomas Hobbes|John Austin|Jean Bodin|Aristotle|Option C|Jean Bodin conceptualized sovereignty as absolute and supreme power that is fundamentally unrestrained by positive laws.|
6.1|How does Thomas Hobbes primarily characterize the sovereign power in his social contract theory|As a limited constitutional trustee bound by popular consent|As an absolute Leviathan with undivided authority to maintain order|As a legal command issued by a determinate superior who receives regular habits of obedience|As a divisible arrangement shared between a monarch and an elected parliament|Option B|Hobbes argued for an absolute Leviathan to escape the state of nature, possessing undivided and supreme authority.|
6.1|According to John Austin's analytical jurisprudence how is sovereignty fundamentally established|Through the moral consensus of a civil society respecting natural rights|Through a divine right bestowed upon monarchs by historical tradition|Through the legal command of a determinate superior who is habitually obeyed by the bulk of society|Through the economic supremacy of the working class over means of production|Option C|Austin defined sovereignty strictly in legal terms as a determinate superior receiving habitual obedience from society's majority.|
6.1|Which characteristic of sovereignty implies that supreme authority cannot be legally transferred or signed away to another entity|Indivisibility|Permanence|Inalienability|Universality|Option C|Inalienability means that the sovereign power cannot be surrendered or alienated without destroying the sovereign entity itself.|
6.1|What distinguishes De Jure sovereignty from De Facto sovereignty in political science|De Jure is recognized constitutional right whereas De Facto is actual physical coercive control|De Jure applies exclusively to democratic states whereas De Facto applies to monarchies|De Jure is temporary emergency power whereas De Facto is permanent statutory legislation|De Jure is held by the electorate whereas De Facto is held exclusively by the judiciary|Option A|De Jure denotes the legitimate legal right to rule, whereas De Facto refers to actual physical and coercive power on the ground.|

6.1|Which attribute of sovereignty dictates that supreme power cannot be legally fragmented or partitioned among competing branches without causing systemic instability|Permanence|Indivisibility|Universality|Absoluteness|Option B|Indivisibility asserts that supreme authority must remain a single unified whole rather than being split into conflicting parts.|
6.1|What does the characteristic of permanence signify regarding a sovereign state|The physical territory of the state can never expand or contract through war|The sovereign authority outlives individual rulers and persists as long as the independent state exists|The laws enacted by a legislature can never be repealed or amended by future generations|The economic resources of the nation must remain permanently nationalized|Option B|Permanence means sovereignty is enduring and continuous, surviving changes in government personnel or individual leaders.|

4.1|What does the concept of 'Verification' demand in behavioural political science?|That all political theories be tested against empirical data and observation|That political leaders be approved by a panel of moral philosophers|That historical texts be interpreted through literary critique|That policies align with traditional constitutional values|Option A|Verification insists that scientific statements and hypotheses must be testable and validated against empirical evidence rather than accepted on dogma.
4.1|Which key principle distinguishes post-behaviouralism from behaviouralism?|An exclusive focus on legislative voting records|A commitment to social relevance and addressing human crises|A rejection of all quantitative research methods|A return to classical Greek political philosophy|Option B|Post-behaviouralism insists that political science must remain socially relevant and actively address real-world human problems rather than hiding behind pure neutrality.
4.1|What is implied by 'Systematization' within the intellectual framework of the behavioural approach?|Linking data collection and theory into a coherent, interrelated body of knowledge|Organizing political parties into hierarchical structures|Structuring government bureaucracies by geographic region|Filing historical documents chronologically in public archives|Option A|Systematization involves organizing research findings and data into coherent, interconnected theoretical frameworks rather than keeping them as isolated facts.
4.1|The methodological emphasis on 'Techniques' in the behavioural credo refers to what aspect of research?|The adoption of sophisticated data-gathering tools such as surveys, polls, and statistical analysis|The rhetorical strategies used in political campaign speeches|The legal procedures for drafting constitutional amendments|The philosophical methods of deductive logic and rhetoric|Option A|Techniques refer to the specialized scientific tools—like surveys, sampling, and statistical analysis—used to gather and analyze empirical political data reliably.

14.1|How does a hierarchical chain of command function in the Weberian bureaucratic model|It establishes a clearly defined system of subordination where lower offices are supervised by higher ones|It allows frontline workers to completely override executive orders during crises|It creates a decentralized network where every bureaucrat acts as an independent authority|It organizes administrative staff into a flat structure with equal decision-making powers|Option B|A hierarchical chain of command establishes a strict scalar system where higher authorities supervise and control lower-ranking offices.
14.1|What is the primary significance of maintaining written files and records in a Max Weber bureaucracy|The administrative management relies on documented archives that preserve institutional memory and precedent|Written records are kept exclusively to punish employees who make clerical errors|Documentation serves only as public entertainment material for local newspapers|Files are discarded annually to prevent the state from archiving historical policy changes|Option A|Written documents and files form the foundation of administrative management, ensuring continuity and consistency through recorded precedents.
14.1|What does Max Weber mean by the principle of impersonality in bureaucratic administration|Officials execute their duties without personal emotional attachments, bias, or favoritism toward clients|Bureaucrats must hide their physical faces behind masks while interacting with the public|Employees are treated as nameless robots with no legal rights or protections|Decision-making is entirely random and detached from any rational legal framework|Option A|Impersonality requires officials to conduct public business sine ira et studio without personal emotion or favoritism.
14.1|Which practice aligns with the merit-based career tenure principle in a Weberian bureaucracy|Staff are selected based on specialized qualifications, examinations, and protected through secure career progression|Employees are hired entirely based on familial loyalty and hereditary succession rights|Workers are fired or promoted every week based on popular public voting campaigns|Positions are distributed as political rewards to campaign donors after an election cycle|Option A|Merit-based career tenure ensures that recruitment depends on specialized professional qualifications and provides job security.
14.1|Why are fixed salaries a critical structural component of Max Webers ideal bureaucratic model|They secure the financial independence of officials and reduce vulnerability to external corruption or bribery|They allow bureaucrats to set their own pay scales without legislative oversight or approval|They ensure that administrative workers earn less than elected politicians at all times|Variable bonuses based on daily customer satisfaction drive aggressive bureaucratic competition|Option A|Fixed salaries ensure officials remain economically secure and professionally independent from external bribes or private interests.
14.1|In the context of Max Webers bureaucracy what does a career orientation imply for the administrative worker|Employment is treated as a lifelong professional calling with systematic promotion tracks and retirement structures|Bureaucrats are expected to switch completely different career industries every three years|Workers view their desk jobs as temporary side projects while pursuing artistic hobbies|Employment terminates automatically after the completion of a single political administration|Option A|Career orientation treats public administration as a primary vocation with structured advancement and long-term security.
14.1|Which of the following represents a direct violation of the Weberian ideal bureaucratic model|A department head assigning a critical regulatory contract to their unqualified personal cousin|An administrative clerk filing official paperwork according to established standard operating procedures|A civil servant passing a rigorous professional qualification examination to earn a promotion|An office supervisor enforcing rules uniformly across all citizens regardless of social status|Option A|Nepotism and favoritism violate the core Weberian principles of meritocracy, impersonality, and objective qualification.
14.1|How do fixed jurisdictional areas contribute to bureaucratic efficiency according to Max Weber|They prevent overlapping jurisdictions, jurisdictional disputes, and confusion over who holds authority|They encourage all employees to constantly interfere in tasks outside their designated departments|They slow down decision-making intentionally through excessive bureaucratic red tape|They allow temporary workers to bypass legal frameworks during unexpected emergencies|Option A|Clear jurisdictional boundaries prevent institutional friction and confusion by assigning distinct, regulated responsibilities to specific offices.
14.1|What is the ultimate organizational goal of combining all components of Max Webers ideal bureaucratic model|To achieve the highest degree of calculability, predictability, technical efficiency, and rational control|To maximize emotional empathy and spontaneous creativity among frontline service workers|To dismantle all forms of state authority in favor of completely decentralized community self-rule|To ensure that political leaders can manipulate administrative rules arbitrarily at any moment|Option A|Weber designed the ideal bureaucratic model to maximize rational-legal authority, calculability, and technical efficiency in administration.

3.1|Which of the following best defines the primary analytical focus of the legalistic approach in political science?|Informal lobbying networks and grassroots social movements|Formal constitutional texts, laws, and official government structures|Socio-economic class struggles and wealth distribution disparities|Bureaucratic corruption and hidden informal power dynamics|Option B|The legalistic approach centers its study on formal institutional frameworks, written constitutions, laws, and the official roles of organs of government.

3.1|Which of the following primary government institutions is central to the legalistic and institutional framework of study?|Revolutionary vanguard cells and underground protest syndicates|Courts, legislatures, and executive administrative organs|Transnational corporations and global market cartels|Autonomous regional mafia networks and criminal syndicates|Option B|The legalistic and institutional framework explicitly prioritizes the study of formal state organs like courts, legislatures, and official government agencies.

3.1|What is a key merit of utilizing the legalistic and institutional approach in political analysis?|It accurately predicts the rise and fall of grassroots social uprisings|It exposes the hidden financial backers of political campaigns|It clearly clarifies formal constitutional rights and jurisdictional limits of the state|It maps out the psychological motivations of individual political leaders|Option C|A major advantage of the legalistic approach is its precision in defining constitutional rights, legal duties, and the clear jurisdictional boundaries of state institutions.
3.1|Which of the following phenomena would a purely legalistic political scientist most likely overlook or underemphasize?|The statutory text of a newly ratified constitutional amendment|The official voting procedures outlined in parliamentary bylaws|Informal backroom bargaining and pressure group influence behind a bill|The formal jurisdictional boundaries established for a supreme court|Option C|Informal backroom negotiations and pressure groups operate outside the formal constitutional framework, making them invisible to a strict legalistic analysis.

4.1|Which academic institution and intellectual movement are historically credited with pioneering the behavioural approach to political science in the 1950s?|The London School of Economics institutional framework|The Chicago school associated with Easton and Lasswell|The Frankfurt school of critical theory and philosophy|The Oxford school of traditional political history|Option B|The behavioural approach emerged strongly in the 1950s through the Chicago school, championed by political scientists like David Easton and Harold Lasswell.
4.1|What is the core methodological focus of the behavioural approach in political science?|Empirical and quantitative study of observable human political behavior|Philosophical analysis of historical political texts and normative ideals|Legalistic evaluation of constitutional documents and institutional charters|Ethical prescription of utopian governance models and moral duties|Option A|Behaviouralism shifts the discipline's focus toward empirical observation, data collection, and quantitative measurement of actual political behavior.
4.1|According to the credo of behaviouralism, what does the principle of regularities imply for political science?|Political phenomena exhibit discoverable uniformities that can be expressed as generalizable theories|Political actions are entirely random and defy any form of scientific categorization|Historical trends repeat themselves in exact cycles every century without variation|Human behavior in governance is strictly guided by legal statutes rather than habits|Option A|The principle of regularities posits that human political behavior displays recurring patterns and uniformities that allow for scientific theory-building.
4.1|How does the behavioural credo define the verification requirement within political research?|Statements and theoretical propositions must be testable and verifiable against empirical data|Research findings are valid purely based on the logical consistency of philosophical reasoning|Academic theories acquire truth value through consensus among political elites|Scientific hypotheses must align with traditional moral and cultural values|Option A|Verification requires that any empirical statement or hypothesis must be capable of being tested and validated against real-world evidence.
4.1|In the context of the behavioural creed, what is the role of quantification in data collection and analysis?|Recording data precisely to allow for rigorous statistical analysis and measurement|Rejecting numerical data in favor of descriptive narrative case studies|Relying exclusively on qualitative interviews without mathematical processing|Using numbers purely for decorative illustration in academic reports|Option A|Quantification involves translating political data into precise numerical terms to facilitate rigorous measurement and statistical hypothesis testing.
4.1|What does value-free inquiry demand from a behavioural political scientist during research?|Separating empirical observation and scientific analysis from personal or moral value judgments|Abandoning all ethical commitments in personal life to pursue a state career|Focusing exclusively on promoting democratic values and social justice globally|Prioritizing the researcher's political ideologies over objective data collection|Option A|Value-free inquiry dictates that researchers must keep their personal, ethical, and political values separate from their empirical investigations.
4.1|What is meant by systematization within the intellectual framework of behaviouralism?|Interrelating data collection, empirical theory-building, and research design into a coherent whole|Organizing physical books in a library according to political sub-disciplines|Filing administrative paperwork for government bureaucratic agencies|Standardizing legislative voting procedures across different nation-states|Option A|Systematization emphasizes that research must be methodical, ensuring that data collection and theory development are closely linked and mutually reinforcing.
4.1|What was the primary critique raised by post-behaviouralism against traditional behaviouralism?|Behaviouralism became overly obsessed with abstract techniques while ignoring urgent real-world social crises|Behaviouralism failed to use enough complex mathematics and statistical software|Behaviouralism was too focused on solving poverty, war, and inequality immediately|Behaviouralism relied excessively on historical texts and normative philosophy rather than data|Option A|Post-behaviouralism emerged because critics felt behaviouralism was overly detached from pressing human crises, arguing that political science must remain socially relevant.
4.1|Which major historical concerns prompted the emergence of the post-behavioural movement?|Poverty, war, inequality, and other pressing human crises threatening society|The desire to return exclusively to legalistic studies of ancient constitutions|A movement to eliminate all empirical and quantitative research from universities|The complete collapse of democratic governance across Western Europe|Option A|Post-behaviouralism insisted that political science must actively address real-world human crises such as poverty, war, and social inequality.

14.1|How does the hierarchical chain of command affect lower-level offices in a Weberian bureaucracy?|It grants lower offices absolute autonomy to overturn directives from upper offices|It subjects lower offices to the supervision, control, and appeal procedures of higher offices|It separates lower offices completely from any interaction with upper management|It transforms lower offices into independent policy-making legislative bodies|Option B|The hierarchical structure ensures strict administrative control by making lower offices accountable to higher authorities through a structured chain of command.
14.1|Which statement best describes the nature of administrative management in a Weberian bureaucracy?|It is based on oral traditions and unwritten cultural customs passed down through generations|It is entirely modern and professional, relying on expert training and thorough knowledge of rules|It is driven by spontaneous revolutionary impulses and charismatic appeals|It is managed through informal social clubs and neighborhood associations|Option B|Management in a Weberian bureaucracy is specialized, professionalized, and grounded in comprehensive knowledge of written rules and administrative procedures.
14.1|What is the ultimate consequence of adopting impersonality and merit-based tenure in a bureaucracy according to Weber?|The creation of an efficient, predictable, and calculable administrative apparatus free from arbitrary power|The complete elimination of all organizational rules in favor of total employee freedom|The transformation of the state into a purely corporate business enterprise driven by profit margins|The decentralization of government into isolated local communes without central coordination|Option A|Impersonality and meritocracy eliminate personal arbitrariness and favoritism, producing a highly rational, predictable, and efficient administrative machine.

4.1|Which academic institution and intellectual tradition are primarily credited with the rise of the behavioural approach in political science during the 1950s|The Oxford School of philosophical idealism|The Chicago School associated with figures like David Easton and Harold Lasswell|The Frankfurt School of critical theory and cultural critique|The classical Athenian tradition of political philosophy|Option B|The behavioural revolution in political science originated primarily from the Chicago School in the 1950s, championed by scholars like David Easton and Harold Lasswell.
4.1|What is the core epistemological objective of the behavioural approach to the study of politics|To establish absolute moral guidelines for governance based on natural law|To evaluate political institutions through historical and philosophical texts|To pursue empirical, quantitative, and scientific study of actual human political behaviour|To construct utopian models of society free from conflict and power struggles|Option C|Behaviouralism shifts the focus from formal institutional and philosophical analysis to the empirical and quantitative study of observable human political actions.
4.1|Which of the following principles forms a central tenet of the credo of behaviouralism as outlined by David Easton|Purely normative evaluation of political systems without empirical backing|Value-free inquiry and the systematic search for testable regularities|Rejection of all quantitative data in favour of qualitative historical interpretation|Exclusively studying legal codes and constitutional documents|Option B|The behavioural credo emphasizes empirical regularities, verification, advanced techniques, quantification, value-free inquiry, and theoretical systematization.
4.1|How does the behavioural approach differ from traditional political science methods in terms of data collection and analysis|It relies exclusively on subjective intuition and personal philosophical reflection|It emphasizes quantification, measurement, and the use of sophisticated analytical techniques|It completely avoids statistical models in favour of literary criticism|It limits its scope to ancient historical texts and legal charters|Option B|Behaviouralism distinguishes itself by heavily utilizing quantification, rigorous measurement tools, and statistical techniques to analyze political phenomena.
4.1|What role does value-free inquiry play within the methodological framework of classical behaviouralism|Values should guide the subjective interpretation of historical political narratives|Values are treated as primary variables that researchers must actively advocate for|Inquiry should be separated from moral or subjective value judgments to maintain objective scientific standards|Values are the ultimate source of all political truth and empirical validation|Option C|Value-free inquiry requires researchers to separate their personal moral judgments from empirical observations to ensure objective and scientific validity.
4.1|Why did the post-behavioural movement emerge as a critique of traditional behaviouralism in political science|Because behaviouralism focused too heavily on solving urgent contemporary societal crises like poverty and war|Because behaviouralism became overly obsessed with methodology and quantification at the expense of social relevance|Because behaviouralism completely rejected the use of empirical data and statistics|Because behaviouralism demanded that all political scientists run for public office|Option B|Post-behaviouralism arose because critics felt behaviouralism had become too detached from real-world crises, hiding behind value-neutrality and excessive methodology.
4.1|Which of the following best describes the core mandate introduced by post-behaviouralism in political science|Political science must remain socially relevant and actively address pressing human crises such as war and inequality|Political science must abandon all quantitative tools and return exclusively to classical philosophy|Political science should avoid taking any stance on social issues to preserve scientific purity|Political science should focus solely on administrative efficiency and bureaucratic procedure|Option A|Post-behaviouralism insisted that political science must not ignore real-world human crises and must use its knowledge to remain socially relevant.
4.1|In the context of the behavioural credo, what is meant by the concept of regularities|The discovery of uniformities and patterns in political behaviour that can be generalized and theorized|The routine scheduling of administrative elections within a democratic framework|The legal constraints placed on political actors by constitutional law|The moral obligations of citizens to obey state laws consistently|Option A|Regularities refer to discoverable uniformities in political behaviour that enable political scientists to formulate generalizations and theories.
4.1|Which prominent political scientist is most closely associated with defining the foundational tenets and credo of behaviouralism|Max Weber|David Easton|Karl Marx|Thomas Hobbes|Option B|David Easton is widely recognized for systematically outlining the intellectual credo and foundational principles of the behavioural approach in political science.
4.1|What primary critique do post-behaviouralists level against the value-free stance of strict behaviouralism|It makes political science completely immune to political corruption and bias|It leads to a dangerous moral conservatism that ignores pressing human suffering and injustice under the guise of neutrality|It ensures that research findings are universally applicable across all historical epochs|It forces political scientists to become active revolutionaries in developing nations|Option B|Post-behaviouralists argued that strict value-free inquiry often served as a conservative defense of the status quo, ignoring moral responsibilities toward human crises.

5.1|Which institutional element acts as the organized agency through which the collective will of the state is formulated, expressed, and executed?|Population|Government|Territory|Constitution|Option B|The government is the institutional machinery or operational agency through which the state makes, applies, and enforces laws across society.
5.1|How does external sovereignty manifest in the behavior of a modern nation-state within the international system?|Through the supreme authority of domestic courts over local criminal infractions|Through the absolute monopoly on the legitimate use of physical force internally|Through the formal recognition of independence and legal equality among other sovereign states|Through the direct provision of public healthcare and social security to citizens|Option C|External sovereignty implies that a state is independent of foreign control and interacts with other sovereign entities on equal legal footing in the international arena.

14.1|Which combination of features explicitly belongs to Max Weber conceptualization of bureaucracy?|Charismatic leadership, divine right, and emotional decision-making|Fixed jurisdictions, hierarchical authority, and written records|Decentralized volunteering, informal norms, and flexible task rotation|Elected rotating committees, open legislative debate, and populist mandates|Option B|Weber ideal type explicitly highlights fixed jurisdictional areas, a strict hierarchy, and comprehensive written files as core pillars.

14.1|Why is merit-based career tenure an essential component of bureaucratic predictability?|It ensures that promotions and employment security are based on professional competence rather than political patronage|It allows lifelong bureaucrats to rewrite national constitutions at will|It guarantees that leadership positions change every election cycle to match public trends|It prevents any form of specialization within government agencies|Option B|Merit-based career tenure secures professional stability and expertise by basing advancement on objective qualifications rather than political favoritism.

3.1|Which of the following best describes the core focus of the Legalistic or Institutional approach in political science?|Informal power dynamics and grassroots social movements|Formal legal rules, constitutional texts, and official government structures|Socio-economic class struggles and wealth distribution|Psychological motivations and voting behavior of individual citizens|Option B|The legalistic or institutional approach centers primarily on the formal structures of government, written constitutions, and codified laws rather than informal behaviors.

3.1|In the context of political science approaches, what distinguishes the institutional perspective from behavioral or socio-economic approaches?|It prioritizes formal institutional design and law over individual behavior or social forces|It exclusively studies the psychological traits of political leaders|It focuses entirely on Marxist interpretations of historical materialism|It relies solely on anthropological studies of ancient tribal societies|Option A|The hallmark of the institutional approach is its focus on formal institutions and legal rules, contrasting with approaches focused on human behavior or socioeconomic pressures.
3.1|What does it mean to say the legalistic approach is often described as static?|It changes its theoretical definitions every single day based on public opinion|It analyzes government structures as fixed arrangements without accounting for continuous evolution|It requires researchers to conduct physical motion experiments on politicians|It measures political phenomena solely through high-speed kinetic data|Option B|A static approach views institutions as fixed snapshots of rules and structures rather than dynamic, evolving entities shaped by ongoing social pressures.
3.1|If a researcher wants to evaluate the official checks and balances between the executive and legislative branches, which approach is most appropriate?|The behavioral approach|The Marxist class-conflict approach|The legalistic or institutional approach|The psychoanalytical approach|Option C|The legalistic or institutional approach is specifically designed to examine formal constitutional mechanisms like checks, balances, and separation of powers.
3.1|Which criticism directly targets the descriptive nature of early institutionalism in political science?|It lacks empirical grounding because it refuses to read government documents|It describes how institutions are supposed to work on paper rather than explaining why or how they actually function in practice|It relies on overly complex mathematical equations to model human psychology|It focuses too much on revolutionary overthrow rather than legal stability|Option B|Early institutionalism was often criticized as merely descriptive because it cataloged formal rules and legal structures without deeply explaining behavioral realities or systemic flaws.
