6.1|Which political theorist defined sovereignty as supreme power over citizens and subjects unrestrained by law?|Thomas Hobbes|Jean Bodin|John Austin|Aristotle|Option B|Jean Bodin conceptualized sovereignty as absolute and perpetual power that is not bound by the positive laws of the state.
6.1|In Thomas Hobbes' political philosophy, the absolute sovereign holding supreme coercive authority is metaphorically referred to as what?|The Social Contract|The Leviathan|The General Will|The Constitutional Monarch|Option B|Hobbes described the absolute sovereign state and ruler as the Leviathan, a powerful monster created to maintain social order and security.
6.1|John Austin's analytical approach defines sovereignty fundamentally through which concept?|The divine right of kings|The moral consensus of society|The legal command of a determinate superior habitually obeyed|The unwritten customary laws of tradition|Option C|Austin viewed sovereignty in legal terms as a habitual obedience given to a specific, determinate human superior who receives no such habitual obedience from others.
6.1|Which characteristic of sovereignty implies that supreme power cannot be legally transferred, granted, or partitioned away to another entity?|Permanence|Indivisibility|Universality|Inalienability|Option D|Inalienability means that the sovereign power is inherent to the state and cannot be permanently alienated or handed over to someone else.
6.1|When a regime maintains absolute, supreme power throughout the entire territorial boundaries of a state without exception, it demonstrates which characteristic of sovereignty?|Universality|De facto control|Popular sovereignty|Legal pluralism|Option A|Universality signifies that sovereignty extends across the entire territory and applies to all individuals and associations within it.
6.1|What distinguishes De Jure sovereignty from De Facto sovereignty?|De jure is based on constitutional or legal right whereas de facto is based on actual physical coercive control|De jure applies only to federal systems whereas de facto applies to monarchies|De jure is temporary whereas de facto is permanent and everlasting|De jure requires popular elections whereas de facto requires hereditary succession|Option A|De jure sovereignty represents the legal and constitutional right to rule, whereas de facto sovereignty represents the practical exercise of power and physical control regardless of legality.
6.1|The British Parliament possesses the ultimate legal authority to make or unmake any law within the UK constitutional framework, illustrating which type of sovereignty?|Political sovereignty|De facto sovereignty|Legal sovereignty|Popular sovereignty|Option C|Legal sovereignty resides in the supreme lawmaking body of the state, which in the UK context is Parliament.
6.1|Who or what is traditionally considered the holder of Political or Popular sovereignty in a representative democracy?|The supreme court justices|The military leadership|The electorate or the people|The permanent civil bureaucracy|Option C|Popular or political sovereignty rests with the citizens or electorate who hold ultimate political influence and democratic control over the government.
6.1|Which characteristic of sovereignty asserts that supreme power is enduring and survives changes in government administrations or specific rulers?|Indivisibility|Permanence|Absoluteness|Legality|Option B|Permanence means sovereignty persists continuously over time, surviving shifts in individual leaders or cabinet regimes just as the state itself persists.
6.1|The idea that sovereignty cannot be fragmented or shared among competing co-equal branches without destroying supreme authority defines which core characteristic?|Indivisibility|Inalienability|Temporality|Particularity|Option A|Indivisibility dictates that supreme power must be unified and cannot be successfully split into rival co-equal supreme authorities within the same state.

7.1|Modern constitutional democracies where power is exercised through codified rules and offices operate primarily under which Weberian authority type?|Charismatic authority|Traditional authority|Legal-Rational authority|Normative authority|Option C|Legal-Rational authority derives its legitimacy from a system of explicit written rules, laws, and institutional offices.
7.1|When a government forces compliance by threatening heavy economic fines and trade embargoes, which concept is primarily being demonstrated?|Legitimate authority|Charismatic devotion|Power through economic sanctions|Traditional succession|Option C|Using economic sanctions and penalties to compel behavior is a core mechanism of power rather than consensual authority.
7.1|Which of the following is a key characteristic unique to Legal-Rational authority?|Belief in the sacred sanctity of immemorial traditions|Devotion to the magnetic heroism of a single individual|Legitimacy established through written constitutional rules and legal procedures|Compliance secured strictly through fear of arbitrary physical violence|Option C|Legal-Rational authority is institutionalized through impersonal, written laws and structural offices rather than personal traits or custom.
7.1|Why might a monarchical system that has lasted for centuries be classified under traditional authority?|Its laws are rewritten by parliament every session|Its right to rule is justified by long-standing customs and inheritance|It relies entirely on the charismatic speeches of the reigning monarch|It rejects all forms of historical continuity in favor of rational codes|Option B|Traditional authority draws its foundational legitimacy from historical continuity, customs, and inherited status.

7.1|Which Weberian authority type is most vulnerable to instability upon the death or departure of the leader?|Legal-Rational authority|Traditional authority|Charismatic authority|Bureaucratic authority|Option C|Charismatic authority is intensely personalized, making succession difficult and often leading to instability when the leader leaves.
3.1|Which of the following best describes the primary focus of the legalistic or institutional approach in political science?|Informal political behavior and grassroots social movements|Formal legal rules, constitutional frameworks, and official government structures|Socio-economic class struggles and wealth distribution disparities|Psychological motivations and voting habits of the electorate|Option B|The legalistic/institutional approach centers heavily on formal constitutional texts, statutes, and institutional structures like courts and legislatures.
3.1|What is a primary methodological limitation of relying solely on the institutional approach to study politics?|It focuses excessively on behavioral surveys and statistical modeling|It relies too much on radical economic determinism and class analysis|It is static and descriptive, often ignoring informal power dynamics and political realities|It completely overlooks the structure and function of judicial systems and legislatures|Option C|By focusing only on formal rules, the institutional approach tends to be static and fails to account for informal power structures or corruption.
3.1|Which key benefit is most directly associated with using the legalistic approach in political analysis?|It provides precise clarity regarding constitutional rights, duties, and jurisdictional limits|It accurately maps out underground economies and informal pressure group networks|It predicts exact voting behavior shifts based on economic inflation indices|It uncovers hidden psychological biases of individual political leaders|Option A|A major merit of the legalistic approach is its ability to clearly define official powers, legal jurisdictions, and formal constitutional rights.
3.1|When evaluating government branches such as legislatures and courts, how does the institutional approach primarily view them?|As fluid networks shaped entirely by external corporate lobbying and media manipulation|As arenas driven primarily by subconscious psychological impulses of individual actors|As static, rule-bound machinery defined strictly by legal and constitutional mandates|As instruments of inevitable revolutionary class warfare and overthrow|Option C|The institutional approach treats formal bodies like legislatures and courts as bound by strict legal structures rather than fluid behavioral networks.
3.1|Which of the following phenomena would a purely institutional political scientist likely overlook or fail to adequately analyze?|The formal amendment procedure outlined in a nation's constitution|The official jurisdictional boundaries separating the executive and the judiciary|The hidden influence of informal pressure groups and backroom political corruption|The statutory text defining the qualifications for holding public office|Option C|Informal pressure groups and hidden political dynamics fall outside the formal rules and texts prioritized by the strict institutional approach.
3.1|Why is the institutional approach frequently criticized for being descriptive rather than analytical?|It focuses on predicting future elections using complex mathematical algorithms|It concentrates on detailing what formal rules state rather than explaining messy behavioral realities|It relies entirely on experimental laboratory simulations of political behavior|It prioritizes abstract philosophical ethics over historical facts and legal codes|Option B|The approach is often labeled descriptive because it painstakingly outlines constitutional structures without deeply analyzing informal behavioral forces.
3.1|How does the legalistic-institutional approach treat socio-economic forces in political systems?|It places them at the absolute center of every legislative voting decision|It treats them as primary drivers of structural constitutional reform|It largely ignores them in favor of formal statutes and official institutional arrangements|It integrates them seamlessly using quantitative economic modeling|Option C|Socio-economic forces, class interests, and informal pressures are generally ignored or marginalized by strict adherents of the legalistic approach.
3.1|Which of the following institutions is a quintessential focus of study under the legalistic approach?|Grassroots protest coalitions and civil disobedience networks|Formal court systems and legislative law-making bodies|Underground revolutionary syndicates and guerrilla factions|Informal community self-help organizations and local charities|Option B|Official government organs like courts and legislatures constitute the core subject matter of institutional political science.
3.1|What distinguishes the institutional approach from more behavioral or sociological approaches to political science?|Its exclusive concentration on official government structures rather than informal human behavior|Its reliance on psychological profiling of individual political candidates|Its focus on mass media influence during electoral campaigns|Its use of anthropological field studies on tribal governance systems|Option A|Unlike behavioral or sociological methods that examine human actions and social pressures, the institutional approach focuses tightly on official government structures.
3.1|Which critique best summarizes the weakness of the institutional approach regarding political change?|It assumes politics never changes because constitutions are permanently immutable documents|It cannot account for how informal power shifts alter political realities beneath static constitutional facades|It relies too heavily on revolutionary upheavals to explain minor policy adjustments|It focuses too much on rapid, unpredictable shifts in public opinion polls|Option B|Because institutional frameworks change slowly, the approach struggles to explain dynamic, informal shifts in political power that occur beneath the surface.

4.1|Which academic institution and era are primarily credited with the development and popularization of the behavioural approach in political science?|The 1950s Chicago school associated with scholars like David Easton and Harold Lasswell|The 18th-century Scottish Enlightenment centered around Edinburgh universities|The 19th-century Oxford philosophical tradition focusing on normative theory|The 20th-century Frankfurt School emphasizing critical social theory|Option A|The behavioural approach emerged strongly in the 1950s through the Chicago school, championed by political scientists like David Easton and Harold Lasswell who emphasized empirical and scientific methods.
4.1|What is the core epistemological focus of the behavioural approach to politics as distinct from traditional institutionalism?|The empirical and quantitative study of observable human political behavior and action|The philosophical deduction of the ideal state through historical legal texts|The normative evaluation of justice based on classical Greek political philosophy|The Marxist interpretation of historical materialism and class struggle in society|Option A|Behaviouralism shifts the primary focus of study away from formal institutional structures toward the empirical, measurable actions and behaviors of individuals within political systems.
4.1|According to the foundational credos of behaviouralism, what does the principle of value-free inquiry demand of researchers?|Separating personal moral and political evaluations from the empirical observation and analysis of data|Ensuring that all political research directly prescribes policies to solve societal crises|Rejecting the use of statistical quantification in favor of subjective narrative interpretations|Prioritizing normative philosophical judgments above quantitative data collection|Option A|Value-free inquiry requires researchers to keep their personal values and moral biases distinct from their objective observation and scientific analysis of political phenomena.
4.1|Which of the following best describes the principle of regularities within the behavioural credo?|Political behavior exhibits discoverable uniformities that can be generalized and expressed in theoretical terms|Political events are completely random occurrences driven entirely by unpredictable human emotions|Institutions evolve purely through historical accidents without any underlying patterns or structures|Political systems never repeat patterns across different cultures or historical periods|Option A|The principle of regularities asserts that human political behavior displays uniform patterns that researchers can identify, explain, and use to build predictive theories.
4.1|What role does quantification play within the methodological framework of the behavioural approach?|It provides precise measurement and mathematical tools to analyze political data rigorously|It serves as a secondary narrative device used only when qualitative historical texts are missing|It acts as an ideological tool designed to promote specific partisan political outcomes|It replaces theoretical frameworks entirely with raw, unorganized mathematical figures|Option A|Quantification is central to behaviouralism because it allows researchers to measure variables precisely, test hypotheses systematically, and analyze political data using statistical methods.
4.1|How does the principle of verification operate within behavioural political science?|Empirical findings and theoretical claims must be tested and validated against observable evidence|Conclusions are accepted as valid purely based on the historical authority of the theorist|Hypotheses are verified through logical deduction independent of real-world data collection|Truth in politics is established through consensus among political elites without testing|Option A|Verification requires that any scientific claim or generalization must be checked, tested, and substantiated using observable, empirical data from the real world.
4.1|What is the main critique that post-behaviouralism raised against classical behaviouralism?|Behaviouralism became overly obsessed with abstract methodology at the expense of addressing urgent real-world human crises|Behaviouralism failed to use any quantitative data or statistical methods in its research output|Behaviouralism completely rejected the scientific method in favor of radical political activism|Behaviouralism focused too heavily on solving poverty, war, and inequality rather than theory|Option A|Post-behaviouralism emerged because critics felt behaviouralism had become too detached from society, prioritizing technique over addressing pressing human problems like war and poverty.
4.1|Which of the following core demands did post-behaviouralism introduce to the discipline of political science?|A renewed commitment to social relevance, action, and addressing contemporary societal problems|An absolute prohibition against using quantitative data or statistical modeling in research|A return to pre-scientific normative philosophy with no regard for empirical observation|A strict adherence to value-free inquiry that forbids political scientists from taking public stances|Option A|Post-behaviouralism insisted that political science must remain socially relevant and actively apply its knowledge to help solve human crises and societal challenges.
4.1|In the context of the behavioural movement, what does the principle of systematization emphasize?|Connecting isolated empirical findings into a coherent, interrelated body of theoretical knowledge|Organizing political documents into chronological historical archives for library storage|Classifying political actors strictly according to their formal legal titles within government|Isolating individual political events without attempting to link them to broader frameworks|Option A|Systematization emphasizes that research data and empirical findings must be integrated into orderly, interconnected theoretical frameworks rather than remaining isolated facts.

7.1|Why is legitimacy considered a crucial element that transforms mere power into authority?|It eliminates the need for any form of economic resources within a state|It replaces all formal constitutional structures with charismatic leadership|It converts coercive dominance into a recognized, accepted right to rule that commands voluntary obedience|It ensures that political leaders can rule indefinitely without public accountability|Option C|Legitimacy provides moral or social justification, turning raw power into accepted authority where obedience is granted willingly rather than extracted through fear.

4.1|Which academic institution and decade are fundamentally associated with the rise of the behavioural approach in political science?|The 1920s Oxford school led by historical institutionalists|The 1950s Chicago school championed by theorists like David Easton|The 1970s Frankfurt school focusing on critical theory|The 1990s Paris school emphasizing post-structuralism|Option B|The behavioural revolution emerged during the 1950s primarily out of the Chicago school, shifting focus toward empirical study.
4.1|Who are two of the most prominent pioneer theorists identified with the behavioural approach in political science?|Karl Marx and Max Weber|David Easton and Harold Lasswell|Jean-Jacques Rousseau and Thomas Hobbes|Niccolò Machiavelli and John Locke|Option B|David Easton and Harold Lasswell are central figures of the Chicago school who heavily shaped behaviouralism.
4.1|What is the core epistemological focus of the behavioural approach to the study of politics?|Normative evaluation of political ideals and justice|Empirical and quantitative analysis of observable human political behaviour|Historical tracing of constitutional legal frameworks|Philosophical speculation on the ideal state|Option B|Behaviouralism prioritizes the empirical, scientific, and quantitative study of actual human actions over normative philosophy.
4.1|According to the credo of behaviouralism, what does the principle of value-free inquiry demand of researchers?|That political science research must be completely detached from ethical judgments and moral preferences|That researchers should actively advocate for socialist policy reforms|That subjective human biases should dictate data collection|That moral values are the ultimate metric for policy success|Option A|Value-free inquiry asserts that scientific political study should avoid moralizing and focus strictly on objective empirical facts.
4.1|Which of the following elements represents a core tenet of the behavioural credo as outlined by David Easton?|Intuitive deduction|Systematization|Dogmatic adherence|Hermeneutic interpretation|Option B|Systematization is a pillar of the behavioural credo, linking data collection and theory building into an orderly framework.
4.1|What role does quantification play within the methodological framework of behaviouralism?|It is considered irrelevant to humanistic studies|It is used exclusively for historical narrative structuring|It provides precise measurement and verification of political phenomena|It serves as a rhetorical device for political campaigning|Option C|Quantification allows behaviouralists to measure political variables precisely and test hypotheses empirically.
4.1|What was the primary critique levelled by post-behaviouralism against traditional behaviouralism?|Behaviouralism relied too heavily on historical archives|Behaviouralism was overly obsessed with pure technique at the expense of addressing urgent real-world social crises|Behaviouralism failed to use enough mathematical equations|Behaviouralism was too focused on curing global poverty and war|Option B|Post-behaviouralism emerged because critics felt behaviouralism ignored real-world crises like war and poverty in pursuit of pure methodology.
4.1|How does post-behaviouralism define the primary social responsibility of political scientists?|To remain strictly neutral and uninvolved in public policy debates|To ensure political science remains socially relevant and actively addresses human crises|To prioritize theoretical abstraction over practical application|To eliminate empirical methods entirely from academic research|Option B|Post-behaviouralism insists that political science must stay socially relevant and apply its knowledge to solve pressing human problems.
4.1|Which pair of concepts best contrasts behaviouralism and post-behaviouralism?|Empirical detachment versus social relevance|Qualitative analysis versus quantitative rejection|Philosophical speculation versus historical legalism|Normative theory versus institutional description|Option A|Behaviouralism emphasized empirical detachment and value-free science, whereas post-behaviouralism demanded social relevance and engagement with crises.
4.1|Which issue areas would a post-behavioural political scientist be most likely to prioritize for urgent academic research?|Poverty, war, and social inequality|Pure abstract model building and statistical formulas|Internal administrative rules of academic departments|Genealogical roots of ancient Greek vocabulary|Option A|Post-behaviouralism specifically demands that political science tackle critical human issues such as poverty, war, and inequality.
8.1|What best defines political legitimacy in the context of political science?|The legal authority to levy taxes and spend public funds without legislative oversight|The psychological conviction among citizens that their rulers possess a moral right to govern|The absolute physical monopoly over the instruments of violence within a state territory|The constitutional capacity of a head of state to dissolve parliament at will|Option B|Legitimacy refers to the psychological acceptance and conviction by the public that the government's exercise of power is morally justified and right.
8.1|Which of the following is considered a primary source of political legitimacy?|Frequent reliance on emergency decrees and martial law|The systematic elimination of opposition parties through legal bans|Transparent elections performance and adherence to the rule of law|The total centralization of economic planning in state hands|Option C|Elections performance and rule of law build trust and provide the procedural and substantive foundations for a government's moral right to rule.
8.1|How does political influence fundamentally differ from coercive power?|Influence relies on persuasion and rational argument rather than the threat of force|Influence can only be exercised by elected officials holding formal government office|Influence requires absolute control over state financial resources to be effective|Influence is illegal in democratic regimes because it bypasses legislative channels|Option A|Political influence shapes decisions through non-coercive means such as persuasion prestige and rational argument rather than force.
8.1|Which mechanism is a classic example of exercising political influence without coercion?|Imposing economic sanctions on a defiant political opponent|Disbanding an unsanctioned public protest using police tactical units|Lobbying lawmakers through evidence-based policy briefs and rational persuasion|Arresting journalists who publish articles critical of current administrative policies|Option C|Lobbying through rational argument and evidence represents political influence because it shapes decisions without applying coercive force.
8.1|Why is legitimacy considered essential for the long-term stability of a political regime?|It ensures the military can easily defeat foreign invaders without external aid|It allows governments to secure compliance primarily through voluntary acceptance rather than costly force|It guarantees that the economy will experience continuous growth and low inflation|It prevents citizens from ever questioning government policies or demanding reforms|Option B|A regime grounded in legitimacy enjoys voluntary compliance which reduces the transaction and enforcement costs associated with pure coercion.
8.1|When a government consistently delivers high public services and economic stability it strengthens which source of legitimacy?|Traditional legitimacy rooted in long-standing hereditary customs|Charismatic legitimacy derived from the extraordinary personal appeal of a leader|Performance legitimacy based on the demonstrable output and effectiveness of the state|Ideological legitimacy stemming from strict adherence to a single dogma|Option C|Performance legitimacy is earned through the effective delivery of governance goods economic growth and administrative competence.
8.1|Which of the following actions best illustrates the exercise of political prestige?|Using a respected public figure's endorsement to sway voter opinion on a referendum|Threatening to cut off legislative funding for districts that vote against a bill|Dispatching state security forces to monitor opposition campaign headquarters|Passing a mandatory decree that overrides local municipal ordinances|Option A|Prestige leverages social standing and respect to shape political opinions and decisions through persuasion rather than coercion.
8.1|In the study of political science how does political influence manifest within legislative bodies?|Through the direct physical intimidation of dissenting lawmakers by party whips|Through reasoned debate coalition building and persuasive negotiation among members|Through the unilateral suspension of legislative rules by executive decree|Through the mandatory expulsion of politicians who fail to align with party ideology|Option B|Within legislatures political influence operates via debate negotiation and persuasion to shape outcomes without relying on coercive threats.
8.1|Which scenario most accurately describes a crisis of legitimacy?|A government wins an election with a narrow margin of five percent of the total vote|Citizens widely perceive the governing regime as corrupt unjust and morally bankrupt|The legislature passes a highly controversial tax reform package late at night|An economic recession leads to a temporary decrease in quarterly tax revenues|Option C|A crisis of legitimacy occurs when the psychological conviction of moral rightness collapses leading citizens to view the regime as fundamentally unjust.
8.1|What role does the rule of law play in establishing and maintaining political legitimacy?|It grants absolute immunity to executive leaders from any form of legal accountability|It ensures that governance is predictable fair and constrained by established legal norms bolstering public trust|It replaces the need for democratic elections by automatically appointing judges to executive posts|It centralizes all legislative judicial and executive powers into a single supreme court|Option B|The rule of law ensures predictability fairness and constitutional limits which reinforces the public's moral conviction that the government is legitimate.
7.1|Which of the following best distinguishes power from authority according to political science concepts?|Power relies purely on voluntary consensus while authority requires physical punishment|Power is the capacity to compel compliance through force or sanctions whereas authority is recognized as a legitimate right to rule|Power is always legally codified in a written constitution while authority is informal and temporary|Power and authority are identical terms describing absolute governmental dominance|Option B|Power involves coercion or the threat of sanctions to compel behavior whereas authority inherently possesses legitimacy and voluntary acceptance of commands.
7.1|An absolute monarch whose right to rule is defended by ancient customs and ancestral lineage derives leadership from which of Weber's types of authority?|Charismatic authority|Legal-rational authority|Traditional authority|Bureaucratic authority|Option C|Traditional authority derives its legitimacy from established customs, long-standing traditions, and hereditary continuity.
7.1|A revolutionary leader who mobilizes millions through exceptional personal magnetism, inspirational rhetoric, and perceived extraordinary qualities exemplifies which form of authority?|Traditional authority|Charismatic authority|Legal-rational authority|Normative authority|Option B|Charismatic authority is founded upon devotion to the exceptional sanctity, heroism, or exemplary character of an individual leader.
7.1|In a modern democratic state, a civil servant issues a directive based strictly on written statutory codes and established office procedures. What type of authority is operating here?|Traditional authority|Charismatic authority|Legal-rational authority|Coercive authority|Option C|Legal-rational authority derives its legitimacy from a system of explicit written rules, laws, and rational procedures tied to institutional offices.
7.1|When a government uses economic sanctions and police enforcement to compel compliance from a rebellious populace without holding any moral legitimacy in their eyes, which concept is primarily at play?|Authority|Legitimacy|Power|Charisma|Option C|Power refers to the ability to compel action or obedience through force, coercion, or sanctions, even in the absence of legitimacy.
7.1|Max Weber's sociological framework categorizes legitimate domination into how many distinct ideal types of authority?|Two types|Three types|Four types|Five types|Option B|Weber famously categorizes legitimate authority into three ideal types: traditional, charismatic, and legal-rational.
7.1|Which of the following scenarios best illustrates the exercise of authority rather than raw power?|A citizen paying taxes because they believe the government has a lawful and moral right to collect them|A shopkeeper handing over cash to an armed robber threatening violence|A corporation threatening to fire employees if they unionize|A foreign military occupying a territory through sheer numbers and weaponry|Option A|Authority requires voluntary recognition of a legitimate right to command obedience, as seen when citizens comply with laws they recognize as lawful.
7.1|What is the foundational basis for obedience under Max Weber's traditional authority?|Belief in the legality of enacted rules|Unquestioning devotion to an individual hero|Habit, custom, and the sanctity of age-old traditions|Economic incentives and material rewards|Option C|Traditional authority relies on the acceptance of status quo customs and historical continuity as the primary justification for rule.
7.1|How does legal-rational authority fundamentally differ from charismatic authority?|Legal-rational is rooted in impersonal legal codes and offices whereas charismatic is rooted in the personal attributes of an individual|Legal-rational is based on hereditary succession while charismatic is based on written constitutions|Legal-rational relies on divine right while charismatic relies on ancient traditions|Legal-rational is inherently unstable while charismatic is permanently institutionalized|Option A|Legal-rational authority binds rulers and ruled to rational, impersonal laws and procedures rather than personal devotion to a leader.
7.1|If a political regime loses its moral standing and widespread acceptance among the public, yet manages to maintain total control solely through fear, coercion, and military surveillance, what has happened to its status?|It retains legal-rational authority but loses power|It retains traditional authority but gains charisma|It retains power while its authority has severely eroded or collapsed|It automatically transitions into charismatic leadership|Option C|Power can persist through pure coercion even when authority and legitimacy have completely vanished from the regime.
9.1|Which of the following best defines an ideology within the context of political science?|A random collection of short-term policy preferences held by individual voters|A coherent set of normative beliefs that explains political reality and offers a blueprint for organization|A strict economic doctrine focused exclusively on maximizing corporate profits in a globalized market|A temporary legal framework used by authoritarian regimes to suppress opposition parties|Option B|An ideology provides a systematic framework of normative beliefs that both interprets political reality and outlines a blueprint for societal and political organization.
9.1|Which political ideology places the highest normative value on individual liberty, free markets, and a limited state?|Socialism|Fascism|Liberalism|Conservatism|Option C|Liberalism prioritizes individual liberties, private property, free-market economics, and a constitutionally limited state apparatus.
9.1|What is the core foundational principle of socialism and communism regarding economic structures?|Absolute state ownership of all media outlets combined with military rule|Collective ownership and the pursuit of socio-economic equality|Strict adherence to traditional feudal hierarchies and hereditary governance|The complete elimination of all industrial production in favor of agrarianism|Option B|Socialism and communism are built upon the collective or public ownership of the means of production to achieve social and economic equality.
9.1|Which prominent political theorist is most closely associated with the conservative defense of traditional social order and gradual, organic change?|Karl Marx|Thomas Hobbes|Edmund Burke|Max Weber|Option C|Edmund Burke is widely recognized as the intellectual founder of modern conservatism, emphasizing organic social order, tradition, and cautious, gradual reform.
9.1|How does fascism fundamentally differ from liberalism regarding the role and scope of government authority?|Fascism advocates for the total subordination of the individual to a totalitarian state supremacy, whereas liberalism limits state power.|Fascism promotes radical egalitarianism through collective ownership, whereas liberalism supports hereditary monarchy.|Fascism seeks the immediate abolition of all state structures, whereas liberalism expands bureaucratic control.|Fascism encourages decentralized local governance and pacifism, whereas liberalism mandates militarism.|Option A|Fascism champions absolute state supremacy and totalitarian control, directly opposing the limited-government and individual-rights tenets of liberalism.
9.1|Which ideological tradition is characterized by the absolute rejection of state authority and hierarchical government structures?|Conservatism|Anarchism|Socialism|Liberalism|Option B|Anarchism is defined by its foundational critique and rejection of all forms of state authority, hierarchy, and compulsory government.
9.1|In the study of political ideologies, what primary function does a normative belief system serve?|It dictates the exact daily weather patterns of a nation|It explains existing political reality while prescribing a preferred future blueprint|It provides a mathematical formula for calculating gross domestic product growth|It replaces the need for any formal constitution or written legal code|Option B|Normative belief systems evaluate how society ought to function, thereby interpreting current reality and mapping out a blueprint for political goals.
9.1|Which of the following ideologies is most directly aligned with the concept of totalitarian supremacy and extreme nationalism?|Socialism|Liberalism|Fascism|Anarchism|Option C|Fascism and Nazism are characterized by extreme nationalism, authoritarianism, and the total dominance of the state over all aspects of public and private life.
9.1|When comparing conservatism and liberalism, what is a primary point of divergence regarding societal change?|Conservatives favor rapid, revolutionary overthrow of all institutions, while liberals want complete stasis.|Conservatives advocate for cautious preservation of tradition and gradual change, while liberals emphasize individual rights and reform.|Conservatives reject all forms of private property, while liberals mandate state-controlled monopolies.|Conservatives promote strict anarchic principles, while liberals enforce totalitarian military rule.|Option B|Conservatism values traditional structures and slow, organic adaptation, whereas liberalism focuses on individual liberty and progressive reform.
9.1|Which political philosophy views the state not as a protector of liberty or a tool for equality, but as an illegitimate and coercive institution that should be dismantled?|Anarchism|Fascism|Conservatism|Socialism|Option A|Anarchism uniquely regards the state as inherently coercive, illegitimate, and unnecessary, advocating for its total dismantling in favor of voluntary cooperation.
10.1|Which of the following best distinguishes a written constitution from an unwritten constitution?|A written constitution is entirely immutable while an unwritten constitution can be amended by simple majority|A written constitution is codified in a single authoritative document whereas an unwritten constitution comprises multiple statutes traditions and judicial precedents|An unwritten constitution lacks any legal force or judicial enforcement mechanism|A written constitution can only exist within a federal system of government|Option B|A written constitution is formally codified into a single foundational document, whereas an unwritten constitution like that of the United Kingdom is a collection of diverse statutes, conventions, and legal precedents.
10.1|What primary structural characteristic defines a rigid constitution compared to a flexible one?|It requires a special, complex, and more difficult amendment procedure than ordinary legislation|It completely prohibits any form of constitutional modification or legislative reform|It can only be suspended or abrogated through a military coup d etat|It requires direct popular referendums for every single administrative decision|Option A|A rigid constitution demands a special, more cumbersome amendment process compared to ordinary laws to protect fundamental governance rules, whereas a flexible constitution is easily altered through standard legislative procedures.
10.1|How does a unitary system of government fundamentally differ from a federal system?|A unitary system concentrates ultimate sovereign power at the national level with sub-national units exercising only delegated powers|A unitary system operates strictly without a written constitution or formal judicial review|A federal system forbids local governments from levying any form of internal taxation|A federal system eliminates the executive branch and vests all authority in a bicameral legislature|Option A|In a unitary state, ultimate legal authority rests with the central government, which may delegate powers to local regions, whereas federalism constitutionally divides power between central and regional governments.
10.1|What is the core philosophical and practical objective of constitutionalism?|To maximize state control over civil society and suppress political opposition|To ensure governance is conducted strictly in accordance with fundamental laws that limit state power to protect civil liberties|To eliminate the judicial and legislative branches in favor of a centralized technocratic council|To guarantee that economic resources are distributed solely through executive decrees|Option B|Constitutionalism is fundamentally about limited government, meaning political power is restrained by fundamental laws to safeguard the rights and freedoms of citizens against arbitrary rule.
10.1|Which key body was established to draft the initial constitutional blueprint that led to Nigeria's 1979 transition to civilian rule?|The Drafting Committee known as the Forty-Nine Wise Men led by Rotimi Williams|The National Liberation Council of military administrators|The Judicial Commission of Inquiry into Federal Electoral Malpractices|The Supreme Council for Islamic Affairs and Customary Law|Option A|The 1979 Constitution drafting process was initiated by the Constitution Drafting Committee consisting of 49 experts under the chairmanship of Chief Rotimi Williams.
10.1|What historical constitutional shift did the Constituent Assembly facilitate in Nigeria leading up to the Second Republic in 1979?|The transition from a parliamentary system to an American-style executive presidential system|The complete abolition of federalism in favor of a unitary centralized state|The replacement of civilian administration with a permanent military directorate|The adoption of a one-party socialist state model modeled after Eastern Europe|Option A|The Constituent Assembly reviewed the draft produced by the 49 wise men and successfully transitioned Nigeria from a British-style parliamentary system to an executive presidential system.
10.1|Why is the United Kingdom frequently cited as the primary example of a nation with an unwritten constitution?|Because its governing laws and conventions are unwritten oral agreements passed down through generations|Because it lacks a single codified constitutional document and relies instead on an accumulation of acts of parliament, common law, and conventions|Because its parliament possesses no authority to pass laws concerning civil liberties or human rights|Because the monarch holds absolute veto power over all judicial and legislative decisions|Option B|The UK has an unwritten constitution because its fundamental principles are not codified into one supreme document but are scattered across acts of parliament, judicial rulings, and unwritten political conventions.
10.1|What is a defining procedural consequence of a rigid constitution?|Ordinary laws can override constitutional provisions if passed by a two-thirds majority|Constitutional amendments demand extraordinary majorities or special ratification processes to prevent hasty alterations|Legislators are legally barred from introducing any constitutional bills during an election year|The judiciary is stripped of its power to interpret constitutional articles|Option B|Rigid constitutions safeguard fundamental laws by requiring special legislative majorities, referendums, or multi-stage ratification processes to make any amendments.
10.1|Which of the following best describes the structural division of power in a federal constitution?|Power is shared constitutionally between a central government and coordinate regional or state governments|Power is held exclusively by regional governments with the central government acting only in an advisory advisory capacity|Power is centralized in the executive branch with regional units serving merely as administrative departments|Power is shared between the military high command and an elected civilian assembly|Option A|A federal constitution establishes a constitutional division of powers where both the central government and regional units derive their authority directly from the constitution and operate coordinately.
10.1|Which phrase best encapsulates the relationship between a constitution and constitutionalism?|A constitution is the legal instrument, while constitutionalism is the political philosophy and practice of limiting state power through that instrument|A constitution and constitutionalism are identical terms with no distinct legal or theoretical differences|Constitutionalism refers exclusively to written documents, whereas a constitution refers to unwritten customs|A constitution applies only to authoritarian regimes, whereas constitutionalism applies only to absolute monarchies|Option A|While a constitution is the foundational document establishing governmental structures, constitutionalism is the active political and legal culture that ensures those powers are genuinely limited to protect human rights.

14.1|How does a hierarchical chain of command function within a Weberian bureaucratic model|Lower offices are supervised and controlled by higher-ranking authorities|Every employee reports directly to the chief executive officer simultaneously|Decisions are made collectively by majority vote across all organizational levels|Field workers operate entirely independently without central oversight|Option B|A hierarchical structure establishes a clear vertical chain of command where higher offices supervise lower ones.
14.1|What is the primary significance of maintaining written files and records in a bureaucratic organization|Administrative acts and decisions are preserved for continuity and accountability|Documents are kept solely to satisfy temporary legal formalities without utility|Records are published publicly to encourage direct democratic participation|Written files replace the need for any formal rules or standard operating procedures|Option A|Written documents and files provide a permanent archive of administrative decisions ensuring organizational memory and accountability.
14.1|Why does Max Weber emphasize impersonality as a core characteristic of an ideal bureaucracy|It ensures officials execute duties objectively without emotional favoritism or bias|It forces employees to abandon all personal identity while outside the workplace|It prevents workers from communicating with one another during working hours|It eliminates the need for any managerial supervision or performance evaluation|Option A|Impersonality ensures that bureaucratic rules are applied uniformly and objectively without personal bias or affection.
14.1|What role does merit-based career tenure play in the Weberian bureaucratic framework|It protects officials from arbitrary dismissal and bases advancement on competence|It guarantees lifetime employment regardless of job performance or misconduct|It ensures that political loyalty is the sole criterion for bureaucratic promotion|It restricts hiring to members of a specific socioeconomic class|Option B|Merit-based career tenure shields civil servants from arbitrary political interference and rewards professional competence.
14.1|How do fixed salaries contribute to the stability of Max Webers ideal bureaucratic model|They provide financial security and reduce the temptation of official corruption|They fluctuate daily based on the overall profitability of the government sector|They depend entirely on the personal discretion of the department head|They are calculated strictly according to the personal wealth of the employee|Option A|Fixed salaries ensure economic independence for officials, reducing vulnerability to bribery and corruption.
14.1|Which feature distinguishes a Weberian bureaucracy from traditional or charismatic forms of authority|Systematic legal rules and rational-organizational structures|Personal loyalty to an individual leader with supernatural qualities|Customary practices handed down through generations without formal codification|Spontaneous decision-making based on immediate emotional appeals|Option A|Weberian bureaucracy is rooted in legal-rational authority defined by systematic rules and structured offices rather than tradition or charisma.
14.1|In the context of Max Webers bureaucratic model what does official-jurisdictional competency entail|The strict limitation of official authority to specific legally defined domains|The freedom of any bureaucrat to override decisions made by executive leaders|The requirement that administrators hold advanced degrees in political philosophy|The authority to manage private business interests alongside public duties|Option A|Jurisdictional competency limits official actions and authority to clearly defined legal boundaries and specialized functions.
14.1|What is a direct consequence of separating bureaucratic administrative staff from the ownership of the means of administration|Officials act as professional administrators rather than private owners of their office tools|Administrators personally own the buildings and computers they use daily|The organization is transformed into a private profit-driven commercial enterprise|Employees are required to purchase their own equipment out of pocket|Option A|Separation from the means of administration ensures that officials operate as professional servants of the organization rather than owners of their positions.
14.1|Which combination of traits fully reflects Max Webers ideal-type bureaucracy according to the study notes|Hierarchy, fixed jurisdictions, written records, impersonality, and merit tenure|Informal networks, charismatic leadership, variable salaries, and emotional appeals|Democratic voting, flexible duties, oral agreements, and political patronage|Temporary structures, decentralized control, subjective judgments, and ad-hoc rules|Option A|The core defining traits of Weberian bureaucracy include fixed jurisdictions, hierarchy, written records, impersonality, and merit-based tenure.

8.1|An environmental advocacy group successfully convinces lawmakers to change a zoning law by presenting scientific research reports. What political concept does this action best demonstrate?|Coercive compliance|Political influence|Legitimacy deficit|Bureaucratic authoritarianism|Option B|Presenting rational arguments and research to shape political decisions without force is a classic manifestation of political influence.
8.1|When a government fails to deliver basic public goods and economic stability, what is most likely to happen to its political standing?|Its legitimacy is reinforced through increased public dependence|Its legitimacy psychological conviction tends to erode among the citizenry|Its political influence is entirely replaced by absolute legal authority|Its use of persuasion automatically increases to compensate|Option B|Legitimacy is heavily tied to performance; chronic governance failures undermine the psychological conviction that rulers have a moral right to govern.
8.1|Which mechanism relies strictly on prestige, rational argument, and lobbying rather than legal mandates or physical punishment?|Sovereign police power|Political influence|Judicial sentencing|Constitutional enforcement|Option B|Political influence encompasses activities like lobbying, persuasion, and leveraging prestige to shape political outcomes without legal coercion.
8.1|Why is the psychological conviction of the governed critical to the study of governance?|It determines the exact financial budget a state can allocate annually|It ensures compliance based on perceived moral right rather than constant physical threat|It prevents citizens from ever questioning judicial interpretations of the constitution|It eliminates the need for formal elections or bureaucratic administration|Option B|A high degree of legitimacy minimizes the need for brute force because citizens voluntarily comply out of a belief in the moral rightness of authority.
8.1|Which of the following best exemplifies the application of political influence in a pluralistic society?|Deploying the national guard to clear a public square|A coalition of business leaders negotiating policy changes through expert testimony|Enacting emergency decrees that suspend civil liberties|A monarch issuing an unchallengeable royal proclamation|Option C|Lobbying and providing expert testimony are standard non-coercive methods of exerting political influence to shape policy decisions.
8.1|If a regime maintains power solely through fear, surveillance, and threat of punishment, what is it predominantly lacking?|Administrative efficiency|Political influence|Legitimacy based on moral right and consent|Financial resources for public infrastructure|Option C|A regime relying purely on fear lacks true legitimacy, which requires the psychological conviction of moral authority and citizen consent.
8.1|How do the concepts of legitimacy and political influence interact within a stable political system?|Legitimacy provides the foundational moral authority that makes political influence more effective and sustainable|Political influence entirely replaces the need for institutionalized legitimacy|Legitimacy is only achieved after an actor successfully lobbies a legislative body|Political influence and legitimacy are mutually exclusive opposites in political theory|Option A|High legitimacy creates an environment of trust and acceptance, enhancing an actor's ability to exercise political influence successfully through persuasion.
9.1|Which of the following best defines an ideology in the context of political science?|A random collection of short-term policy preferences and emotional public reactions|A coherent set of normative beliefs that explains political reality and offers a blueprint for organization|A strict set of economic formulas used exclusively to maximize corporate market growth|A temporary coalition of political parties formed solely to win an upcoming election|Option B|An ideology provides a structured, normative framework that interprets reality and guides political structures and actions.
9.1|Which core principle distinguishes classical liberalism from other major political ideologies?|The absolute supremacy of the totalitarian state over all individual liberties|The complete elimination of private property in favor of collective ownership|A strong emphasis on individual liberty, free markets, and a limited state|The preservation of traditional societal hierarchies through rapid revolutionary upheaval|Option C|Liberalism prioritizes individual freedoms, free-market economics, and minimal government intervention in daily life.
9.1|Who is most famously associated with the conservative defense of traditional order and gradual, organic social change?|Karl Marx|Edmund Burke|Benito Mussolini|Jean-Jacques Rousseau|Option B|Edmund Burke is widely recognized as the foundational thinker of modern conservatism, emphasizing tradition and caution toward radical reform.

9.1|Which ideology is characterized by the complete rejection of state authority and hierarchical government?|Conservatism|Fascism|Liberalism|Anarchism|Option D|Anarchism fundamentally stands for the abolition of the state and all forms of coercive hierarchical authority.
9.1|In a liberal political framework, what is the expected role of the state regarding economic and social affairs?|To tightly control all pricing, manufacturing, and distribution of consumer goods|To act as a limited referee ensuring basic rules while allowing free markets and personal liberty to flourish|To abolish private enterprise and replace it with centralized bureaucratic planning boards|To enforce strict cultural homogeneity and traditional religious laws across the population|Option B|Liberalism favors a limited state whose primary purpose is to protect individual rights and maintain a stable framework for free markets.
9.1|Which concept is central to the socialist critique of capitalist economic systems?|The belief that free markets naturally eliminate all social inequalities without intervention|The view that private ownership creates structural inequality that must be resolved through collective ownership|The idea that societal traditions should dictate economic output regardless of technological efficiency|The principle that totalitarian governance is required to maintain industrial production rates|Option B|Socialists argue that private ownership of resources leads to exploitation and inequality, necessitating collective control.
9.1|What is the conservative stance toward rapid or revolutionary political change, as historically articulated by thinkers like Edmund Burke?|Rapid change is necessary to purge society of historical injustices and modernize institutions instantly|Change should be approached with extreme caution, favoring organic evolution and preservation of established traditions|Political systems must be completely dismantled and rebuilt every generation to stay relevant|Change is entirely unnecessary because traditional institutions are completely flawless|Option B|Conservatism values continuity and stability, viewing rapid or radical disruption of traditions as dangerous to social order.
9.1|How do fascism and liberalism fundamentally differ regarding the relationship between the individual and the collective?|Both ideologies view the individual as entirely subordinate to the economic goals of international corporations|Liberalism champions individual liberty and limited government, whereas fascism subordinates the individual to total state supremacy|Liberalism advocates for collective ownership of property, while fascism promotes pure laissez-faire capitalism|Both ideologies seek the total abolition of national borders and centralized government bureaucracies|Option B|Liberalism centers on individual autonomy and rights, whereas fascism demands total submission of the individual to the fascist state.
10.1|What is the core defining principle of constitutionalism in political science?|Governance based strictly on the unwritten traditions of a sovereign parliament|The absolute concentration of state power in an executive president without judicial oversight|Governance according to a fundamental law that limits state power to protect civil liberties|The total absence of any written legal framework to allow maximum legislative flexibility|Option C|Constitutionalism requires that government authority is derived from and limited by a fundamental law, ensuring that civil liberties are protected against arbitrary state action.
10.1|Which classification best describes a constitution that can be amended through the same simple legislative process as ordinary laws?|Rigid constitution|Flexible constitution|Federal constitution|Unwritten constitution|Option B|A flexible constitution does not require special, rigorous amendment procedures and can be altered through standard legislative processes just like ordinary laws.
10.1|What is a primary characteristic of an unwritten constitution as exemplified by the United Kingdom?|It is entirely contained within a single supreme codified document ratified by a constituent assembly|It consists of a collection of statute laws, judicial precedents, and constitutional conventions rather than a single document|It forbids the judiciary from ever interpreting any matters related to governance or civil rights|It makes all forms of governmental change permanently impossible without a nationwide referendum|Option C|The UK constitution is unwritten because it is uncodified, drawing its authority from a mix of historical statutes, court judgments, and unwritten conventions.
10.1|In a federal system of government as opposed to a unitary system, how is political power structurally distributed?|Power is concentrated exclusively in a single central national government that can dissolve regional bodies at will|Power is divided constitutionally between a central national government and coordinate regional or state governments|Power is shared equally among independent city-states without any overarching federal authority|Power is held entirely by traditional monarchs who delegate administrative duties to regional governors|Option B|Federalism features a constitutional division of powers between central and regional governments, where neither level can unilaterally abolish the other.
10.1|What distinguishes a rigid constitution from a flexible one?|A rigid constitution requires special, complex, and more difficult amendment procedures than ordinary legislation|A rigid constitution can never be amended under any circumstances once it has been ratified|A rigid constitution lacks any mechanism for judicial review or constitutional enforcement|A rigid constitution exists only within unitary states governed by a single parliamentary body|Option A|Rigid constitutions safeguard fundamental principles by mandating special, stringent legislative thresholds or referendums for any amendments.

10.1|Which of the following best defines a unitary system of government?|A system where all governmental power is concentrated in a central authority, with any regional units exercising only delegated powers|A system where regional states possess absolute sovereignty and can veto any national federal laws|A system where executive and legislative powers are strictly separated with a dual presidency model|A system where power is divided equally between two coordinate levels of government by a supreme legal document|Option A|In a unitary system, the central government holds ultimate supremacy, and any local or regional administrative units exist solely as agents of the center.
10.1|Why is a written constitution typically associated with a higher degree of constitutional rigidity?|Because written documents are physically printed on parchment that cannot be altered physically|Because a written constitution usually outlines a formal, demanding process for making amendments to its text|Because written constitutions are only adopted by totalitarian regimes that forbid any future legal changes|Because written constitutions rely exclusively on unwritten social conventions for their daily interpretation|Option B|Written constitutions generally require specialized, formal amendment procedures to ensure stability and protect the fundamental framework from fleeting political whims.
10.1|What was the major structural shift in Nigeria's governance introduced by the 1979 Constitution created under the transition process?|Moving from a federal structure to a strictly unitary administrative state without regional governments|Adopting an Executive Presidential system in place of the previous Westminster parliamentary model|Abolishing the judiciary and transferring all legal dispute resolution powers to the executive branch|Replacing the written constitution with an unwritten system modeled strictly after the United Kingdom|Option B|The 1979 Constitution marked a historic transition for Nigeria by replacing the British-style Westminster parliamentary system with an American-style Executive Presidency.

12.1|How does a coup d'État fundamentally differ from a revolution in terms of political dynamics?|Coups involve mass public uprisings while revolutions are restricted to the military|Coups are peaceful reforms whereas revolutions are illegal takeovers|Coups are illegal top-level seizures of power without systemic restructuring whereas revolutions overturn the entire social and political system|Coups aim at economic redistribution while revolutions focus exclusively on foreign policy|Option C|A coup d'État is an elite or military-led seizure of state power from the top without necessarily altering the underlying socio-economic structures, unlike a comprehensive revolution.|
12.1|Which of the following best describes evolutionary or reformist political change?|A rapid and violent restructuring of society|A peaceful, gradual process of altering policies and institutions within existing legal frameworks|An illegal military takeover of government ministries|A sudden collapse of state authority triggered by foreign invasion|Option B|Evolutionary and reformist changes occur peacefully and incrementally within the established constitutional and legal boundaries rather than through sudden systemic destruction.|
12.1|What is a primary characteristic that separates a military coup d'État from other forms of political transition?|It is always initiated by civilian labor unions|It represents a sudden, illegal intervention from within the state apparatus, specifically by armed forces|It requires a decade-long nationwide guerrilla war before execution|It focuses entirely on replacing municipal tax laws rather than executive leadership|Option B|A coup d'État is executed internally by elements of the state's own security apparatus, making it an illegal top-level seizure of executive power.|
12.1|Which of the following is cited as a major systemic cause for military intervention in politics?|Excessive judicial independence and transparency|Widespread political corruption and chronically rigged elections|Overwhelming economic prosperity and low inflation rates|Complete ethnic and cultural homogeneity across society|Option B|Persistent political corruption and fraudulent elections create severe legitimacy crises for civilian governments, often providing the military with a pretext to intervene.|
12.1|How can severe ethnic polarization act as a catalyst for military rule?|It forces the legislature to dissolve political parties voluntarily|It creates deep societal fractures that civilian leaders may fail to manage, leading the military to step in under the guise of national unity|It guarantees that elections will always result in coalition governments without conflict|It eliminates the need for any formal state budget or bureaucracy|Option B|Deep ethnic polarization destabilizes fragile states by undermining national cohesion, prompting military officers to claim they are restoring order above sectarian divides.|
12.1|When a nation experiences a severe economic collapse, how does this typically influence the likelihood of military intervention?|It decreases military influence because the army lacks financial resources|It increases the vulnerability of civilian regimes as public dissatisfaction and institutional decay create a power vacuum exploited by armed forces|It automatically triggers a peaceful democratic transition to a monarchy|It forces the state to disband its armed forces entirely to save money|Option B|Economic collapse erodes the performance legitimacy of civilian governments, making it easier for the military to justify intervention as a rescue mission to save the economy.|
