12.1|Which statement accurately contrasts evolutionary change with revolutionary change?|Evolutionary change is violent while revolutionary change is peaceful|Evolutionary change relies on gradual, peaceful adaptation within the system whereas revolutionary change employs systemic violence to dismantle the old order|Evolutionary change requires foreign military intervention unlike revolution|Evolutionary change focuses only on military coups while revolution focuses on elections|Option B|The core distinction lies in the method and depth of change: evolutionary change is gradual and peaceful within existing structures, whereas revolution is rapid, systemic, and violent.|
14.1|Which characteristic of Max Weber's ideal bureaucratic model ensures that administrative duties are distributed predictably among distinct offices?|Hierarchical chain of command|Fixed jurisdictional areas|Merit-based career tenure|Impersonality in official interactions|Option B|Fixed jurisdictional areas establish regularized official duties and clear divisions of labor, ensuring organizational tasks are distributed predictably.
14.1|How does a hierarchical chain of command function within a Weberian bureaucracy?|It guarantees lifetime employment regardless of performance|It mandates that every lower office is supervised by a higher one|It requires all public records to be archived indefinitely|It separates personal assets from official administrative budgets|Option B|A hierarchical chain of command ensures organizational control by establishing a clear structure where each lower office is under the control and supervision of a higher one.
14.1|What is the primary purpose of maintaining written files and records in a Weberian bureaucracy?|To ensure public transparency for democratic elections|To provide a permanent, cumulative memory and accountability for administrative actions|To calculate precise production quotas for industrial workers|To prevent employees from receiving fixed salaries|Option B|Written documents form the administrative archive or files, providing a permanent and continuous record of official decisions and organizational memory.
14.1|In the context of Max Weber's bureaucracy, what does the principle of impersonality imply?|Administrators should act based on personal friendships|Decision-making must be governed by abstract rules rather than personal feelings or favoritism|Bureaucrats are expected to remain completely anonymous to citizens|Officials do not receive fixed salaries or career tenure|Option B|Impersonality ensures that administrative operations and management are executed objectively according to abstract rules, eliminating personal bias or emotional favoritism.
14.1|Which feature of Max Weber's model protects bureaucrats from arbitrary dismissal and political interference?|Fixed jurisdictional areas|Written files and records|Merit-based career tenure and fixed salaries|Hierarchical chain of command|Option C|Merit-based career tenure and fixed professional salaries provide financial security and job stability, insulating public officials from arbitrary political pressures.
14.1|When a public official applies standard operating procedures uniformly to all citizens without showing favoritism, which Weberian principle is being demonstrated?|Fixed jurisdictional areas|Hierarchical chain of command|Impersonality|Merit-based career tenure|Option C|Impersonality requires administrative acts to be conducted without regard to personal feelings, treating all individuals uniformly according to established rules.
14.1|What is a defining consequence of dividing administrative work into fixed jurisdictional areas in a bureaucracy?|It eliminates the need for written documentation|It creates a specialized division of labor with assigned official duties|It allows any employee to perform any managerial task interchangeably|It ensures that officials own the administrative tools they use|Option B|Fixed jurisdictional areas define the scope of authority and responsibilities for each office, creating a structured and predictable division of labor.
14.1|Why are fixed salaries considered a vital component of the Weberian ideal bureaucratic model?|They encourage bureaucrats to accept bribes for extra income|They ensure financial independence and reduce vulnerability to corruption|They link a worker's pay directly to daily public popularity|They replace the need for formal written files and records|Option B|Fixed salaries provide secure, predictable compensation, reducing the temptation for financial corruption and reinforcing professional independence.
14.1|Which organizational feature best describes the vertical authority structure in a Weberian bureaucracy?|Horizontal networking|Democratic voting assemblies|Hierarchical chain of command|Decentralized local autonomy|Option C|The hierarchical chain of command establishes a vertical pyramid of authority where higher offices supervise and direct lower offices.
14.1|How does a merit-based system primarily contribute to the functioning of a Weberian bureaucracy?|By selecting officials based on technical competence and professional qualifications|By rotating political leaders after every election cycle|By ensuring that bureaucratic positions are inherited through family lineage|By allowing citizens to directly elect middle-management bureaucrats|Option A|Merit-based selection ensures that personnel are appointed based on proven qualifications and technical competence rather than political patronage.
3.1|Which of the following best describes the core focus of the legalistic or institutional approach in political science?|Informal social movements and grassroots protest networks|Formal constitutional texts, legal rules, and official government structures|Socio-economic class struggles and wealth distribution disparities|Underground political syndicates and corruption rings|Option B|The legalistic or institutional approach focuses primarily on formal legal frameworks, written constitutions, and the designated structures of government such as legislatures and courts.
3.1|What is a primary analytical advantage or merit of utilizing the institutional approach to political science?|It accurately predicts revolutionary uprisings in developing nations|It exposes covert economic lobbying and hidden corporate influence|It provides clear clarification of constitutional rights and jurisdictional boundaries|It maps the psychological behavior of individual voters during elections|Option C|A major merit of the institutional approach is its ability to clearly outline and clarify constitutional rights, legal duties, and the jurisdictional limits of governing organs.
3.1|Which of the following represents a significant limitation of the legalistic/institutional approach?|It is excessively dynamic and changes too rapidly to track|It completely ignores informal power dynamics and socio-economic forces|It relies too heavily on statistical econometric modeling of human behavior|It requires extensive fieldwork tracking illegal underground organizations|Option B|The approach is criticized for being static and overly descriptive because it neglects informal power structures, social dynamics, and economic forces that shape actual politics.
3.1|How does the institutional approach typically view the role of pressure groups and political corruption?|As the primary driving force behind all legal evolution|As central variables that must be measured in every constitutional case|As secondary phenomena or external factors largely ignored by its formal focus|As structural necessities required for a legislature to function effectively|Option C|Because the institutional framework concentrates strictly on official rules and state organs, informal entities like pressure groups and corruption are typically overlooked or minimized.
3.1|An analyst studying a state by strictly reading its written constitution, legislative statutes, and court rulings is utilizing which methodology?|The behavioral revolution model|The Marxist class-conflict framework|The legalistic / institutional approach|The radical postmodernist critique|Option C|The exclusive reliance on written constitutions, legal statutes, and formal courts defines the core of the legalistic or institutional approach.
3.1|Why is the legalistic or institutional approach often characterized as static in political analysis?|It focuses heavily on permanent structural changes while ignoring continuity|It assumes government institutions operate in a vacuum without real-world feedback loops|It relies on fixed legal texts and formal rules rather than capturing fluid, everyday political behaviors|It prohibits researchers from updating constitutional amendments over time|Option C|The approach is deemed static because it concentrates on written laws and official charters, which change slowly, rather than capturing the fluid and evolving nature of actual political life.
3.1|Which government bodies are typically placed at the center of study within the institutional approach?|Trade unions, labor syndicates, and revolutionary cells|Legislatures, executives, and formal judicial courts|Mass media conglomerates and corporate boards of directors|International non-governmental organizations and guerrilla factions|Option B|The institutional approach directs its core analytical attention toward official state organs like legislatures, courts, and executive branches.
3.1|What is a major consequence of the institutional approach's neglect of socio-economic forces?|It creates an overly idealized picture of how government functions in practice|It leads to an over-reliance on Marxist economic determinism|It forces researchers to conduct expensive sociological surveys|It makes constitutional law completely obsolete in modern states|Option A|By ignoring socio-economic realities and informal power, the institutional approach often paints a formalistic and idealized picture that does not match real-world political operations.
3.1|Which criticism most directly targets the descriptive nature of the traditional institutional approach?|It relies excessively on complex mathematical equations and game theory|It merely describes what formal rules exist rather than explaining why political actors behave the way they do|It focuses too much on predicting future geopolitical conflicts|It discards historical context entirely in favor of futuristic simulations|Option B|The approach is frequently criticized as being overly descriptive because it catalogs formal structures and legal rules without deeply explaining underlying behavioral motivations.
3.1|In the context of political science approaches, how do institutionalists view official government documents?|As useless pieces of propaganda designed to mask elite rule|As the fundamental blueprint through which political life and state power must be understood|As minor side-notes compared to grassroots mobilization|As temporary guidelines that hold no real binding authority over citizens|Option B|Institutionalists view official documents and constitutional texts as the central framework and foundational blueprint governing state authority and political organization.
4.1|Which intellectual movement in political science emerged during the 1950s associated with the Chicago school to emphasize empirical and quantitative observation?|Marxism|Behaviouralism|Institutionalism|Post-Behaviouralism|Option B|Behaviouralism emerged in the 1950s primarily through the Chicago school, shifting focus toward empirical observation and quantitative analysis of political actions.
4.1|Who are two of the prominent scholars most closely associated with the foundational development of the behavioural approach in political science?|Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels|David Easton and Harold Lasswell|Max Weber and Woodrow Wilson|Aristotle and Plato|Option B|David Easton and Harold Lasswell are foundational figures of the behavioural approach who advanced systematic and empirical analysis in political science.
4.1|According to the credo of behaviouralism, what type of inquiry should political science strive to maintain regarding normative judgments?|Value-free inquiry|Ideologically driven advocacy|Philosophically absolute inquiry|Theologically bound analysis|Option A|A core tenet of the behavioural credo is value-free inquiry, aiming to separate empirical observation from personal or moral preferences.
4.1|Which of the following best represents a core pillar of the behavioural credo regarding data collection and analysis?|Intuitive speculation|Historical storytelling|Quantification and techniques|Qualitative philosophical interpretation|Option C|Quantification and advanced research techniques are central components of the behavioural approach to ensure precise measurement of political phenomena.
4.1|What is a primary criticism or driving concern that led to the emergence of post-behaviouralism against pure behaviouralism?|An excessive focus on poverty and international war|A neglect of social relevance and pressing human crises|An over-reliance on historical legal texts|A refusal to use quantitative methods|Option B|Post-behaviouralism emerged because critics felt behaviouralism became too obsessed with methodology and ignored urgent real-world crises like war and inequality.
4.1|Which principle of the behavioural credo asserts that political science should seek to discover uniformities in human behavior that can be expressed in generalized theories?|Verification|Regularities|Systematization|Value-free inquiry|Option B|The principle of regularities posits that observable political behaviors exhibit uniform patterns that can lead to generalized scientific theories.
4.1|In the context of the behavioural approach, what does the principle of verification entail?|Accepting traditional wisdom without testing|Relying purely on intuitive legal deductions|Testing and confirming knowledge against empirical evidence|Validating claims solely through ethical philosophy|Option C|Verification requires that theoretical propositions and claims be rigorously tested and supported by empirical evidence.
4.1|How does the behavioural approach view the relationship between data collection and theory construction?|As entirely separate and unrelated endeavors|As integrated components leading to systematization|As obstacles to objective political analysis|As dependent exclusively on historical interpretation|Option B|Systematization in behaviouralism connects data collection and theory construction into an orderly, coherent body of scientific knowledge.
4.1|What core demand did post-behaviouralists make regarding the role of political scientists in society?|They must remain completely detached neutral observers|They must actively engage in addressing social crises and human survival|They must abandon all quantitative and empirical methods|They must focus exclusively on formal institutional structures|Option B|Post-behaviouralists argued that political science must remain socially relevant and take responsibility for helping solve major human crises.
4.1|Which academic hub is historically credited with driving the development of the behavioural revolution in political science during the 1950s?|The Oxford school of philosophy|The Chicago school|The Paris institute of political studies|The Berlin historical school|Option B|The Chicago school served as the primary epicenter for the behavioural revolution in political science during the 1950s.

5.1|The aggregate body of individuals inhabiting a state, regardless of whether they hold active political rights, refers to which element of statehood?|Electorate|Citizenship class|Population|Bureaucracy|Option C|Population is the human element or collective citizenry residing within the territorial jurisdiction of the state.
5.1|When a government establishes social security systems and unemployment benefits, it is primarily expanding which dimension of its operational mandate?|Coercive apparatus|Constituent duties|Ministrant obligations|Sovereign prerogatives|Option C|Social security and welfare programs belong squarely to ministrant functions, which aim to improve public welfare and living standards.
6.1|Which political theorist defined sovereignty as supreme power over citizens and subjects that is unrestrained by law?|Thomas Hobbes|Jean Bodin|John Austin|John Locke|Option B|Jean Bodin established the foundational modern concept of sovereignty as a supreme authority that is inherently unrestrained by human laws.
6.1|According to Thomas Hobbes in his theory of the Leviathan, what primary characteristic must sovereign power possess to maintain social order?|Absolute and undivided authority|Shared governance with an elected parliament|Temporary control subject to periodic voter renewal|Decentralized federalism across regional provinces|Option A|Hobbes argued that sovereignty must be absolute and concentrated in a single Leviathan to prevent society from relapsing into a violent state of nature.
6.1|How does John Austin conceptualize the source of sovereign authority within a state?|As a moral imperative rooted in natural law|As a social contract established by divine right|As the command of a determinate superior who receives habitual obedience|As the collective will of the general public expressed through voting|Option C|Austin defined sovereignty strictly in legal positivist terms, viewing it as the command given by a determinate political superior whom the bulk of society habitually obeys.
6.1|If a government holds supreme power because it successfully exercises physical coercive control over a territory despite lacking constitutional legitimacy, which type of sovereignty does it possess?|De Jure sovereignty|Legal sovereignty|De Facto sovereignty|Popular sovereignty|Option C|De Facto sovereignty refers to actual physical control and enforcement capacity on the ground, regardless of whether it holds formal constitutional authorization.
6.1|Which characteristic of sovereignty asserts that supreme power cannot be legally transferred, surrendered, or ceded to another entity?|Permanence|Indivisibility|Inalienability|Universality|Option C|Inalienability means that the sovereign power is inherent to the state and cannot be permanently handed over or transferred away without destroying the state itself.
6.1|What distinguishes legal sovereignty from political or popular sovereignty within a state structure?|Legal sovereignty resides in the supreme lawmaking body like parliament whereas popular sovereignty resides with the electorate.|Legal sovereignty controls military forces while political sovereignty controls the judiciary.|Legal sovereignty is temporary whereas political sovereignty lasts forever.|Legal sovereignty applies only to international treaties whereas political sovereignty applies to local ordinances.|Option A|Legal sovereignty rests in the supreme legal organ empowered to enact laws such as a parliament, whereas political or popular sovereignty lies behind the legal facade with the electorate.
6.1|Which attribute of sovereignty means that supreme authority extends over all individuals and associations within the territorial boundaries of the state?|Permanence|Universality|Indivisibility|Absoluteness|Option B|Universality signifies that the jurisdiction of the sovereign authority covers every person, group, and institution operating within the defined borders of the state.
6.1|What does the characteristic of permanence imply regarding the nature of sovereign authority?|It automatically expires when a specific political leader dies.|It lasts only as long as the ruling political party maintains a legislative majority.|It persists continuously across changes in government administrations or regimes as long as the state exists.|It can be suspended during national emergencies without affecting the underlying political structure.|Option C|Permanence means sovereignty outlives individual rulers and governments, enduring continuously as a core attribute of the sovereign state.

7.1|What is the defining characteristic of legal-rational authority as categorized by Max Weber|Obedience is given to a leader due to exceptional personal heroism|Compliance is rooted in ancient customs and historical practices|Rule is enforced strictly through economic sanctions and physical force|Power is legitimized by written constitutional rules and established offices|Option D|Legal-rational authority is built upon systematic, written rules, laws, and institutional offices rather than traditions or individual personalities.
7.1|How does authority fundamentally differ from power based on the study session notes|Authority requires physical force while power requires moral consent|Authority represents legitimate right to command obedience while power relies on compelling compliance via sanctions|Authority is temporary and unstable while power is permanent and constitutional|Authority exists only in democratic states while power exists only in monarchies|Option B|Authority is distinguished by its legitimacy and voluntary recognition, whereas power can rely entirely on coercion and sanctions without consent.

3.1|Which of the following is considered a core merit of the legalistic approach to political study?|It provides clear boundaries for constitutional rights and jurisdictional limits|It accurately predicts revolutionary uprisings and social upheavals|It exposes hidden networks of corruption and informal lobbying|It measures the psychological impact of media on voter turnout|Option A|A major advantage of this approach is that it clearly defines legal boundaries constitutional rights and the formal jurisdictions of different branches of government.
3.1|A major limitation of the legalistic and institutional approach is that it tends to be static and what else?|Descriptive rather than explanatory regarding real power dynamics|Overly reliant on quantitative statistical regression models|Obsessed with Marxist interpretations of economic production|Capable of predicting every future constitutional crisis|Option A|Critics argue that the approach is overly static and descriptive focusing on how institutions are written rather than explaining how power actually operates in practice.
3.1|When studying a legislature using the legalistic approach a scholar would primarily examine which of the following?|The formal constitutional powers and procedural rules of lawmaking|The personal friendships and behind-the-scenes compromises among members|The corporate campaign donations influencing election outcomes|The socioeconomic backgrounds and racial demographics of the candidates|Option A|The legalistic approach directs attention toward formal constitutional provisions legislative procedures and written rules rather than informal social interactions.
3.1|Which political phenomenon is most likely to be completely overlooked by a strict institutionalist researcher?|Informal pressure groups and underground political networks|Official parliamentary voting records and bills passed into law|Supreme Court rulings on federal jurisdiction and statutory interpretation|Formal executive decrees and presidential vetoes|Option A|Because institutionalists focus strictly on official government bodies they often ignore informal actors such as pressure groups and shadow power structures.
3.1|Why might the legalistic approach be criticized for ignoring socio-economic forces?|It assumes laws operate in a vacuum without considering economic inequality or class interests|It refuses to read any literature written by economists or sociologists|It relies entirely on psychological profiling of individual politicians|It claims that society has no impact whatsoever on the creation of courts|Option A|The approach is often critiqued for treating legal texts as autonomous while ignoring how socio-economic inequalities and wealth shape political outcomes.
3.1|How does the institutional approach treat the judiciary?|As a formal constitutional arbiter bound by written statutes and precedent|As a mere tool of violent revolution and class warfare|As an informal social club driven entirely by personal friendships|As an irrelevant actor with no real impact on state power|Option A|The legalistic framework views the judiciary through the lens of formal legal authority constitutional interpretation and statutory application.
3.1|Which factor is typically neglected by scholars who rely exclusively on the legal-institutional framework?|Widespread bureaucratic corruption and bribery scandals|Constitutional amendments passed by a national legislature|Official boundary limits defined for local government districts|Written procedures required to impeach an executive official|Option A|Corruption and informal clientelism bypass written legal rules making them hard to capture using a purely legalistic or institutional model.
3.1|In the context of political science approaches what distinguishes the institutional focus from a behavioral focus?|Institutions study formal rules while behavioralism studies actual human actions and attitudes|Institutions focus on economics while behavioralism focuses exclusively on law|Institutions ignore governments while behavioralism studies only constitutions|Institutions are entirely outdated while behavioralism is the only valid method|Option A|The institutional approach prioritizes formal structures and rules whereas behavioralism emphasizes the empirical study of human behavior attitudes and actions within politics.
3.1|If a researcher wants to understand why a government functions differently in practice than its constitution suggests which approach is most helpful?|Moving beyond the legalistic approach to examine informal power dynamics and socio-economic forces|Sticking strictly to the text of the constitution to find the hidden meaning|Ignoring all modern political science and studying ancient philosophy exclusively|Assuming that all written laws are always fully enforced without exception|Option A|Since the legal-institutional approach misses informal dynamics and socio-economic realities researchers must look beyond it to capture the full picture of political life.
4.1|Which institution and academic era are primarily credited with the rise of the behavioural approach in political science?|The 1950s Chicago school associated with theorists like David Easton and Harold Lasswell|The 18th-century Scottish Enlightenment focusing on moral philosophy and political economy|The classical Greek academy emphasizing normative statecraft and virtue|The 19th-century European institutionalism centered on legal-formal constitutions|Option A|The behavioural approach emerged strongly during the 1950s Chicago school through the pioneering work of scholars like David Easton and Harold Lasswell who emphasized empirical observation.
4.1|What core methodological shift did the behavioural approach introduce to the study of politics?|A strict focus on empirical observation and quantitative measurement of human political behavior|A primary reliance on philosophical reflection and ethical evaluation of the good society|An exclusive concentration on formal constitutional documents and legal structures|A rejection of scientific inquiry in favor of historical narrative analysis|Option A|Behaviouralism shifted the focus of political science away from pure legal-formalism toward the empirical and quantitative study of actual human political behavior.
4.1|According to the foundational tenets of behaviouralism, what does the principle of value-free inquiry demand of researchers?|That political science research should separate subjective ethical evaluations from empirical observation|That scientists must completely eliminate personal moral responsibility from all social actions|That political institutions should operate without any ideological guidance or leadership|That researchers must abandon any attempt to study public policy outcomes|Option A|Value-free inquiry in behaviouralism requires researchers to keep their personal values and subjective moral judgments distinct from empirical data collection and analysis.
4.1|Which of the following is explicitly recognized as part of the core credo of behaviouralism?|Systematization|Historical relativism|Normative prescription|Philosophical idealism|Option A|Systematization is one of the key pillars of the behavioural credo, alongside regularities, verification, techniques, quantification, and value-free inquiry.
4.1|How does behaviouralism view the pursuit of regularities in political science?|As the search for generalized patterns and uniformities in political behavior that can be tested|As the enforcement of strict uniformity in political opinions among citizens|As the belief that political systems never change over time|As the reliance on unverified historical traditions to guide policy|Option A|The search for regularities involves identifying recurring patterns and uniformities in political behavior that can lead to generalizable scientific theories.
4.1|What role do quantitative techniques play within the behavioural approach to politics?|They allow researchers to measure, analyze, and verify empirical political data precisely|They serve as a substitute for qualitative historical context and narrative depth|They are utilized primarily to validate ideological preferences in public policy|They represent an outdated method replaced by post-modern literary criticism|Option A|Quantification and advanced research techniques are central to behaviouralism for measuring and verifying empirical claims rigorously.
4.1|What primary critique led to the emergence of post-behaviouralism in political science?|That behaviouralism became too detached from urgent real-world human crises like poverty and war|That behaviouralism relied excessively on philosophical ethics and neglected empirical data|That behaviouralism focused too heavily on reforming corrupt government institutions|That behaviouralism rejected the use of statistical methods and mathematical models|Option A|Post-behaviouralism arose because critics felt strict behaviouralism was overly obsessed with neutral methods while ignoring pressing societal crises such as war and poverty.
4.1|What core commitment does post-behaviouralism demand from political scientists regarding social relevance?|That political science must actively address societal problems and maintain social relevance|That researchers must remain neutral observers and avoid practical applications of their work|That the discipline should abandon scientific methods entirely in favor of political activism|That political science should focus exclusively on theoretical abstraction and model building|Option A|Post-behaviouralism insists that political science must remain socially relevant and actively apply its knowledge to solve major human problems.
4.1|In the context of the behavioural credo, what does the verification principle entail?|The ability to test, replicate, and substantiate empirical research findings |The absolute legal validation of government statutes by judicial review|The philosophical justification of democratic norms through rational debate|The historical confirmation of ancient political doctrines through textual analysis|Option A|Verification requires that scientific claims and research findings must be open to empirical testing, replication, and validation.
4.1|How does post-behaviouralism modify or react to the traditional behavioural emphasis on value-free inquiry?|It argues that pure value-free neutrality is insufficient when human crises demand ethical engagement and relevance|It completely endorses value-free inquiry as the only valid scientific methodology|It rejects all empirical data collection in favor of purely normative philosophy|It claims that values can be mathematically measured and quantified like physical objects|Option A|Post-behaviouralism challenges strict value-free inquiry by arguing that political scientists have a moral responsibility to address human crises and remain socially relevant.

4.1|Which key theorist is most closely identified with the intellectual development of behaviouralism and post-behaviouralism?|David Easton|Max Weber|Karl Marx|Thomas Hobbes|Option A|David Easton is a central figure who helped shape behaviouralism and later called for the post-behavioural revolution to ensure social relevance.
4.1|What is the primary epistemological focus of the behavioural approach to politics?|Empirical and quantitative study of observable human political behavior|Philosophical inquiry into ideal forms of justice and governance|Historical analysis of ancient institutional constitutions|Normative evaluation of moral duty and political obligation|Option A|Behaviouralism prioritizes empirical observation and quantification rather than purely normative or abstract philosophical theorizing.
4.1|Which of the following is explicitly listed as a core tenet in the credo of behaviouralism?|Value-free inquiry|Revolutionary action|Moral absolutism|Historical teleology|Option A|Value-free inquiry is a foundational pillar of the behavioural credo, aiming to separate personal values from scientific observation.
4.1|According to the behavioural credo, what role does verification play in political research?|Claims must be tested and confirmed against observable empirical data|Conclusions are derived purely through deductive philosophical reasoning|Theories are validated through historical consensus and tradition|Truth is established via subjective interpretation and narrative meaning|Option A|Verification requires that political assertions undergo rigorous empirical testing rather than relying on unproven assumptions.
4.1|How does behaviouralism view the role of quantification in political analysis?|Using statistical measurements and mathematical tools to analyze political data|Rejecting numerical data in favor of deep qualitative case studies|Focusing exclusively on literary critiques of political speeches|Employing legalistic interpretations of statutory law|Option A|Quantification is a core tenet of behaviouralism, relying heavily on statistics and numerical measurement to study behavior.

4.1|What is the main critique that post-behaviouralism raised against traditional behaviouralism?|It became overly detached from pressing real-world crises like poverty and war|It relied too heavily on qualitative interviews and narrative histories|It failed to use any mathematical or statistical methods whatsoever|It ignored the importance of value-free scientific inquiry|Option A|Post-behaviouralists argued that an obsession with pure technique led behaviouralism to neglect urgent societal problems like war and inequality.
4.1|What did post-behaviouralism insist political science must actively maintain?|Social relevance and active engagement with human crises|Strict political neutrality and complete detachment from public policy|Exclusive concentration on theoretical methodology over practical issues|A complete rejection of empirical data in favor of moral philosophy|Option A|Post-behaviouralism demanded that political science remain socially relevant and apply its tools to address real human challenges.
4.1|Which of the following best captures the transition from behaviouralism to post-behaviouralism?|A shift from value-free technical obsession to actionable social responsibility|A movement away from empirical data toward ancient philosophical traditions|An abandonment of all quantitative methods in favor of pure intuition|A strict return to institutional legalism and historical description|Option A|Post-behaviouralism did not discard behavioural techniques, but rather added a demand for action, relevance, and societal problem-solving.

3.1|What is the primary analytical focus of the legalistic or institutional approach in political science?|Informal networking and grassroots community organizing|Formal constitutional texts, legal rules, and official government structures|Socio-economic class struggles and wealth distribution disparities|Psychological behavioral patterns of individual voters and politicians|Option B|The legalistic or institutional approach centers its analysis strictly on formal rules, constitutional architecture, and official institutions like legislatures and courts.
3.1|Which of the following institutions is a primary subject of study under the institutional approach to political science?|Labor unions and underground resistance networks|Corporate boardrooms and transnational conglomerates|Courts and legislative assemblies|Religious congregations and cultural fraternities|Option C|Courts, legislatures, and executive offices are the foundational formal governmental bodies examined by institutional theorists.
3.1|What is considered a major merit of utilizing the legalistic/institutional approach?|It accurately maps the informal flow of corruption and bribery|It clarifies constitutional rights, duties, and jurisdictional limits|It predicts the exact outcomes of revolutionary class warfare|It uncovers hidden psychological motives of political actors|Option B|A core strength of the legal framework is its ability to provide clear, precise definitions of constitutional rights, official powers, and jurisdictional boundaries.
3.1|Which of the following represents a primary limitation of the legalistic/institutional approach?|It relies excessively on dynamic mathematical models of economic behavior|It is static, overly descriptive, and ignores informal power dynamics|It focuses too much on spontaneous revolutionary uprisings|It completely disregards the written text of constitutions|Option B|The approach is criticized for being static and purely descriptive, failing to capture how real-world power operates outside formal rules.
3.1|How does the institutional approach typically treat pressure groups, lobbying factions, and informal socio-economic forces?|It places them at the center of all political decision-making models|It views them as primary agents of systemic economic transformation|It largely overlooks or ignores their impact within formal institutional mechanics|It evaluates them strictly through quantitative behavioral surveys|Option C|Because it confines its focus to official structures, the institutional approach tends to ignore or minimize informal forces like pressure groups.

3.1|What is a likely consequence of relying solely on the institutional approach to understand a developing nation's political reality?|You will capture every instance of underground black-market financial transactions|You may mistake ideal constitutional provisions for actual political practices|You will accurately forecast every spontaneous citizen protest movement|You will understand the psychological trauma of every voter|Option B|Focusing only on institutional text can create a distorted, idealised picture that masks corruption, clientelism, and how power is actually exercised.

4.1|What is the primary methodological focus of the behavioural approach to politics?|Normative evaluation of political ideals|Historical analysis of legal constitutions|Empirical and quantitative study of human political behavior|Philosophical inquiry into justice and equality|Option C|Behaviouralism shifts away from purely legal-institutional or philosophical methods, prioritizing the empirical and quantitative study of observable political behavior.|
4.1|According to the core credo of behaviouralism, what type of inquiry should political scientists pursue?|Value-free inquiry|Radical ideological activism|Historical narrative reconstruction|Legalistic document interpretation|Option A|A foundational tenet of the behavioural credo is value-free inquiry, which emphasizes objective, scientific observation free from subjective moral biases.|
4.1|Which key intellectual figure is prominently associated with the development of the behavioural approach?|David Easton|Karl Marx|Thomas Hobbes|Jean-Jacques Rousseau|Option A|David Easton, alongside Harold Lasswell, is recognized as a central figure in shaping and formalizing the behavioural approach in political science.|
4.1|What does the 'Verification' principle entail within the behavioural credo?|Accepting traditional wisdom without testing|Proving political claims through observable data and testing|Relying purely on intuitive philosophical reasoning|Prioritizing ethical arguments over factual evidence|Option B|Verification requires that political claims and hypotheses be rigorously tested and validated against empirical, observable data rather than accepted on authority.|
4.1|What does the 'Quantification' element of behaviouralism demand of political data?|Translating political phenomena into numerical form for precise measurement|Describing political events using descriptive poetry|Avoiding numbers to preserve qualitative richness|Using historical anecdotes as ultimate proof|Option A|Quantification involves measuring political phenomena numerically to allow for precise statistical analysis and comparison.|
4.1|What core limitation or critique led to the emergence of post-behaviouralism?|An excessive focus on solving immediate poverty and war|A neglect of social relevance in favor of pure methodology and abstraction|A complete rejection of empirical data collection|An over-reliance on ancient Greek philosophy|Option B|Post-behaviouralism emerged because critics felt behaviouralism became too obsessed with technique and quantification while ignoring urgent real-world human crises.|
4.1|Which goal is explicitly championed by post-behaviouralism in contrast to strict behavioural value neutrality?|Maintaining total detachment from societal problems|Abandoning all scientific methods completely|Remaining socially relevant and actively addressing human crises like war and poverty|Reverting back to medieval scholasticism|Option C|Post-behaviouralists insisted that political science must remain socially relevant and actively address pressing human crises such as poverty, war, and inequality.|
4.1|Which concept is part of the core credo of behaviouralism alongside regularities and verification?|Systematization|Revolutionary overthrow|Normative dogma|Historical relativism|Option A|Systematization is a pillar of the behavioural credo, aiming to integrate empirical findings into a coherent, interconnected theoretical framework.|
4.1|How does behaviouralism view the search for 'Regularities' in politics?|As an impossible and undesirable task|As discoverable uniformities in human political behavior that can be generalized|As purely random events with no pattern|As historical accidents unique to each century|Option B|Behaviouralism assumes that human political behavior exhibits discoverable regularities and patterns that can be generalized and expressed as theories.|

14.1|What is the primary purpose of maintaining impersonality in the execution of official duties under Weber's model|To ensure policy is administered without personal bias or emotional favoritism toward clients|To allow bureaucrats to express personal moral judgments when enforcing harsh laws|To encourage close personal friendships between officials and citizens to build trust|To give individual workers the freedom to bend rules based on personal empathy|Option A|Impersonality means that administrative tasks are conducted sine ira et studio without hatred or passion, ensuring equal and objective treatment for everyone.

14.1|What structural consequence does a strict hierarchical chain of command have on a bureaucracy|It establishes clear lines of responsibility and accountability for every administrative action|It eliminates all forms of communication between top leadership and ground-level workers|It forces every employee to report directly to the chief executive officer simultaneously|It transforms the organization into a decentralized network of independent local units|Option A|A strict hierarchy establishes precise supervisory relationships, making it clear who is accountable for every decision and subordinate action.
14.1|Why are fixed salaries considered essential for public officials in Max Weber's bureaucratic theory|To provide financial independence and reduce susceptibility to bribery or graft|To ensure that bureaucrats can become wealthy business owners outside of work hours|To tie the personal income of government workers directly to the profitability of the state|To allow administrators to set their own pay rates based on how many cases they close|Option A|Fixed salaries ensure that officials are financially secure and professionalized, minimizing incentives for corrupt behavior or extortion.
14.1|Which statement best describes the nature of fixed jurisdictional areas in public administration|Official duties are clearly bounded by specific laws, rules, and administrative regulations|Employees can choose which tasks they want to complete on any given morning|Jurisdictions expand or contract fluidly based on the personal charisma of the director|Departments overlap completely to encourage cross-functional competition and innovation|Option A|Fixed jurisdictional areas mean that the scope of authority and responsibilities for each office is clearly delimited by legal regulations.
14.1|What role do written rules and files play regarding the permanence of a bureaucratic organization|They allow the organization to persist independently of the specific individuals currently holding office|They trap the organization in rigid procedures that prevent any future adaptation or reform|They serve as secret documents that only top political leaders are allowed to interpret|They act as temporary guidelines that expire at the end of each fiscal year|Option A|Written records create an institutional memory that outlasts any single bureaucrat, ensuring organizational continuity and predictability over time.

3.1|When evaluating the branches of government, an institutionalist scholar would primarily examine which of the following?|The unwritten social norms guiding public opinion on TikTok|The official constitutional powers and operational rules of legislatures and courts|The personal psychological background of individual citizens voting in elections|The economic productivity of trade unions operating behind the scenes|Option B|Institutionalists look directly at official government bodies, specifically focusing on the constitutional design and formal procedures of institutions like courts and legislatures.
3.1|Why might the Legalistic Approach be criticized for overlooking real-world corruption?|Because corruption is always explicitly legalized in written constitutional texts|Because official institutional rules rarely reflect how power is actually exercised in practice|Because corruption only occurs in non-governmental organizations and private firms|Because legal frameworks completely eradicate bribery through strict statutory wording|Option B|Formal rules on paper often hide the reality of political corruption and informal bargaining, which institutional frameworks fail to capture.
3.1|In the context of the Institutional Approach, pressure groups and interest groups are typically viewed as what?|The primary focus of constitutional textual analysis|The supreme governing authority above the legislature and courts|External actors or informal forces whose operations are often ignored by strict institutionalists|The formal statutory creators of international trade law|Option C|Because strict legal-institutional approaches focus heavily on formal government machinery, they tend to overlook or minimize informal actors like pressure groups.
3.1|Which analytical tool is most essential to a researcher employing the Legalistic Approach?|Public opinion survey data and behavioral polling metrics|Constitutional documents, statutory laws, and court rulings|Ethnographic field notes from underground political resistance groups|Statistical regression models tracking household income disparity|Option B|The legalistic approach relies fundamentally on reading and interpreting formal legal documents, constitutional texts, and judicial precedents.
3.1|How does the Legalistic Approach differ fundamentally from modern behavioral or socio-political approaches?|It focuses purely on human emotions rather than state laws|It prioritizes formal institutional design and written law over informal behavioral dynamics|It rejects the existence of written constitutions entirely|It exclusively studies international economic trade balances without government involvement|Option B|While behavioral and socio-political approaches study actual human behavior and social forces, the legalistic approach restricts itself to formal rules and structures.
3.1|What impact does the static nature of the Legalistic Approach have on political analysis during times of rapid social upheaval?|It enables the researcher to forecast cultural revolutions with high accuracy|It makes the analysis comprehensive by capturing shifting public sentiments|It limits the ability to explain sudden changes because it relies on rigid, established rules|It forces the study to focus on underground revolutionary cells rather than parliaments|Option C|Because the approach is static and relies on written rules, it struggles to adapt to or explain rapid, fluid changes driven by social unrest or informal politics.
3.1|An analysis of the separation of powers between the executive and legislative branches based strictly on a country's written constitution is an example of which approach?|The Legalistic / Institutional Approach|The Marxist Class Struggle Approach|The Rational Choice Economic Approach|The Psychoanalytical Leadership Approach|Option A|Analyzing explicit constitutional provisions regarding the separation of powers is the hallmark of the legalistic and institutional approach.
4.1|Which academic institution and intellectual tradition are primarily credited with the rise of the behavioural approach in political science during the 1950s?|The Oxford School emphasizing historical institutionalism|The Chicago School associated with scholars like David Easton and Harold Lasswell|The Frankfurt School focusing on critical theory and cultural critique|The Paris School centered on structuralism and existentialism|Option B|The behavioural revolution in political science emerged in the 1950s primarily out of the Chicago School, championed by prominent figures like David Easton and Harold Lasswell.
4.1|What is the core methodological focus of the behavioural approach to the study of politics?|Normative evaluation of political ideals and justice|Historical narrative analysis of institutional evolution|Empirical and quantitative investigation of observable human political behavior|Philosophical deduction of the ideal state|Option C|Behaviouralism shifts the focus of political science away from pure legalism or philosophy toward the empirical and quantitative study of actual human behavior within politics.
4.1|According to the credo of behaviouralism as outlined by David Easton, what does the principle of regularities imply?|Political phenomena exhibit discoverable uniformities that can be expressed in generalizations or theories|All political actions are entirely random and unpredictable|Political systems operate independently of human psychological inputs|Political behavior cannot be studied through scientific frameworks|Option A|The principle of regularities asserts that human political behavior displays discoverable uniformities that allow political scientists to formulate valid generalizations and theories.
4.1|In the context of the behavioural creed, what does the tenet of verification require of political research?|Data and conclusions must be subject to rigorous testing and re-examination against observable evidence|Findings must align with traditional philosophical doctrines|Theories must be accepted based on the authority of classical theorists|Hypotheses must rely exclusively on intuitive deductions|Option A|Verification mandates that any scientific statement or conclusion must be open to rigorous empirical testing and validation against observable data.
4.1|Why did behaviouralists place a heavy emphasis on quantification and measurement in political science?|To eliminate all ethical dilemmas from public policy|To render data amenable to precise statistical analysis and precise expression|To replace qualitative historical texts with mathematical poetry|To ensure political science remains entirely divorced from sociology|Option B|Quantification allows political scientists to record data with precision and utilize advanced statistical methods to analyze political trends and behavior accurately.
4.1|What does the value-free inquiry pillar of behaviouralism demand from researchers?|That investigators separate their personal moral evaluations and ideological preferences from their empirical observations|That political science ignore all questions regarding human values|That researchers actively promote specific political ideologies in their findings|That scientific studies focus exclusively on moral philosophy|Option A|Value-free inquiry insists that researchers must keep their personal ethical views and biases separate from the objective gathering and analysis of empirical data.
4.1|How does the systematization tenet characterize the relationship between theory and research in behaviouralism?|Theory and research should exist as completely isolated academic pursuits|Theory should serve as a sterile framework devoid of practical application|Data collection and theoretical development must be closely intertwined and mutually supportive parts of scientific inquiry|Research should precede theory by at least one century|Option C|Systematization emphasizes that research and theory should not be isolated; rather, data collection must feed into coherent theoretical frameworks and vice versa.
4.1|What primary critique did post-behaviouralism level against traditional behaviouralism in political science?|Behaviouralism was too focused on immediate social crises like poverty and war|Behaviouralism became overly obsessed with technical methodology at the expense of addressing urgent real-world human problems|Behaviouralism rejected the use of quantitative data entirely|Behaviouralism abandoned empirical observation in favor of pure mysticism|Option B|Post-behaviouralism emerged because critics felt behaviouralism had become hyper-focused on technical methods and neutral data, neglecting pressing social issues like war, poverty, and inequality.
4.1|Which of the following best represents the central maxim or core demand of the post-behavioural movement?|Knowledge must be actionable and politically neutral simultaneously|Intellectual inquiry should prioritize methodological purity over social relevance|Political science must remain socially relevant and actively address human crises|Research should abandon all empirical tools in favor of rhetorical debate|Option C|Post-behaviouralism insists that political science cannot remain detached or neutral regarding major human crises, demanding that intellectual work maintain social relevance.
4.1|Which scholar is most famously associated with the articulation and leadership of both the behavioural revolution and the subsequent post-behavioural shift in political science?|Max Weber|David Easton|Karl Marx|Thomas Hobbes|Option B|David Easton played a foundational role in defining the behavioural approach in the 1950s and later led the "creative outburst" of post-behaviouralism, urging the discipline to address societal crises.

4.1|Which key figure is most closely associated with the foundational development of the behavioural approach in political science?|David Easton|Karl Marx|Max Weber|Aristotle|Option A|David Easton is a central figure of the behavioural revolution who helped systematize its core tenets and Credo.
4.1|According to the Credo of Behaviouralism, what does the principle of verification entail?|Relying purely on historical narratives and philosophical debates|Testing and establishing the validity of political generalizations empirically|Accepting political claims based on institutional prestige|Valuing subjective interpretations over measurable facts|Option B|Verification in behaviouralism requires that statements and generalizations about political behavior be testable and empirically validated.
4.1|What does the behavioural tenet of quantification emphasize in political research?|Eliminating all mathematical models from social inquiry|Expressing data and research findings numerically wherever possible to achieve precision|Relying strictly on qualitative case studies|Avoiding statistical analysis in favor of descriptive texts|Option B|Quantification involves recording and analyzing political data numerically to enhance precision, measurement, and data handling.
4.1|What is the core meaning of value-free inquiry within the behavioural approach?|Taking active political stances on social crises|Separating the researcher's personal moral and political values from empirical data collection and analysis|Rejecting all moral frameworks in society|Prioritizing ethical philosophy over scientific observation|Option B|Value-free inquiry asserts that scientific political research should be objective and uncorrupted by the investigator's personal moral or political beliefs.
4.1|What does the concept of systemization represent in the context of the behavioural credo?|Isolating individual political events as completely unique phenomena|Closely tying theory and research together to build coherent, interconnected frameworks of knowledge|Randomly gathering disconnected political facts|Abandoning theoretical structures for pure data accumulation|Option B|Systematization emphasizes that research and theory must be closely interlinked to construct systematic, coherent scientific explanations.
4.1|Which pillar of the behavioural credo focuses on discovering uniformities and patterns in human political actions that can lead to generalizable theories?|Regularities|Verification|Techniques|Quantification|Option A|Regularities refer to discoverable uniformities in political behavior that can be expressed in generalized theories or explanations.
4.1|Why did post-behaviouralism emerge as a critical reaction against traditional behaviouralism?|Because behaviouralism focused too heavily on solving immediate global crises like poverty and war|Because behaviouralism was perceived as overly fixated on methodology at the expense of addressing urgent social problems and human crises|Because behaviouralism completely rejected the use of statistics and data|Because behaviouralism advocated for violent revolution over reform|Option B|Post-behaviouralism emerged because critics felt behaviouralism's obsession with value-free technique made it socially irrelevant to real-world crises like war and poverty.
4.1|Which primary demand did post-behaviouralists place on the discipline of political science?|Political science must remain socially relevant and actively address pressing human crises|Political science must abandon all empirical research entirely|Political science must return exclusively to legal-formal institutional studies|Political science must eliminate all qualitative methods from academia|Option A|Post-behaviouralism insisted that political science must be socially relevant, meaning it cannot remain neutral in the face of major human and societal crises.
4.1|Which of the following best describes the fundamental difference between behaviouralism and post-behaviouralism?|Behaviouralism focused on normative philosophy while post-behaviouralism focused on mathematics|Behaviouralism emphasized objective, value-free empirical measurement while post-behaviouralism demanded social relevance and action regarding human crises|Behaviouralism rejected data collection while post-behaviouralism embraced strict positivism|Behaviouralism was developed in Europe while post-behaviouralism originated in ancient Greece|Option B|Behaviouralism prioritized value-free empirical science, whereas post-behaviouralism argued that scholars must apply their knowledge to solve real-world moral and social problems.

8.1|Which of the following is traditionally considered a primary source of political legitimacy?|Mandatory military conscription laws of the state|Absolute economic self-sufficiency and isolationism|Regular democratic elections and adherence to the rule of law|Strict suppression of opposition political organizations|Option C|Elections and the rule of law serve as vital institutional mechanisms that generate popular consent and build the psychological conviction of legitimacy.
8.1|How is political influence fundamentally distinguished from coercion in political science?|Influence relies on persuasion and rational argument rather than the threat or use of force|Influence is exclusively exercised by unelected bureaucrats instead of elected politicians|Coercion is a formal constitutional power restricted entirely to the judicial branch|Coercion requires the consent of the governed whereas influence bypasses public opinion|Option A|Political influence involves shaping political decisions and behaviors through persuasion prestige and rational arguments without relying on coercive force.
8.1|Which mechanism is explicitly cited as a non-coercive method of shaping political decisions?|Imposition of emergency martial law decrees|Lobbying lawmakers and building public coalitions|Confiscation of private property for state utilization|Deploying armed forces to suppress civil disobedience|Option B|Lobbying represents a core method of political influence where actors shape outcomes through advocacy and persuasion rather than physical force.
8.1|When a government maintains legitimacy primarily through its ability to deliver public goods and economic stability, which source is it leveraging?|Traditional dynastic succession frameworks|Charismatic personal authority of a single leader|Performance-based governance and output legitimacy|Ideological indoctrination through state-controlled media|Option C|Performance acts as a key source of legitimacy when rulers earn moral authority by successfully governing and delivering positive societal outcomes.
8.1|What role does the rule of law play in establishing political legitimacy?|It guarantees that citizens will never question executive decisions|It provides a predictable and moral framework that justifies the exercise of authority|It eliminates the need for holding regular competitive public elections|It centralizes all economic resources under direct control of the judiciary|Option B|Adherence to the rule of law ensures that power is exercised according to established, transparent, and fair rules, reinforcing the moral right to govern.
8.1|Which scenario best exemplifies the application of political influence in a democratic system?|A dictator outlawing opposition parties to secure unanimous votes|A citizen advocacy group shifting public opinion on environmental policy through open debate|A supreme court judge handing down a mandatory minimum prison sentence|A police commissioner deploying riot control units to clear a public square|Option B|Advocacy groups utilize persuasion and public argument to influence policy outcomes without applying coercive force.
8.1|Why is the psychological conviction of the ruled considered essential to the concept of legitimacy?|It forces citizens to obey laws regardless of their personal ethical beliefs|It measures the exact financial cost of maintaining a national security apparatus|It transforms raw power into accepted authority by generating voluntary moral recognition|It replaces the necessity of a written national constitution or legal code|Option C|Legitimacy resides in the minds of the citizens; it is the internal acceptance that power is rightfully and morally held, turning mere power into authority.
8.1|Which tactic is least likely to be associated with political influence as defined in the study session notes?|Engaging in persuasive public speaking during a legislative debate|Threatening political opponents with physical violence or imprisonment|Utilizing professional prestige to build consensus around a policy proposal|Lobbying government officials with data and rational policy arguments|Option B|Threatening physical violence or imprisonment is a form of coercion, which stands in direct contrast to non-coercive political influence.
8.1|How do elections contribute directly to the reinforcement of political legitimacy?|By replacing all legal frameworks with temporary popular votes|By providing a peaceful and institutionalized process for citizens to grant consent to rulers|By ensuring that government policies remain completely immune to public criticism|By concentrating executive and legislative powers into a single governing office|Option B|Elections provide a structured, participatory mechanism through which citizens confer moral authority and consent upon their chosen leaders.

9.1|Why do conservative thinkers generally advocate for cautious, gradual social change rather than radical transformation?|Because they believe human reason can perfectly redesign society overnight|Because established traditions contain accumulated wisdom that prevents societal chaos|Because they seek immediate and complete abolition of private property|Because they view the state as an inherently evil entity that must be destroyed instantly|Option B|Conservatives value tradition and historical continuity, arguing that sudden, radical changes risk destroying the functional fabric of society.

12.1|How does a coup d'état fundamentally differ from a revolution in terms of political dynamics?|A coup d'état is a violent mass uprising aiming for total socioeconomic restructuring while a revolution is an elite-level takeover|A coup d'état is an illegal top-level military seizure of existing power structures whereas a revolution is a profound, structural, and often violent systemic overturn|A coup d'état always leads to a democratic transition while a revolution always establishes military authoritarianism|A coup d'état involves civilian participation while a revolution is strictly restricted to armed forces personnel|Option B|A coup d'état targets the apex of government leadership illegally without necessarily altering the underlying socioeconomic fabric, unlike a revolution which fundamentally transforms the political system.
12.1|When a military faction executes a sudden, extra-constitutional removal of a sitting government, this specific act is best classified as a:|Revolution|Social movement|Coup d'état|Constitutional reform|Option C|A coup d'état is defined as an illegal, top-level seizure of state power, typically executed by the military against the current administration.

12.1|What distinguishes a coup d'état from a revolutionary change regarding mass participation?|Coups are typically executed by a small, elite military faction from within the state apparatus, whereas revolutions involve broad-based mass mobilization|Coups require millions of citizens to vote in a referendum while revolutions are executed entirely by foreign powers|Coups are always non-violent while revolutions are strictly peaceful legal procedures|Coups permanently transform class relations while revolutions only change executive leadership names|Option A|Coups are narrow, top-down elite events carried out by armed forces units, whereas revolutions fundamentally rely on deep, widespread popular participation.
14.1|Which of the following best characterizes the principle of impersonality within Max Weber's ideal bureaucratic model?|Decisions are made based on personal friendships and political loyalty|Administrative actions and interactions are governed by official rules rather than personal feelings or biases|Employees are treated differently depending on their social status outside the organization|Clients receive specialized treatment based on individual charisma and emotional appeal|Option B|Impersonality ensures that officials carry out their duties objectively and without emotional attachment or favoritism, relying strictly on standardized rules.
14.1|What is a defining structural feature of a Weberian bureaucracy regarding its authority framework?|A fluid horizontal network where authority is shared equally among all workers|A rigid hierarchical chain of command where lower offices are supervised by higher ones|A decentralized system of local governance driven by direct citizen participation|An informal leadership structure based on shifting alliances and temporary projects|Option B|A hierarchical chain of command is foundational to bureaucracy, ensuring clear lines of supervision, accountability, and control from top to bottom.
14.1|How does the Weberian model of bureaucracy handle official administrative acts and communications?|Through oral traditions passed down informally between generations of workers|Through private personal journals kept by individual administrators in their homes|Through comprehensive written files and records that preserve organizational memory|Through public town hall speeches delivered directly by bureaucrats to citizens|Option C|Written files and records are essential to modern bureaucracy because they ensure continuity, accountability, and a reliable documentation trail of official actions.
14.1|What criterion is fundamental for appointment and career advancement within a merit-based bureaucratic system?|Family lineage and aristocratic background within the political sphere|Personal financial investments and private capital ownership in the agency|Demonstrated professional competence, qualifications, and formal examinations|Length of personal acquaintance with the current political executive in power|Option C|Merit-based career tenure ensures that positions are filled by qualified professionals based on technical competence rather than political patronage or personal connections.
14.1|Which characteristic defines the jurisdictional areas of offices within a Max Weber ideal bureaucracy?|Fixed and officially defined domains of duties and authority governed by laws or administrative regulations|Flexible task distributions that change daily depending on the mood of the department head|Voluntary responsibilities that employees can accept or reject based on personal interest|Randomly assigned duties that rotate weekly among all available personnel regardless of training|Option A|Fixed jurisdictional areas mean that official duties are clearly distributed among offices, preventing overlap and ensuring clear specialization and responsibility.
14.1|Why are fixed salaries considered a vital component of Max Weber's bureaucratic model?|They allow bureaucrats to engage in high-risk financial speculation on the side|They eliminate the financial vulnerability of officials and reduce incentives for bribery and corruption|They tie an official income directly to the daily number of citizens they successfully turn away|They enable employees to set their own pay rates according to their perceived importance|Option B|Fixed salaries provide economic security and professional independence, helping to insulate bureaucrats from corrupt practices like taking bribes for official favors.
14.1|In the context of Max Weber's theory, bureaucracy is best understood as a form of organization that emphasizes which of the following?|Charismatic leadership and emotional inspiration|Traditional customs and hereditary succession rights|Rational-legal authority and systematic efficiency|Revolutionary transformation and social upheaval|Option C|Weberian bureaucracy is the ultimate organizational expression of rational-legal authority, prioritizing calculated efficiency, predictability, and formal rules.
14.1|Which scenario directly violates the principles of a Max Weber ideal bureaucracy?|An official is promoted based strictly on scoring the highest on a civil service examination|An administrator processes a permit application using standard operating procedures without knowing the applicant personally|A department head fires a qualified worker to give the position to a close personal family member|A government agency maintains detailed archives of every transaction and policy decision made over the past decade|Option C|Promoting a family member violates the core bureaucratic tenets of merit-based career tenure, impersonality, and objective qualification standards.
14.1|What role do written rules and files play in maintaining bureaucratic organizational structure?|They serve merely as historical curiosities with no practical bearing on daily decisions|They establish a stable, predictable framework that outlives individual officeholders|They are used exclusively to prosecute whistleblowers and limit public transparency|They create confusion and slow down processes to prevent any work from getting completed|Option B|Written files and documents create institutional memory and operational stability, ensuring that the organization functions consistently regardless of personnel turnover.
14.1|Which statement accurately describes the career structure of officials within a Max Weber ideal bureaucracy?|Employment is treated as a lifetime or long-term career with guaranteed tenure and predictable promotion tracks|Jobs are temporary volunteer roles that individuals hold for only a few weeks before rotating out|Positions are won through high-stakes public popularity contests held every calendar year|Employment is purely casual, with workers hired and fired arbitrarily on a daily basis|Option A|A career orientation with secure tenure and regularized advancement is a core pillar that professionalizes bureaucrats and protects them from arbitrary dismissal.

6.1|Which political theorist defined sovereignty as supreme power over citizens and subjects unrestrained by law?|Thomas Hobbes|Jean Bodin|John Austin|John Locke|Option B|Jean Bodin pioneered the modern concept of sovereignty, describing it as supreme power that is fundamentally unrestrained by positive laws.

7.1|Why is charismatic authority often considered inherently unstable or precarious over the long term?|It relies entirely on permanent written constitutions that are difficult to amend|It is invariably tied to the mortal life and extraordinary qualities of a single individual|It depends on predictable economic sanctions that eventually deplete state resources|It is restricted by rigid hereditary customs that prevent rapid political innovation|Option B|Charismatic authority tends to be unstable because it lacks a permanent institutional structure and relies on the unique presence of a charismatic leader.

8.1|Which of the following best defines political legitimacy in the context of political science?|The physical capacity of a state to enforce laws using military and police forces|The psychological conviction among citizens that their rulers possess a moral right to govern|The legal authorization granted exclusively through international diplomatic recognition|The economic capability of a government to provide continuous welfare benefits to citizens|Option B|Legitimacy is fundamentally a psychological belief and acceptance by the governed that the exercise of political power is morally justified and right.
8.1|How does political influence fundamentally differ from coercion?|Influence relies on physical force or the explicit threat of deprivation while coercion relies on laws|Influence shapes decisions through persuasion prestige and rational argument without coercive force|Influence can only be exercised by elected officials whereas coercion is used by bureaucrats|Influence is an illegal political tactic whereas coercion is a constitutionally protected power|Option B|Political influence achieves compliance or shapes decisions through voluntary persuasion and authority rather than through the use or threat of force.
