14.1|What is the foundational purpose of the hierarchical chain of command in Max Weber's ideal bureaucratic model|To ensure a firmly ordered system of subordination where lower offices are supervised by higher ones|To foster democratic debate and equal voting power among all ranks of civil servants|To decentralize decision-making so that frontline workers can operate without administrative oversight|To establish a rotating leadership structure that prevents long-term career tenure|Option B|A hierarchical chain of command establishes a clearly defined system of authority and subordination, ensuring that lower offices are strictly supervised and directed by higher ones.
14.1|Why are written files and records considered indispensable to the operation of a Max Weber ideal bureaucracy|They form the basis of modern official management and ensure administrative continuity and accountability|They serve primarily as historical artifacts to be archived for academic researchers and biographers|They act as public newspapers to keep citizens informed of daily political debates and legislative intent|They allow individual bureaucrats to alter official policies secretly without leaving a digital trace|Option A|Written documents and files ensure that administrative operations are continuous, traceable, and conducted according to established, repeatable precedents.
14.1|How does impersonality manifest in the day-to-day operations of a Weberian bureaucratic organization|Officials execute their administrative duties without personal emotional attachment, bias, or favoritism toward clients|Public servants are expected to suppress their personal identities by wearing identical uniforms at all times|Decisions are made collectively by random citizens rather than trained professionals to ensure absolute neutrality|Bureaucrats interact with citizens strictly through automated artificial intelligence without human intervention|Option A|Impersonality ensures that administrative tasks are executed sine ira et studio (without hatred or passion), treating all clients equally and objectively based on rules.
14.1|What is the primary significance of merit-based career tenure within Max Weber's bureaucratic theory|It protects public officials from arbitrary political interference and ensures professional competence|It guarantees that employees can never be dismissed from their jobs under any circumstances whatsoever|It replaces the need for a hierarchical chain of command by granting permanent autonomy to all workers|It ensures that executive leadership positions are filled exclusively through popular public elections|Option A|Merit-based career tenure safeguards administrative stability and professional neutrality by insulating civil servants from political patronage and arbitrary firing.
14.1|In the context of Max Weber's bureaucracy what does the existence of fixed salaries signify for the administrative official|It provides regular, predictable financial compensation that reinforces their professional independence and status|It acts as a performance-based commission where income fluctuates wildly based on daily case closures|It represents a secondary source of income while officials rely primarily on private commercial enterprises|It serves as a temporary stipend until the official transitions into elected political office|Option A|Fixed salaries ensure that bureaucrats are financially secure and professionalized, reducing the temptation of corruption or reliance on fees.
14.1|Which organizational outcome is most directly produced by combining fixed jurisdictional areas with a strict hierarchy|A predictable, specialized, and coordinated division of labor capable of efficient large-scale administration|An unpredictable administrative environment where tasks overlap and responsibilities are constantly contested|A decentralized network of autonomous communes operating completely independent of central authority|A flexible, ad hoc crisis response team that disregards standard operating procedures to innovate rapidly|Option A|Fixed jurisdictions and a strict hierarchy work together to create a specialized division of labor and clear accountability across large organizations.
14.1|How does a bureaucratic model rooted in written files differ fundamentally from traditional governance systems|It relies on documented, impersonal legal precedents and universal rules rather than oral traditions or arbitrary royal whim|It prioritizes charismatic emotional appeals over institutional continuity and systematic record-keeping|It depends entirely on hereditary lineage and familial loyalty to distribute administrative responsibilities|It rejects all forms of written law in favor of instantaneous public referendums on every administrative decision|Option A|Written files replace arbitrary, oral, or traditional decision-making with transparent, documented, and rule-bound administrative continuity.
14.1|Which of the following best describes the structural relationship between a lower office and a higher office in a Weberian hierarchy|The lower office operates under the control and supervision of the higher office with a formal right of appeal upwards|The lower office functions as an independent entity that can veto directives issued by the higher office|The lower office holds superior technical expertise and commands the higher office on strategic matters|The lower office and higher office operate as horizontal peers with no supervisory obligations between them|Option A|The hierarchical chain of command inherently requires lower offices to be supervised and directed by higher offices, maintaining a clear top-down supervisory flow.
14.1|What is a core theoretical consequence of implementing impersonality and merit-based selection in public administration|The elimination of nepotism and particularistic favoritism in favor of universalistic, rational-legal application of rules|The complete eradication of all administrative errors and inefficiencies within complex government agencies|The transformation of the bureaucracy into a legislative body that writes laws rather than executes them|The privatization of all public services to maximize corporate profitability and market competition|Option A|Impersonality and merit-based selection ensure that public administration operates on universalistic, rational-legal criteria rather than personal connections or political favoritism.

4.1|According to David Easton and other behaviouralists, what does the 'Verification' tenet of the behavioural credo require?|Testing and confirming empirical generalizations against observable data|Deriving political truths strictly through logical deduction and intuition|Accepting classical philosophical texts as self-evident axioms|Relying on elite consensus to validate political theories|Option A|Verification entails testing and confirming scientific assertions and empirical generalizations against real-world, observable data.|
4.1|What role do values play in traditional behavioural inquiry according to its core credo?|Inquiry should strive to be value-free to maintain scientific objectivity|Values must dictate the primary normative goals of public policy research|Values are the central variable used to measure institutional performance|Ethical frameworks should override empirical data when results conflict|Option A|A core tenet of behaviouralism is value-free inquiry, aiming to separate personal biases from empirical political analysis.|
4.1|Which of the following is considered a core pillar of the behavioural credo in political science?|Systematization of knowledge through theory and research integration|Qualitative narrative interpretation of historical political epochs|Philosophical speculation on the ultimate purpose of government|Normative prescription of utopian political arrangements|Option A|Systematization—linking research findings into coherent theoretical frameworks—is a fundamental pillar of the behavioural credo alongside quantification and verification.|
4.1|What was a primary critique raised by post-behaviouralists against traditional behaviouralism?|It ignored pressing social crises such as poverty, war, and inequality in favor of abstract quantification|It relied too heavily on historical archives and classical philosophical texts|It rejected the use of statistical tools and mathematical modeling in research|It was overly focused on prescribing radical revolutionary changes to society|Option A|Post-behaviouralists argued that behaviouralism's obsession with value-free quantification made it irrelevant to urgent human crises like war and poverty.|

4.1|Why did post-behaviouralism insist that political science must remain socially relevant?|Because retreating into value-neutral technocracy fails to address real-world human suffering|Because empirical data collection is fundamentally impossible without ideological bias|Because historical texts provide all necessary solutions to modern political problems|Because quantitative techniques are scientifically invalid in studying human beings|Option A|Post-behaviouralism emerged to demand action, arguing that political science must actively address crises like poverty and inequality rather than hide behind neutral technocracy.|
4.1|Which of the following best characterizes the shift from behaviouralism to post-behaviouralism?|A supplement adding social action and crisis-relevance to empirical methodology|A complete abandonment of quantitative data in favor of pure moral philosophy|A return to ancient Greek institutionalism and legalism|The elimination of the scientific method from political studies|Option A|Post-behaviouralism did not completely discard behavioural techniques, but rather added a commitment to value, action, and social relevance.|

3.1|Why might a political scientist criticize the legalistic institutional approach for lacking explanatory depth regarding real-world policy outcomes?|Because official laws on paper often diverge significantly from actual political practice|Because it relies entirely on mathematical models rather than legal texts|Because it focuses too much on temporary public opinion polls|Because it completely rejects the existence of constitutions|Option A|A major shortcoming is the gap between legal theory on paper and how power is actually exercised in practice, which formal institutionalism misses.

4.1|Which school of thought is primarily credited with the rise of the behavioural approach in political science during the 1950s?|The Frankfurt School|The Chicago School|The Oxford School|The Paris School|Option B|The behavioural approach in political science emerged primarily from the Chicago School in the 1950s through scholars like David Easton and Harold Lasswell.
4.1|What is the primary methodological focus of the behavioural approach to politics?|Normative evaluation of political ideals|Historical analysis of state constitutions|Empirical and quantitative study of human political behavior|Philosophical inquiry into justice and ethics|Option C|Behaviouralism shifts the focus of political science away from pure institutional or normative philosophy toward the empirical and quantitative study of observable political behavior.
4.1|According to David Easton and the proponents of behaviouralism, what does the creedal element of 'value-free inquiry' mean?|Research must completely ignore ethical considerations|Scientific explanations should be kept analytically distinct from ethical evaluations|Political scientists should never hold personal political opinions|Research must be funded exclusively by neutral private entities|Option B|Value-free inquiry in behaviouralism dictates that scientific explanations and empirical observations must be kept analytically distinct from subjective moral or ethical evaluations.
4.1|Which of the following best describes the credo of behaviouralism as advanced by its Chicago school proponents?|Regularities, Verification, Techniques, Quantification, Value-free inquiry, Systematization|Intuition, Hermeneutics, Dialectics, Narrative, Speculation, Ideology|Tradition, Authority, Revelation, Dogma, Absolutism, Historicism|Morality, Teleology, Metaphysics, Abstraction, Prescription, Universalism|Option A|The core credo of behaviouralism centers around systematic qualities like regularities, verification, advanced techniques, quantification, value-free inquiry, and systematization.
4.1|What was the primary reaction of post-behaviouralism toward traditional behaviouralism?|It rejected all forms of empirical data collection|It argued that political science must remain socially relevant and address crises like poverty and war|It demanded an exclusive return to medieval political philosophy|It claimed that quantification was the only valid goal of science|Option B|Post-behaviouralism arose to challenge the hyper-fact-oriented detachment of behaviouralism, insisting that political science must stay socially relevant and tackle pressing human crises.
4.1|Who are the prominent theorists most closely associated with the foundation of the behavioural approach in political science?|Karl Marx and Max Weber|David Easton and Harold Lasswell|Thomas Hobbes and John Locke|Aristotle and Plato|Option B|David Easton and Harold Lasswell are foundational figures of the 1950s behavioural movement who pushed for empirical, scientific methods in political science.
4.1|In the context of the behavioural creed, what does 'systematization' entail?|Interrelating data and theory in a coherent, orderly body of knowledge|Randomly collecting political facts without any theoretical framework|Solely focusing on historical anomalies and singular events|Deriving political laws purely from legal statutes|Option A|Systematization refers to the necessity of interrelating collected data and theoretical propositions into a coherent, organized, and cumulative body of scientific knowledge.
4.1|Why did post-behaviouralists criticize the strict value-free requirement of early behaviouralism?|They believed it blinded researchers to urgent human problems and real-world crises|They thought it made computers too expensive to use in research|They argued that values were the only things that could be mathematically measured|They wanted political science to become a branch of pure mathematics|Option A|Post-behaviouralists argued that an obsession with value-free neutrality often resulted in social irrelevance, ignoring critical real-world crises like war, poverty, and inequality.
4.1|What role does quantification play within the behavioural approach to politics?|It is entirely dismissed as unscientific|It is used to measure, analyze, and test political phenomena precisely|It serves solely as a decorative addition to qualitative essays|It replaces the need for any data collection whatsoever|Option B|Quantification is a core pillar of behaviouralism, providing the mathematical and statistical tools needed to measure and test political behavior precisely.
4.1|Which key issue prompted the emergence of post-behaviouralism in political science?|An excess of funding for political campaigns|The failure of behaviouralism to address major societal crises such as war and poverty|The sudden disappearance of quantitative data worldwide|A legal ban on the use of surveys and interviews|Option B|Post-behaviouralism emerged because critics felt behaviouralism was too narrowly focused on abstract methodology while ignoring urgent real-world crises like war, poverty, and inequality.

6.1|Which core characteristic of sovereignty ensures that the supreme power covers all individuals and associations within the defined territorial jurisdiction?|Universality|Permanence|Absoluteness|Indivisibility|Option A|Universality means that the sovereign authority extends uniformly over all persons, groups, and property located within the state's borders.

6.1|What does the characteristic of indivisibility imply regarding supreme state power?|Power can be freely split among rival provincial governors|Supreme authority cannot be fragmented into competing co-equal supreme branches without causing conflict|Sovereignty must be divided equally between church and state|Authority is split permanently between foreign and domestic actors|Option C|Indivisibility insists that supreme power must remain unified in a single ultimate source, as splitting supreme authority invites legal paralysis and civil war.
7.1|Which of the following best distinguishes power from authority in political science?|Power relies purely on voluntary consent while authority requires physical force|Power is the probability of imposing one's will despite resistance whereas authority involves recognized legitimacy|Authority is exclusively economic while power is strictly normative and legal|Power and authority are interchangeable terms used to describe state coercion|Option B|Power involves compelling obedience through force or sanctions regardless of consent, whereas authority is the socially recognized right to command.

7.1|Why does Max Weber argue that legal-rational authority is the most stable and bureaucratically efficient form of domination in modern states?|It relies on unpredictable personal devotion rather than fixed rules|It is based on impersonal rules and institutional offices rather than fickle human personalities or rigid customs|It functions entirely without any laws or formal administrative structures|It requires absolute physical violence to maintain continuous public compliance|Option B|Legal-rational authority anchors legitimacy in institutional offices and predictable written rules, avoiding the instability of personal charisma.
7.1|If citizens follow a government directive solely because they believe the government has the rightful moral and legal title to issue it, they are responding to what concept?|Coercive power|Authority|Economic compulsion|Normative coercion|Option B|Authority is defined precisely as the recognized, legitimate right to command obedience, which elicits voluntary compliance.
7.1|Which of the following scenarios best demonstrates normative power as a mechanism of compulsion?|Cutting off a nation's trade access to bankrupt its economy|Deploying military troops to suppress a domestic uprising|Using shared moral values and social pressure to shame an actor into compliance|Inheriting political office through an ancient royal bloodline|Option C|Normative power operates through shared values, ethics, and social pressure rather than physical force or financial sanctions.
7.1|What happens to charismatic authority over time, according to sociological theories building on Weber's typology?|It naturally disappears without ever transforming|It inevitably undergoes routinization into either traditional or legal-rational authority|It becomes permanent and immune to institutionalization|It automatically converts into purely economic power structures|Option B|Charismatic authority is inherently unstable and tends to routinize into traditional or legal-rational forms as the original leader's movement institutionalizes.

14.1|Which of the following best characterizes Max Weber's concept of fixed jurisdictional areas within an ideal bureaucracy|Official duties are distributed in a stable, systematic manner regulated by laws or administrative rules|Tasks are rotated randomly among employees to prevent institutional corruption and burnout|Responsibilities shift fluidly based on the political whims of the currently elected executive|Authority is decentralized entirely to local community leaders to maximize direct citizen participation|Option A|Fixed jurisdictional areas ensure that official duties are clearly defined and systematically regulated by established rules.
14.1|How does a hierarchical chain of command function within the Weberian bureaucratic model|It establishes a clearly ordered system of subordination where lower offices are supervised by higher ones|It creates a decentralized network where every official operates with absolute autonomy and equal power|It forms a flat structure focused entirely on peer-to-peer collaboration without supervisory layers|It relies on temporary committees that dissolve after every policy decision is finalized|Option A|A hierarchical chain of command ensures organizational control through a structured system of superior and subordinate offices.
14.1|What role do written files and records play in a Max Weber ideal bureaucracy|They serve as the foundational material that makes administrative actions continuous and traceable over time|They act primarily as public propaganda tools used to sway voters during national election cycles|They are strictly forbidden to protect the personal privacy of government officials and citizens|They are treated as temporary notes that must be destroyed immediately after a meeting concludes|Option A|Written documents ensure that administrative actions and historical precedents remain continuous and transparent.
14.1|In the context of Max Weber's bureaucracy, what does the principle of impersonality imply regarding administrative management|Officials conduct business without personal bias or emotional attachment based on abstract rules|Administrators are encouraged to form deep personal friendships with citizens to foster trust|Decisions are made entirely according to the personal moral compass and intuition of the bureaucrat|Public servants are treated as faceless machines with zero human rights or legal protections|Option A|Impersonality ensures that officials administer rules objectively, free from emotional bias or favoritism.

14.1|Which feature is a direct consequence of fixed salaries for bureaucrats in Max Weber's theory|It separates the official from ownership of the administrative means of production and office management|It ensures that public servants can collect unlimited private donations from corporate lobbyists|It forces government employees to rely solely on commission-based fees collected directly from citizens|It turns every bureaucrat into an independent business owner operating for personal profit|Option A|Fixed salaries ensure financial security and independence, preventing officials from exploiting office resources for private gain.

14.1|How does the principle of specialized training or professional qualification align with Weberian bureaucracy|Bureaucratic positions are filled based on specialized competence rather than political patronage or favoritism|Officials are chosen randomly through a civic lottery system regardless of their education or skill level|Anyone from the general public can walk into an office and perform complex administrative duties instantly|Training is completely discouraged to keep administrative processes simple and unsophisticated|Option A|Weberian bureaucracy requires officials to possess specialized qualifications to ensure efficient administrative execution.
14.1|What is a primary institutional benefit of maintaining written files and records in public administration|It preserves organizational memory and allows for consistent application of rules across different time periods|It guarantees that administrative procedures take three times longer than necessary to complete|It prevents any citizen from ever challenging a government decision in a court of law|It allows bureaucrats to easily alter historical data to hide policy failures from the public|Option A|Comprehensive written records maintain institutional continuity and accountability over the long term.

4.1|What primary criticism led to the emergence of post-behaviouralism in political science?|Behaviouralism was too focused on solving immediate societal crises like poverty and war|Behaviouralism neglected empirical methods in favor of pure moral philosophy|Behaviouralism became too abstract and detached from addressing real-world human crises|Behaviouralism rejected the use of quantitative data entirely|Option C|Post-behaviouralists argued that an excessive fixation on pure technocratic quantification made behaviouralism irrelevant to urgent societal crises such as war and inequality.
4.1|What did post-behaviouralism insist political science must prioritize to remain legitimate?|Social relevance and active engagement with human problems|Strict isolation from public policy debates|Exclusive reliance on historical textual analysis|The complete elimination of quantitative tools|Option A|Post-behaviouralism championed the idea that knowledge must be socially relevant, urging political scientists to tackle pressing real-world issues.
4.1|Which issue area is cited as a major crisis that post-behaviouralism argued political science needed to address?|The decline of classical Greek philosophy|Poverty and war|The codification of ancient Roman law|The translation of medieval political texts|Option B|Post-behaviouralism arose precisely to redirect scholarly attention toward urgent contemporary crises like poverty, war, and social inequality.
4.1|How does post-behaviouralism view the relationship between values and empirical research compared to strict behaviouralism?|It argues that action and values are inescapable, and research must be put to service for human betterment|It completely outlaws any form of quantitative measurement in political studies|It maintains that values have no place whatsoever in academic inquiry|It claims that historical documents are the only valid source of political truth|Option A|Unlike strict behavioural value-free purism, post-behaviouralism asserts that values are vital because knowledge must guide constructive social action and human betterment.

1.1|Which major development in political science shifted the focus toward scientific observation and quantifiable human behavior?|The Classical paradigm shift|The Behavioural revolution|The Marxist economic awakening|The Machiavellian secular split|Option B|The Behavioural revolution introduced empirical methods statistical analysis and a focus on observable human political behavior rather than just formal institutions.|
1.1|Which ancient Greek thinker is most closely associated with idealistic utopian philosophy prior to Aristotle's empirical classification?|Plato|Heraclitus|Thucydides|Xenophon|Option A|Plato is renowned for his philosophical idealism and utopian vision of the just state outlined in The Republic.|
3.1|Which of the following best defines the core focus of the legalistic approach in political science?|Informal social movements and grassroots protests|Formal constitutional texts and official government structures|Socio-economic inequalities and class struggle dynamics|Hidden economic interests driving public policy decisions|Option B|The legalistic approach focuses primarily on formal legal rules, constitutional texts, and official government institutions like legislatures and courts.
3.1|What is a primary analytical advantage of utilizing the institutional approach in political analysis?|It accurately predicts revolutionary movements|It explains how informal pressure groups shape policy|It clarifies constitutional rights and jurisdictional limits of government|It measures the psychological motivations of voters|Option C|By focusing on institutional structures and rules, this approach provides clarity regarding formal constitutional rights and the jurisdictional limits of various branches of government.
3.1|Which of the following is a major limitation associated with the legalistic and institutional approach?|It relies excessively on unpredictable revolutionary actions|It is overly dynamic and constantly changes with political moods|It is static and descriptive because it ignores informal power dynamics|It focuses too much on underground corruption networks|Option C|The institutional approach is often criticized for being static and overly descriptive, failing to account for informal power dynamics that shape actual political behavior.
3.1|An analyst studying a government solely by reading its written constitution and legislative rulebooks is applying which approach?|The behavioral approach|The Marxist class-conflict approach|The legalistic institutional approach|The pluralist interest-group approach|Option C|Reading only written constitutions and formal rulebooks characterizes the legalistic institutional approach, which prioritizes official rules over practical realities.
3.1|When political scientists critique the legalistic approach for ignoring pressure groups and corruption, they are pointing out its neglect of what factor?|Formal legal procedures|Informal power dynamics and socio-economic forces|Constitutional jurisdictional limits|Official legislative voting records|Option B|A core limitation of this framework is its oversight of informal power dynamics, socio-economic forces, and interest groups that operate outside official structures.
3.1|Which pair of entities would be of primary interest to a researcher using the institutional approach?|Labor strikes and corporate lobbying firms|Courts and legislatures|Revolutionary cells and guerrilla militias|Social media influencers and protest organizers|Option B|Courts and legislatures are formal government institutions that sit at the very center of the legalistic and institutional framework of study.
3.1|Why might a purely institutional analysis fail to explain why a specific law is effectively ignored in practice?|Because constitutions are always flexible documents|Because it ignores informal corruption, enforcement gaps, and political realities|Because legal texts are written in ambiguous foreign languages|Because courts always declare unconstitutional laws void immediately|Option B|Institutional analysis often misses the gap between law on paper and law in action because it overlooks informal practices, enforcement failures, and corruption.
3.1|How does the institutional approach typically treat the study of politics?|As a struggle between socioeconomic classes|As a set of formal rules, offices, and legal procedures|As a psychological reaction to environmental stimuli|As a chaotic web of unorganized social protests|Option B|The framework views political life through the lens of formal rules, established offices, and structured legal procedures rather than fluid social movements.
3.1|What is the consequence of the legalistic approach focusing heavily on static constitutional frameworks?|It becomes unable to capture dynamic political changes and informal behaviors|It automatically incorporates all modern technological advancements|It guarantees absolute political stability in developing nations|It successfully eliminates bureaucratic corruption within the state|Option C|Because it relies on static descriptions of rules, the approach struggles to capture dynamic political shifts, behavioral adaptations, and informal political influences.
3.1|Which of the following elements would a strict institutionalist most likely exclude or downplay in their research?|Legislative voting procedures|Constitutional amendments|Informal lobbying and backroom political bargaining|Judicial review mechanisms|Option C|Informal lobbying and backroom political bargaining are typical examples of informal power dynamics that the legalistic institutional approach tends to ignore.
4.1|Which academic institution and decade are primarily associated with the rise of the behavioural approach in political science?|The Oxford school of the 1930s|The Chicago school of the 1950s|The Frankfurt school of the 1920s|The Parisian school of the 1960s|Option B|The behavioural approach originated primarily through the Chicago school during the 1950s, emphasizing empirical and scientific methods.
4.1|Who are two of the prominent scholars most closely associated with the development of behaviouralism in political science?|Karl Marx and Max Weber|David Easton and Harold Lasswell|Thomas Hobbes and John Locke|Jean-Jacques Rousseau and Montesquieu|Option B|David Easton and Harold Lasswell were key figures who championed the behavioural revolution and the study of observable political behavior.
4.1|What is the primary epistemological focus of the behavioural approach to politics?|Normative evaluation of political ideals|Historical tracing of constitutional origins|Empirical and quantitative study of human political behavior|Philosophical contemplation of justice and the state|Option C|Behaviouralism shifts the focus away from pure normative philosophy toward empirical, observable, and measurable patterns of human political action.
4.1|According to the credo of behaviouralism, what type of inquiry should political science strive to maintain?|Value-free inquiry|Radical ideological critique|Dogmatic partisan inquiry|Intuitive speculative inquiry|Option A|A core tenet of the behavioural credo is value-free inquiry, aiming to separate personal biases from scientific observation and analysis.
4.1|Which of the following is explicitly listed as a core component of the behavioural credo?|Verification|Revelation|Intuition|Metaphysics|Option A|Verification is a fundamental pillar of the behavioural credo, requiring that empirical assertions be tested and proven through systematic data.
4.1|In the context of the behavioural approach, what does systematization refer to?|Relating data and findings into a coherent, interconnected body of theory|Relying strictly on historical narratives without theoretical frameworks|Rejecting all previous political philosophies in favor of chaos|Organizing political parties based on geographic representation|Option A|Systematization involves linking empirical research findings into an interconnected body of theory to explain political phenomena comprehensively.
4.1|What role do measurement and advanced tools play in the behavioural framework?|They are considered irrelevant to human political motivation|They form the basis of quantification and specialized techniques|They are replaced entirely by qualitative historical case studies|They are used solely for ethical evaluation of policy outcomes|Option B|Quantification and specialized techniques are vital to behaviouralism for measuring political phenomena precisely and objectively.
4.1|What was a major catalyst or critique that led to the emergence of post-behaviouralism?|A desire to return exclusively to medieval political philosophy|The need for political science to remain socially relevant and address crises like poverty and war|An absolute rejection of any form of data collection or voting analysis|The complete eradication of quantitative methods in academic research|Option B|Post-behaviouralism arose because scholars insisted that political science must address urgent human crises like poverty, war, and inequality rather than just abstract methodology.
4.1|How does post-behaviouralism expand upon or modify pure behaviouralism?|It completely abandons empirical research in favor of poetry|It balances empirical rigor with a commitment to social relevance and action|It restricts political studies only to laboratory experiments|It prohibits the study of public policy and international relations|Option B|Post-behaviouralism does not discard behavioural tools, but insists they be applied to solve real-world societal problems and human crises.
4.1|Which of the following best captures the transition from behaviouralism to post-behaviouralism?|A shift from strictly value-free empirical mechanics toward socially engaged problem-solving|A complete return to ancient Greek metaphysical speculation|The total elimination of statistics and quantitative modeling from universities|A movement toward endorsing specific political parties in elections|Option A|Post-behaviouralism broadened the scope of behaviouralism by demanding that empirical research also serve a purpose in addressing real-world societal crises.
6.1|Which characteristic of sovereignty asserts that supreme power cannot be transferred, given away, or alienated to another entity?|Indivisibility|Permanence|Inalienability|Absoluteness|Option C|Inalienability means that the sovereign power is inherent to the state and cannot be legally handed over or transferred to any other body.
6.1|How does Thomas Hobbes primarily characterize the sovereign authority known as the Leviathan?|A constitutional magistrate bound by a social contract|An absolute power necessary to maintain order and prevent the state of nature|A temporary emergency dictator subject to periodic voter recall|A representative assembly sharing power with a judicial council|Option B|Hobbes argued for an absolute Leviathan to enforce covenants, establish civil peace, and rescue humanity from the chaotic state of nature.
6.1|Which type of sovereignty refers to supreme legal authority that is recognized and exercised through constitutional and legislative channels?|De Facto sovereignty|Popular sovereignty|De Jure sovereignty|Political sovereignty|Option C|De jure sovereignty denotes the legal, legitimate, and constitutional right to rule, regardless of day-to-day physical control.
6.1|According to John Austin's command theory of law, what constitutes the sovereign?|A determinate human superior who receives habitual obedience from the bulk of a given society|An abstract moral consensus derived from natural law traditions|The collective electorate expressing its supreme will through referendums|An unwritten constitution upheld by historical judicial precedents|Option A|Austin defined sovereignty through a legal positivist lens as a determinate superior receiving habitual obedience rather than a moral or divine entity.
6.1|If a military junta seizes physical power through a coup d'état and maintains coercive control despite lacking constitutional legitimacy, what type of sovereignty do they possess?|De Jure sovereignty|Legal sovereignty|De Facto sovereignty|Popular sovereignty|Option C|De facto sovereignty represents pure physical and coercive control over a territory, even when it lacks formal de jure constitutional authorization.
6.1|Which dimension of sovereignty emphasizes that supreme political power is unlimited by internal man-made laws?|Permanence|Absoluteness|Universality|Indivisibility|Option B|Absoluteness means the sovereign is bound by neither the commands of predecessors nor its own laws, possessing supreme authority.
6.1|In a modern democratic system, where does political or popular sovereignty conceptually reside?|With the permanent civil service bureaucracy|With the supreme court justices|With the electorate or the people|With the reigning monarch or chief executive|Option C|Political or popular sovereignty locates the ultimate source of political authority and legitimacy within the electorate or the citizenry.
6.1|Which property of sovereignty ensures that supreme power does not lapse or terminate with the death of a particular ruler or a change in government?|Universality|Inalienability|Permanence|Indivisibility|Option C|Permanence signifies that sovereignty endures continuously across time, surviving shifts in administration or leadership regimes.
6.1|Which characteristic implies that sovereign power cannot be legally fragmented or divided among competing branches without destroying the core concept of supremacy?|Absoluteness|Indivisibility|Permanence|Universality|Option B|Indivisibility posits that supreme power must remain whole and centralized, as dividing sovereignty creates conflicting final authorities.

7.1|Which of the following best distinguishes power from authority according to the study session materials?|Power relies solely on legal documents while authority relies on economic wealth|Power is the ability to compel action through sanctions or force whereas authority is a recognized legitimate right to command|Power requires voluntary consent from citizens whereas authority requires physical coercion|Power and authority are identical concepts used interchangeably by Max Weber|Option B|Power involves coercion or sanctions to compel compliance whereas authority is specifically defined as a recognized and legitimate right to command obedience.
7.1|A government official holds office because their family has ruled the nation for centuries through established customs. Under Max Weber's typology, this form of rule represents which type of authority?|Charismatic authority|Legal-rational authority|Traditional authority|Coercive authority|Option C|Traditional authority derives its legitimacy from long-standing customs, traditions, and hereditary lineage rather than written rules or personal heroism.
7.1|When citizens obey a political leader primarily because they are deeply inspired by the leader's extraordinary personal heroism and exceptional character, what type of authority is being exhibited?|Traditional authority|Legal-rational authority|Economic authority|Charismatic authority|Option D|Charismatic authority is based on devotion to the exceptional sanctity, heroism, or exemplary character of an individual leader.
7.1|A police officer issues a speeding ticket based strictly on written traffic codes and established constitutional statutes. This scenario exemplifies which of Max Weber's types of authority?|Legal-rational authority|Traditional authority|Charismatic authority|Normative power|Option A|Legal-rational authority is rooted in a system of written rules, laws, and impersonal legal offices rather than custom or personal devotion.
7.1|Which of the following forms of power relies on the manipulation of material rewards, wealth, or financial penalties to influence actor B's behavior?|Normative power|Economic power|Charismatic power|Traditional power|Option B|Economic power involves using material resources, wealth, or financial sanctions to compel an actor to act in a certain way.
7.1|If a government successfully forces compliance from a resistant population purely through military threats and physical punishment, which foundational concept from the study session is primarily at play?|Authority|Legal-rational legitimacy|Power|Traditional succession|Option C|Power encompasses the use of force or sanctions to compel compliance, distinguishing it from legitimate authority which gains voluntary obedience.
7.1|Which characteristic is strictly unique to authority as opposed to raw power?|The ability to inflict severe economic sanctions|The capacity to deploy military forces|The presence of recognized legitimacy and right to command|The reliance on personal charisma alone|Option C|Authority is fundamentally characterized by the recognition of legitimacy, meaning those commanded feel an obligation to obey.
7.1|Max Weber's sociological classification of authority specifically divides legitimate domination into how many distinct types?|Two types|Three types|Four types|Five types|Option B|Max Weber categorizes legitimate authority into three distinct types: traditional, charismatic, and legal-rational.
7.1|Which of the following choices best represents an application of normative power in a political or social setting?|Imposing a heavy tax penalty on non-compliant corporations|Threatening military invasion against a rival territory|Using shared moral values and social pressure to compel compliance|Handing down a monarchy through hereditary succession|Option C|Normative power operates through shared values, ethics, and social norms to influence behavior rather than physical force or financial rewards.
7.1|Why does Max Weber's concept of legal-rational authority depend heavily on written constitutional rules and impersonal offices?|Because written rules ensure that obedience is owed to the legally established office and laws rather than to a person's hereditary status or personal charm|Because written rules eliminate the need for any form of government enforcement or police sanctions|Because written rules are exclusively created by charismatic leaders during times of revolution|Because written rules prevent any possibility of political conflict or societal disagreement|Option A|Legal-rational authority anchors legitimacy in formal, written laws and structural offices, ensuring stability independent of specific individuals.
8.1|What best defines political legitimacy in the context of political science?|A legal requirement enforced by military tribunals|The psychological conviction among citizens that rulers possess a moral right to govern|The absolute physical monopoly over the instruments of state violence|An economic measurement of a nation-wide gross domestic product per capita|Option B|Legitimacy is fundamentally defined as the psychological conviction and social belief that those in power hold a legitimate, moral right to rule.|
8.1|Which of the following is considered a primary source of political legitimacy?|Coercive intimidation and secret police surveillance|Regular elections, effective government performance, and adherence to the rule of law|Financial speculation and corporate stock market valuations|Unilateral military deployment without legislative oversight|Option B|Sources of legitimacy derive from societal acceptance built through fair elections, reliable state performance, and upholding the rule of law.|
8.1|How does political influence primarily differ from coercive power?|Influence relies on persuasion, prestige, and rational argument rather than the threat or use of force.|Influence is exclusively exercised by unelected bureaucratic technocrats.|Coercive power requires widespread public consensus to function effectively.|Influence has no measurable impact on legislative policy outcomes.|Option A|Political influence achieves compliance or alignment through persuasion and prestige, bypassing the need for coercive physical force.|
8.1|When a citizen obeys a government directive simply because they believe the regime operates fairly and morally, what concept is being demonstrated?|Coercive compliance|Legitimacy|Totalitarian indoctrination|Economic rationalism|Option B|Believing that a government operates fairly and morally builds the psychological conviction known as legitimacy, leading to voluntary compliance.|
8.1|Which of the following activities is a classic manifestation of political influence?|Lobbying lawmakers using rational arguments and persuasive data|Imprisoning political dissidents without a formal trial|Invading a neighboring territory to annex contested land|Imposing an emergency economic blockade by executive decree|Option A|Lobbying through persuasion and rational argument exemplifies political influence because it shapes decisions without applying coercive force.|
8.1|If a government loses its legitimacy, what is the most likely long-term consequence for the regime?|Increased economic productivity across all industrial sectors|An immediate expansion of international diplomatic alliances|Heightened reliance on raw coercion and potential civil instability|Complete dissolution of formal geographic borders overnight|Option C|When psychological conviction and moral right to govern fade, regimes typically must rely increasingly on coercion to maintain control, often risking instability.|
8.1|Which term describes the capacity to shape political decisions through prestige and persuasion without forcing compliance?|Bureaucratic hierarchy|Totalitarianism|Political influence|Autocratic sovereignty|Option C|Political influence is precisely the ability to shape policy and decisions through non-coercive means like prestige, lobbying, and rational argument.|
8.1|Why are regular elections often viewed as a vital pillar of modern state legitimacy?|They guarantee that no economic recessions will ever occur.|They provide a peaceful mechanism for citizens to authorize leaders and validate their moral right to govern.|They completely eliminate the need for any legislative or judicial branches.|They ensure that all citizens receive equal financial compensation.|Option B|Regular elections allow citizens to participate in choosing leadership, thereby reinforcing the psychological conviction that the government rules with consent.|
8.1|In the study of governance, how does rule of law contribute directly to legitimacy?|By ensuring that rulers are bound by legal frameworks rather than arbitrary whims, fostering public trust|By allowing executive leaders to bypass constitutional restrictions during a crisis|By prioritizing the personal wealth of elected officials over public welfare|By eliminating all forms of political opposition permanently|Option A|The rule of law enhances legitimacy by demonstrating that leaders are constrained by predictable, fair legal rules, building public trust and moral authority.|
8.1|Which scenario best illustrates the exercise of political influence rather than raw power?|A diplomat convincing a foreign minister to sign a treaty through persuasive negotiation|A dictator forcing political opponents into exile under threat of execution|A police officer arresting a suspect for armed robbery|A supreme court judge sentencing a convicted felon to prison|Option A|Diplomatic negotiation relies on persuasion and argument to shape outcomes, distinguishing it from the direct threat or application of state coercion.|
9.1|Which of the following best defines an ideology in the context of political science?|A random collection of short-term policy reactions|A coherent set of normative beliefs explaining reality and offering a blueprint for political organization|An absolute scientific law that dictates exact historical outcomes|A temporary campaign slogan used by political parties during elections|Option B|An ideology provides a structured, normative framework that interprets social reality and guides how political systems ought to be organized.
9.1|Which core principle distinguishes liberalism from other major political ideologies?|The absolute supremacy of the totalitarian state|The total abolition of private property and currency|The prioritization of individual liberty free markets and a limited state|The complete rejection of any form of constitutional governance|Option C|Liberalism centers heavily on individual liberties, capitalist market dynamics, and minimizing government intervention in personal and economic spheres.
9.1|What is the foundational economic and social objective of socialism and communism according to the study materials?|The preservation of traditional feudal hierarchies|Collective ownership and the pursuit of socio-economic equality|The establishment of an unregulated laissez-faire market system|The complete rejection of public institutions in favor of total private control|Option B|Socialism and communism emphasize dismantling class stratification through collective ownership of resources to achieve true equality.
9.1|Who is the prominent historical theorist closely associated with traditional conservatism and the defense of gradual change?|Karl Marx|Adolf Hitler|Edmund Burke|Michail Bakunin|Option C|Edmund Burke is widely recognized as the father of modern conservatism, emphasizing organic societal growth, traditions, and caution toward radical reform.
9.1|How does fascism or nazism view the role of the state in human life and society?|As an unnecessary evil that should be immediately dismantled|As a limited entity responsible only for protecting individual contract rights|As a totalizing authority where state supremacy overrides all individual interests|As a neutral arbiter that stays out of cultural and economic matters|Option C|Fascism and Nazism champion a totalitarian state model where individual existence is entirely subordinated to the collective power and glory of the state.
9.1|Which political ideology fundamentally rejects all forms of state authority and hierarchical government?|Conservatism|Anarchism|Socialism|Liberalism|Option B|Anarchism stands apart by advocating for the complete elimination of the state, viewing all hierarchical government authority as illegitimate and oppressive.
9.1|In a democratic-capitalist society, a political party advocating for extensive deregulation, low taxation, and private enterprise alignment is drawing primarily from which tradition?|Liberalism|Fascism|Anarchism|Communism|Option A|Advocating for free markets and a limited state directly reflects core liberal principles concerning economic freedom and limited government.
9.1|If a political regime nationalizes all major industries, abolishes private capital accumulation, and attempts to eliminate class distinctions, which ideology is it primarily executing?|Conservatism|Fascism|Liberalism|Socialism/Communism|Option D|Collective ownership of the means of production and the pursuit of a classless society are the hallmark definitions of socialist and communist systems.
9.1|When a conservative political theorist argues against rapid, revolutionary constitutional overhauls in favor of preserving established societal customs, what core concept are they utilizing?|Totalitarian state supremacy|Traditional order and gradual change|Collective worker ownership|Absolute individual anarchy|Option B|Conservatism prioritizes preserving historical continuity, traditional social orders, and instituting changes only gradually and organically.
9.1|Which ideology views society not as a collection of independent individuals, but as an organic entity whose supreme expression is realized through a powerful, centralized dictatorial apparatus?|Fascism|Liberalism|Anarchism|Socialism|Option A|Fascism constructs an organic view of the nation-state where individual liberties are crushed in favor of absolute state supremacy and totalitarian control.
10.1|What is the core defining principle of constitutionalism in political governance?|The absolute supremacy of the legislature over the judiciary|Governance strictly according to fundamental law that limits state power and protects civil liberties|The total absence of any written legal framework in modern states|The complete centralization of state administration under a unitary system|Option B|Constitutionalism requires that government power be limited by a fundamental law to safeguard citizens' civil liberties against arbitrary rule.
10.1|Which classification best describes a constitution that requires a special, arduous legislative procedure for amendment?|Flexible constitution|Unwritten constitution|Rigid constitution|Unitary constitution|Option C|A rigid constitution demands special legislative procedures and supermajorities for amendments, distinguishing it from flexible ones.
10.1|What is a primary characteristic of an unwritten constitution, as exemplified by the United Kingdom?|It is completely unrecorded and exists only as oral tradition among judges|It is contained in a single, sacred document ratified by a constituent assembly|It is derived from a collection of statutes, judicial precedents, and conventions rather than a single document|It can never be amended or altered under any circumstances whatsoever|Option C|An unwritten constitution is not codified in a single document but is sourced from multiple statutes, customs, and judicial precedents.
10.1|How does a unitary system of government structurally distribute constitutional power?|By dividing sovereignty equally between regional states and a central government|By concentrating all ultimate governing authority in a single central national government|By abolishing all local authorities and delegating power solely to international bodies|By granting independent veto power to each provincial legislature over national laws|Option B|A unitary system concentrates constitutional power within a central national government, which may delegate administrative duties to lower units.
10.1|What role did Chief Rotimi Williams play in the evolution of Nigeria's constitutional history?|He served as the sole military dictator during the transition to the executive presidency|He led the committee known as the 49 Wise Men in the Constitutional Drafting Committee for the 1979 Constitution|He drafted the 1960 independence constitution without any legislative consultation|He successfully abolished the federal system of government in favor of a monarchy|Option B|Chief Rotimi Williams headed the famous 49 Wise Men of the Constitutional Drafting Committee that laid the groundwork for Nigeria's 1979 Constitution.
10.1|Which institutional body immediately succeeded the Constitutional Drafting Committee to finalize the framework for Nigeria's 1979 Constitution?|The British Colonial Office|The Supreme Military Council|The Constituent Assembly|The Federal Executive Council|Option C|The Constituent Assembly reviewed and debated the draft produced by the Constitutional Drafting Committee to transition Nigeria toward an executive presidency.
10.1|What significant structural change in governance did the 1979 Nigerian Constitution introduce?|A shift from a parliamentary system to an American-style executive presidential system|A complete transition from a federal structure to a strict unitary state|The establishment of a hereditary monarchy with lifetime legislative powers|The adoption of an unwritten constitution modeled after the United Kingdom|Option A|The 1979 Constitution marked Nigeria's historical institutional transition from a British-style parliamentary system to an executive presidency.
10.1|Which of the following is a primary feature of a flexible constitution?|It can be amended through the same simple majority process used for ordinary legislation|It requires a referendum and a two-thirds majority of all regional states to change|It is immutable and permanently blocks any legal or social reforms|It is strictly prohibited from containing any provisions regarding human rights|Option A|A flexible constitution allows amendments through standard legislative procedures without requiring special, arduous ratification hurdles.
10.1|Which constitutional category best describes a system where legislative and executive powers are shared between a central government and regional constituent units?|Unitary constitution|Flexible constitution|Federal constitution|Unwritten constitution|Option C|A federal constitution constitutionally divides powers between a central national government and regional or state governments.
10.1|Why is constitutionalism considered distinct from simply having a constitution?|A constitution can exist formally on paper without effectively limiting state power or protecting rights, whereas constitutionalism demands active limitation of power|Constitutionalism only applies to unwritten systems like the United Kingdom|A constitution is a temporary decree while constitutionalism is a permanent military doctrine|Constitutionalism forbids any form of executive authority in government|Option A|Having a constitution does not guarantee constitutionalism if the governing authorities ignore its limitations and trample civil liberties.
12.1|Which form of political change is characterized by a gradual, peaceful process of institutional adjustment rather than a sudden systemic overthrow?|Revolutionary change|Evolutionary or reformist change|Coup d'état|Military interventionism|Option B|Evolutionary or reformist change occurs gradually and peacefully through existing institutional frameworks, contrasting with violent or abrupt systemic shifts.
12.1|How does a coup d'état fundamentally differ from a social revolution in terms of political transformation?|A coup is a top-level seizure of state power without a deep transformation of socioeconomic structures, whereas a revolution involves a fundamental, systemic overturn.|A coup always incorporates widespread popular participation, while a revolution is strictly carried out by elite military units.|A revolution occurs overnight through constitutional means, whereas a coup takes decades of evolutionary reform.|A coup replaces economic systems completely, whereas a revolution only replaces individual political figures.|Option A|A coup d'état is typically an elite, top-level seizure of government leadership that leaves underlying social and economic structures largely intact, unlike a full revolution.

14.1|Which of the following best characterizes Max Weber's concept of fixed jurisdictional areas within a bureaucracy|Official duties are distributed in a stable, regulated manner defined by administrative rules|Positions are assigned randomly based on daily administrative workloads|Jurisdictions shift dynamically according to shifting political priorities|Tasks are shared equally among all workers regardless of departmental specialization|Option A|Weber's model requires clearly defined spheres of competence and official duties distributed predictably according to established regulations.
14.1|How does a hierarchical chain of command function in a Weberian bureaucratic model|Higher offices supervise and control lower offices in a graded system of authority|All administrative workers share absolute horizontal equality in decision-making|Power is decentralized entirely to local field units to maximize autonomy|Subordinates maintain absolute veto power over directives issued by executive superiors|Option A|A hierarchical structure ensures strict vertical subordination, where each lower office is controlled and supervised by a higher one.
14.1|What role do written files and records play in the ideal bureaucratic model according to Max Weber|Administrative acts and decisions are recorded in writing to ensure organizational memory and continuity|Files are kept exclusively for confidential personal evaluations of top executives|Written documentation is discouraged to maintain verbal flexibility in governance|Records are used solely for public historical exhibitions rather than daily administration|Option A|Weber emphasized that administrative operations and decisions are preserved in writing to maintain a permanent and traceable operational record.
14.1|What is the functional purpose of impersonality in Max Weber's bureaucratic theory|To administer official business without bias, personal affection, or emotional favoritism|To strip all workers of individuality and mandate identical personal lifestyles off-duty|To prevent employees from communicating with anyone outside their specific department|To ensure that citizens receive preferential treatment based on personal connections|Option A|Impersonality ensures that bureaucratic officials execute their duties neutrally and objectively, free from personal bias or emotional attachments.
14.1|Why is career tenure a fundamental component of the merit-based Weberian bureaucracy|It protects officials from arbitrary dismissal and secures professional independence in public service|It guarantees that employees can never be disciplined for poor job performance|It forces civil servants to remain in the same entry-level position for their entire lives|It ensures that political leaders can replace the entire administration after every election cycle|Option A|Career tenure provides job security, allowing bureaucrats to act objectively and professionally without fear of political retaliation or arbitrary firing.
14.1|Which factor primarily determines recruitment and advancement in a Weberian bureaucratic structure|Technical qualifications, specialized training, and demonstrated merit|Personal loyalty to the reigning political party or executive leader|Family lineage, social status, and aristocratic background|Length of personal acquaintance with senior departmental directors|Option A|Weberian bureaucracies rely strictly on merit-based recruitment where individuals are selected based on specialized qualifications and formal training.
14.1|How are salaries structured for officials in the classical Weberian ideal bureaucratic model|Regular, fixed monetary compensation paid directly by the organization rather than fees from clients|Voluntary donations collected directly from citizens seeking government services|Variable commissions based on the number of bureaucratic forms processed daily|Unpaid volunteer status supported by private outside business investments|Option A|Weber specified that officials receive fixed monetary salaries determined by their rank, rendering them financially independent from citizen fees or client bribes.
14.1|Which of the following represents a core structural attribute of Max Weber's bureaucracy|Rational-legal authority backed by systematic rules and structured hierarchy|Charismatic leadership based on emotional appeals and traditional customs|Decentralized tribal governance driven by customary communal practices|Direct democratic voting by all citizens on every administrative regulation|Option A|Weberian bureaucracy is the organizational manifestation of rational-legal authority, operating through codified rules, hierarchy, and legal procedures.
14.1|In the context of Max Weber's bureaucratic model, what does official duty require of an administrator|Full-time commitment to official responsibilities as a primary occupational career|Part-time volunteer participation alongside private commercial enterprises|Temporary service rendered only during times of acute national crisis|Occasional advisory contributions dictated purely by personal convenience|Option A|Weber defined bureaucracy as a professionalized vocation requiring the official's full-time dedication to administrative duties as a primary career.
14.1|What is a primary systemic outcome of implementing the Weberian bureaucratic model in public administration|Enhanced administrative predictability, calculability, efficiency, and formal equality before rules|Increased unpredictability and reliance on spontaneous emotional decision-making|Total elimination of all administrative paperwork and regulatory documentation|Frequent executive disruptions caused by arbitrary personal patronage appointments|Option A|The combination of fixed rules, hierarchy, and impersonality is designed to maximize administrative predictability, efficiency, and formal equality.

10.1|What is the core philosophical objective of constitutionalism in a democratic state?|Centralizing total authority within the executive branch|Governing according to fundamental laws that limit government power to protect liberties|Ensuring the absolute supremacy of judicial review over legislative acts|Eliminating the need for a formal legislative assembly|Option B|Constitutionalism fundamentally entails governance constrained by supreme laws to prevent tyranny and safeguard the civil liberties of citizens.
10.1|Which country serves as the classic textbook example of a state operating under an unwritten constitution?|United States|Nigeria|United Kingdom|Canada|Option C|The United Kingdom is universally recognized for utilizing an unwritten (or uncodified) constitution comprised of various historical documents, conventions, and laws.
10.1|How does a flexible constitution differ primarily from a rigid constitution?|It can be amended through the same simple legislative process as ordinary laws|It cannot be modified under any political circumstances|It requires a special referendum for every minor administrative change|It is always unwritten and purely customary|Option A|Flexible constitutions do not require special, rigorous amendment procedures and can be altered by the regular legislative body using standard lawmaking procedures.
10.1|What was the popular designation given to the 49 eminent members of the Constitution Drafting Committee (CDC) led by Chief Rotimi Williams in Nigeria?|The Constituent Assembly|The Wise Men|The Executive Council|The National Patriots|Option B|Chief Rotimi Williams headed the 49-member Constitution Drafting Committee (CDC), famously referred to as the 49 Wise Men, which laid the groundwork for Nigeria's 1979 Constitution.
10.1|Which institutional body was specifically responsible for debating, reviewing, and ultimately transitioning Nigeria to the 1979 Executive Presidential system?|The Supreme Military Council|The Constituent Assembly|The Judicial Service Commission|The Federal Executive Council|Option B|Following the work of the CDC, the Constituent Assembly was convened to debate and finalize the framework that transitioned Nigeria to an Executive Presidency in 1979.
10.1|In a federal constitutional arrangement, how is power formally distributed?|Concentrated solely within the central government authority|Divided constitutionally between a central government and regional or state units|Retained exclusively by local municipal governments|Delegated entirely at the discretion of the judiciary|Option B|A federal constitution establishes a constitutional division of powers between the central national government and constituent state or regional governments.
10.1|What is the defining characteristic of a unitary system of constitutional governance?|All governmental power is legally vested in a single central authority|Power is shared equally between provinces and the national capital|Regional governments hold absolute veto power over national statutes|The constitution explicitly forbids central government intervention in local affairs|Option A|In a unitary system, ultimate governmental power resides centrally, and any regional or local bodies derive their authority entirely from the central government.
10.1|Which major institutional shift marked the introduction of the 1979 Constitution in Nigeria under the transition program?|Shift from a parliamentary system to an executive presidential system|Shift from a federal structure to a strictly unitary state|Shift from a written code to an entirely unwritten constitutional convention|Shift from civilian rule to a lifelong military dictatorship|Option A|The 1979 Constitution notably discarded the British-style parliamentary model in favor of an American-style Executive Presidential system of government.
14.1|Which of the following best characterizes Max Weber's concept of fixed jurisdictional areas within a bureaucracy|Duties and responsibilities are clearly distributed and officially defined for every office holder|Tasks are assigned dynamically based on daily political whims and executive moods|Responsibilities shift fluidly among workers depending on personal friendships|Jurisdictions overlap entirely to encourage cross-departmental competition|Option A|Weberian bureaucracy relies on a formal division of labor where official duties are strictly circumscribed by rules and regulations.
14.1|How does the hierarchical chain of command function in a Weberian bureaucratic structure|Lower offices are directly supervised and controlled by higher-ranking authorities|Every employee operates as an independent agent answerable only to the general public|Authority flows horizontally across departments with no distinct supervisory layer|Decision-making power is concentrated entirely at the lowest administrative tier|Option B|A strict hierarchy establishes a clear pyramid of authority where each lower office is subordinate to a higher one.
14.1|What is the significance of written files and records in Max Weber's model of bureaucracy|They form the permanent memory of the administration and ensure operational continuity|They are used exclusively as historical artifacts for public museums and libraries|They serve as temporary notes that are routinely discarded at the end of each fiscal week|They are optional guidelines that administrators can choose to ignore at will|Option A|Written documentation ensures that administrative acts, decisions, and rules are recorded and preserved systematically.
14.1|Why does Max Weber emphasize impersonality in the execution of official bureaucratic duties|To eliminate personal bias, favoritism, and emotional attachments in administrative decisions|To ensure that public officials form deep personal bonds with the citizens they serve|To allow administrators to bypass official rules based on individual moral judgments|To encourage subjective political favoritism toward high-ranking politicians|Option C|Impersonality ensures that clients and citizens are treated according to objective rules rather than personal feelings.
14.1|What is the primary rationale for merit-based career tenure in a Weberian bureaucracy|To protect officials from arbitrary dismissal and secure professional, politically neutral service|To ensure that jobs are distributed exclusively among ruling family members and political allies|To guarantee that employees can be fired instantly whenever a new political party wins an election|To encourage high employee turnover to prevent workers from mastering their jobs|Option B|Career tenure based on merit protects administrative professionals from partisan interference and political turnover.
14.1|Which administrative feature ensures that bureaucrats remain financially secure and independent of bribery|Fixed salaries paid directly by the organization rather than fees collected from clients|Commission-based pay derived directly from the number of citizens served daily|Voluntary donations collected from local businesses to cover operating expenses|Unpredictable stipends distributed based on the success of political campaigns|Option A|Fixed salaries prevent bureaucrats from extorting fees directly from citizens and promote institutional integrity.
14.1|In the context of Weberian bureaucracy what does fixed jurisdictional authority prevent among administrative offices|Duplication of effort and jurisdictional conflicts through clear demarcation of duties|Cooperation and communication between different departments and regional branches|The implementation of any standardized rules across different government agencies|The appointment of qualified personnel to specialized administrative roles|Option C|Clearly defined jurisdictions eliminate operational overlap and clarify institutional boundaries.
14.1|What distinguishes a bureaucratic organization from a traditional or charismatic administrative structure according to Weber|Reliance on legal-rational authority, written rules, and structural hierarchy rather than personal loyalty|Dependence on the divine right of kings and hereditary succession of office holders|Adherence to emotional appeals and spontaneous revolutionary zeal from followers|Absence of any formal rules or records in favor of oral traditions|Option A|Weberian bureaucracy is rooted in legal-rational authority characterized by systematic rules and formal structures.
14.1|Why are official records considered indispensable to the functioning of a modern bureaucracy|They provide a cumulative reference for past decisions to maintain consistency and accountability|They are designed primarily to slow down administrative processes and create paperwork|They serve as secret documents that must be hidden permanently from public oversight|They replace the need for any formal laws or legislative statutes passed by parliaments|Option A|Administrative acts require documented precedents to ensure procedural consistency and legal accountability.
14.1|How does the hierarchical structure of a bureaucracy affect communication and accountability within the organization|It channels directives downward and reports upward through clearly established formal pathways|It encourages chaotic, peer-to-peer messaging that bypasses all official supervisors entirely|It confines all communication strictly to informal social networks outside the workplace|It eliminates the need for any oversight by senior management over lower-level workers|Option A|The chain of command structures official communication to maintain strict supervision and operational control.

12.1|How does a coup d'etat fundamentally differ from a revolution in terms of political dynamics?|A coup is a top-level military seizure of power without systemic social transformation while a revolution is a violent and total overhaul of the social structure|A coup always results in democratic elections while a revolution establishes a military dictatorship|A coup is carried out by the civilian masses while a revolution is orchestrated exclusively by elite military officers|A coup requires long-term ideological planning while a revolution happens spontaneously overnight|Option A|A coup d'etat is an illegal, top-level change in government leadership without altering the underlying socio-economic system, whereas a revolution fundamentally transforms the entire political and social order.
12.1|Which of the following best describes the core mechanism of a coup d'etat?|Grassroots mobilization of labor unions|A sudden, illegal seizure of state power from within the existing elite structure, often by the military|A prolonged constitutional amendment process approved by a referendum|Foreign military intervention and annexation|Option B|A coup d'etat relies on a swift, elite-level maneuver, typically executed by the armed forces or security apparatus, to depose the current leadership.
12.1|What is a primary distinguishing feature of revolutionary political change?|It occurs strictly through legal parliamentary procedures|It involves a violent and fundamental overturn of the existing political, economic, and social systems|It is initiated exclusively by career bureaucrats seeking minor tax reforms|It maintains the existing institutional status quo without altering class relations|Option B|Revolutionary change is defined by its radical, systemic scope and the use of violent force to completely replace the established ruling class and social structure.

12.1|An economic collapse characterized by hyperinflation, mass unemployment, and acute scarcity often serves as a catalyst for military rule for what reason?|It proves the perfection of free-market capitalism|It destroys the legitimacy of the incumbent civilian government and incites popular despair, allowing the military to seize power amid public disillusionment|It forces the military to disband due to a lack of resources|It instantly resolves all ideological disputes among political factions|Option B|Severe economic failure erodes public trust in civilian leaders, creating an environment where military intervention is often greeted with initial public relief.

12.1|Which of the following scenarios represents an evolutionary rather than a revolutionary or coup-induced political change?|A junta suspends the constitution and deposes the president at dawn|Citizens elect a new parliament that gradually amends the tax code over several years|A guerrilla army overthrows the capital and nationalizes all private property|A faction of generals arrests the cabinet ministers and imposes martial law|Option B|Gradual, legal policy changes enacted through established legislative processes represent evolutionary or reformist political development.
