3.1|Which of the following best defines the core focus of the legalistic or institutional approach in political science?|Informal political networks and street-level bureaucracy|Formal legal rules constitutional texts and official government institutions|Socio-economic class struggles and wealth distribution disparities|Cultural norms and psychological motivations of voters|Option B|The legalistic or institutional approach centers primarily on formal legal frameworks constitutional documents and structural organs of the state like legislatures and courts.
3.1|What is a primary analytical advantage of applying the legalistic or institutional approach to political analysis?|It accurately predicts revolutionary movements and sudden regime collapses|It measures the exact psychological impact of campaign advertisements on voters|It clearly clarifies constitutional rights and formal jurisdictional limits of power|It captures the hidden influence of underground economic markets on policy|Option C|By focusing on written laws and structural rules this approach provides clarity regarding official constitutional rights and the legal boundaries of institutional power.
3.1|Which of the following is considered a major limitation of the legalistic or institutional approach?|It relies too heavily on quantitative survey data and polling metrics|It ignores informal power dynamics socio-economic forces and pressure groups|It refuses to examine written constitutions or legislative acts|It overestimates the role of individual political psychology in governance|Option B|A core critique of institutionalism is its static and descriptive nature which overlooks informal power structures corruption and external socio-economic pressures.
3.1|Why is the legalistic approach frequently criticized as being static?|Because it changes its fundamental definitions of government every election cycle|Because it focuses exclusively on volatile political protests and riots|Because it views political structures through a fixed formal lens rather than accounting for evolving political dynamics|Because it mandates that constitutions remain unamendable over time|Option C|The approach is labeled static because it treats legal texts and institutional designs as rigid blueprints while missing the fluid and dynamic reality of politics.
3.1|How does the institutional approach typically view the role of courts and legislatures?|As secondary actors completely subordinate to corporate lobbying groups|As minor cultural symbols with no real impact on policy implementation|As central formal organs responsible for upholding constitutional rules and making laws|As temporary revolutionary committees designed to overthrow traditional authority|Option D|In the institutional framework legislatures and courts are studied as the core formal machinery of the state responsible for legal enactment and adjudication.
3.1|Which phenomenon is most likely to be overlooked by a strict adherent to the legalistic approach?|The formal veto procedure exercised by a chief executive|The statutory text defining the jurisdiction of a supreme court|Informal backroom bargaining and corruption among political elites|The official amendment process outlined in a national constitution|Option C|Informal elite negotiations and corrupt practices operate outside official legal rules and are thus missed by purely institutional analyses.
3.1|What distinguishes the institutional approach from approaches that emphasize socio-economic forces?|Institutionalism focuses on formal state structures rather than class distributions or economic production|Institutionalism rejects the study of any written documents whatsoever|Institutionalism prioritizes Marxist economic theory over legal codes|Institutionalism exclusively analyzes international trade agreements|Option A|While socio-economic approaches look at material wealth and class relations institutionalism concentrates on formal rules and governmental bodies.
3.1|In the context of political science methodologies how is the descriptive nature of the institutional approach generally evaluated?|As a revolutionary breakthrough that explains political psychology|As a useful baseline for mapping formal structures but insufficient for explaining full political behavior|As an entirely useless framework that provides false constitutional data|As the only valid method for measuring public opinion trends|Option B|Descriptiveness allows scholars to map out formal structures clearly but limits the approach's ability to explain the underlying behavioral drivers of politics.
3.1|Which of the following would a legalistic-institutional researcher study to understand a government?|The social media sentiment of average citizens during an election|The official constitutional text outlining executive powers and legislative procedures|The psychological trauma experienced by marginalized socio-economic groups|The underground economy operating outside state tax codes|Option B|Constitutional texts and formal executive-legislative rules are the primary empirical data sources for legalistic-institutional scholars.
3.1|What blind spot does the legalistic approach share regarding interest groups and political parties?|It assumes parties and interest groups do not exist because they are not part of the physical judiciary|It fails to account for how external pressure groups and lobbies informally shape the legislative process|It overemphasizes revolutionary uprisings at the expense of parliamentary debate|It measures party loyalty using advanced econometric modeling|Option B|Because it focuses strictly on official institutions the legalistic approach often misses how external pressure groups informally influence policy outcomes.

14.1|Which of the following best characterizes Max Weber's concept of fixed jurisdictional areas within a bureaucracy|Official duties are distributed in a stable, systematic manner regulated by laws or administrative rules|Tasks are assigned dynamically based on daily political whims and executive discretion|Responsibilities shift constantly among workers depending on peer collaboration and informal agreements|Jurisdictions are determined purely by personal relationships between the leader and subordinates|Option A|Fixed jurisdictional areas mean that official duties are clearly defined and systematically distributed by rules, ensuring predictability and accountability.
14.1|How does the hierarchical chain of command function in a Weberian ideal bureaucratic model|Lower offices are supervised and controlled by higher ones in a clearly structured pyramid of authority|All administrative decisions are made collectively through democratic voting by all organizational members|Authority is decentralized completely to local field agents without any oversight from a central office|Supervisors have nominal status while day-to-day decisions are dictated entirely by external political sponsors|Option A|A hierarchical chain of command establishes a strict, pyramid-shaped system of subordination where every lower office is controlled by a higher one.
14.1|What is the primary significance of maintaining written files and records in a Weberian bureaucracy|Administrative acts and decisions are preserved in writing to ensure organizational memory and legal continuity|Written documents serve primarily as historical literature for academic research outside the agency|Records are kept solely to satisfy temporary public relations campaigns and media requests|Files are optional notes used informally by individual bureaucrats during private meetings|Option A|Written files and records ensure that administrative acts, decisions, and rules are documented for transparency, continuity, and accountability.
14.1|In the context of Max Weber's bureaucracy, what does the principle of impersonality imply|Officials discharge their official duties without regard for personal affections, biases, or individual emotions|Bureaucrats must remain completely anonymous to the public and hide their legal identities|Decision-making is entirely random and detached from any established legal frameworks or policies|Employees are treated as disposable machinery with no human rights or workplace protections|Option A|Impersonality means that administrative tasks are executed objectively and uniformly, without personal bias or emotional favoritism.
14.1|What role does merit-based career tenure play within the Max Weber ideal bureaucratic model|It ensures officials are appointed and promoted based on professional qualifications, examinations, and proven competence|It guarantees that political appointees can fire any career civil servant at any time without justification|It forces employees to remain in the exact same entry-level position for the entirety of their working lives|It bases promotions exclusively on family lineage, personal loyalty to the regime, and social wealth|Option A|Merit-based career tenure protects civil servants from arbitrary dismissal and ensures that advancement depends on professional competence rather than political patronage.
14.1|Why are fixed salaries a fundamental structural component of Weberian bureaucratic organizations|They provide financial independence, reducing the temptation of corruption and ensuring loyalty to the office|They allow administrators to engage in private entrepreneurial ventures using state resources on the side|They tie the personal income of bureaucrats directly to the daily profits or losses of the government agency|They ensure that administrative workers are compensated strictly through fees collected directly from citizens|Option A|Fixed salaries provide predictable financial security, which minimizes administrative corruption and reinforces professional dedication to the office.

14.1|How do written files and records directly contribute to the stability and efficiency of a bureaucracy according to Weber|They allow the modern office to operate based on accumulated precedents, institutional memory, and codified rules|They create bureaucratic red tape that intentionally slows down all governmental operations to discourage citizens|They enable administrators to alter past laws secretly without leaving a trace of the original legislation|They function primarily as advertising material to promote the agency's political achievements to voters|Option A|Written records anchor the bureaucracy in established rules and precedents, ensuring long-term institutional stability and consistent administration.
14.1|What is a direct consequence of implementing the rule of impersonality in bureaucratic administration|Clients receive standardized and predictable treatment regardless of their personal social status or wealth|Public officials prioritize the personal needs of wealthy citizens over ordinary citizens to gain favors|Bureaucrats exercise arbitrary power based on their personal moods and subjective moral judgements|Government agencies become highly individualized and customize every single procedure for each person|Option A|Impersonality ensures that rules are applied uniformly to all citizens, preventing favoritism and guaranteeing equal treatment under the law.
14.1|Which key feature distinguishes a Weberian bureaucratic career from political appointments or elected office|Career tenure based on professional qualifications and examinations rather than political loyalty or election cycles|Total freedom to alter core constitutional laws based on shifting public opinion polls and electoral mandates|Temporary status tied strictly to the tenure of the current executive head of state or ruling political party|Appointment derived entirely from personal wealth, aristocratic birthright, or charismatic leadership appeal|Option A|Weberian career tenure is anchored in professional expertise and merit-based advancement rather than short-term political alignments or election results.

5.1|Providing public healthcare, universal education, and social security safety nets are examples of which category of state functions?|Ministrant functions|Constituent functions|Essential functions|Coercive functions|Option A|Ministrant functions are optional or welfare-oriented services undertaken by the government to advance the social well-being and economic development of its citizens.
5.1|If a government deploys its armed forces to repel an external invasion or conducts formal diplomatic negotiations with another nation, which type of state function is it executing?|Constituent function|Ministrant function|Welfare function|Subsidiary function|Option A|National defense and foreign relations fall squarely under constituent functions, which protect the state from external threats and secure its borders.
5.1|How do ministrant functions fundamentally differ from constituent functions in modern political science?|Ministrant functions focus on social welfare and economic development whereas constituent functions focus on basic order and defense|Ministrant functions are legally prohibited in democratic systems while constituent functions are mandatory|Ministrant functions can only be performed by private corporations whereas constituent functions are exclusive to citizens|Ministrant functions are temporary emergency measures whereas constituent functions are permanent daily activities|Option A|Ministrant functions center on enhancing societal welfare and provisioning services, while constituent functions protect the foundational existence and security of the state.

4.1|Which intellectual movement in political science primary originated from the Chicago School during the 1950s and emphasized empirical observation of individual political actors?|Behaviouralism|Post-Behaviouralism|Institutionalism|Structural Functionalism|Option A|Behaviouralism emerged in the 1950s through scholars at the Chicago School who advocated for studying human political behavior empirically.
4.1|How does the credo of Behaviouralism define the concept of value-free inquiry in political research?|Political science must separate moral judgments and personal values from objective empirical analysis|Ethical values should dictate the selection of research methodologies|Value judgments are the ultimate goal of political analysis|Scientific techniques cannot be applied to human subjects without value statements|Option A|Value-free inquiry asserts that researchers must remain objective and separate personal moral values from empirical political observation.
4.1|Which key principle of the Behavioural credo focuses on expressing political data through numerical measurement and statistical tools?|Quantification|Verification|Systematization|Regularities|Option A|Quantification refers to the process of measuring political phenomena numerically and using statistical techniques for data analysis.
4.1|How did Post-Behaviouralism primarily critique the strict application of the Behavioural approach?|It argued that Behaviouralism ignored urgent social crises like poverty and war in favor of methodological purity|It claimed that Behaviouralism relied too heavily on qualitative historical analysis|It asserted that Behaviouralism overemphasized normative philosophical ideals|It criticized Behaviouralism for rejecting quantitative techniques and statistical measurements|Option A|Post-Behaviouralism critiqued Behaviouralism for prioritizing technique over substance while ignoring real-world crises such as war, poverty, and social inequality.
4.1|Which feature of the Behavioural credo insists that empirical claims and conclusions must be tested and validated against observable evidence?|Verification|Systematization|Integration|Regularities|Option A|Verification requires that all scientific propositions and theoretical generalizations be grounded in and tested against observable political facts.
4.1|According to Post-Behavioural theorists, what should be the fundamental purpose of political science research?|Addressing pressing human crises and maintaining social relevance|Developing abstract theories unburdened by contemporary social problems|Eliminating all practical applications to preserve academic neutrality|Focusing exclusively on formal state institutions and legal frameworks|Option A|Post-Behaviouralism demands that political research actively engage with real-world human crises and retain social relevance.
4.1|In the Behavioural approach, what does the concept of regularities suggest about political behavior?|There are observable patterns in human political behavior that can be expressed as general principles|Political actions are completely random and impossible to predict scientifically|Human political decisions are determined entirely by rigid legal statutes|Every political action is completely unique and cannot be generalized|Option A|The assumption of regularities posits that human political actions exhibit recurring patterns that allow for theoretical generalizations.

4.1|What does the term systematization mean within the context of the Behavioural credo?|Research and theory building must be closely linked in a coherent logical framework|Data collection should occur without any underlying theoretical framework|Political research must be restricted to historical case studies|Empirical findings must be immediately converted into normative public policies|Option A|Systematization stresses that empirical research and theoretical construction must interact systematically to build coherent political knowledge.
4.1|A political scientist attempts to resolve ongoing social inequality by prioritizing practical action and relevance over pure quantitative precision. Which approach is this researcher applying?|Post-Behaviouralism|Traditional Behaviouralism|Formal Legalism|Classical Normative Theory|Option A|Post-Behaviouralism emphasizes action, social relevance, and solving urgent human problems like inequality over mere technical sophistication.

12.1|Which of the following best describes a revolutionary change?|A rapid, violent, and total systemic overturn of existing political and social structures|A peaceful adjustment of policy guidelines through legislative debate|A stealthy midnight replacement of a single cabinet minister by the armed forces|An incremental constitutional amendment passed by a democratic legislature|Option A|Revolutionary change is defined by its rapid, often violent nature and its goal of completely replacing the existing socioeconomic and political order.

12.1|What distinguishes a coup d'etat from other forms of political change regarding the actors involved?|It is exclusively executed by grassroots peasant uprisings|It involves the illegal seizure of state power by top-level military or internal security elements|It is conducted through transparent, universally ratified public referendums|It is managed entirely by international corporate conglomerates|Option B|A coup d'etat is specifically characterized by the illegal overthrow of top-level state leadership from within the state apparatus, typically by the armed forces.

3.1|What is the primary analytical focus of the legalistic institutional approach in political science|Informal social networks and community norms|Formal constitutional texts and official government structures|Socio-economic class struggles and wealth distribution|Psychological motivations of individual voters|Option B|The legalistic or institutional approach centers primarily on formal rules, constitutional documents, and established state organs like legislatures and courts.
3.1|Which of the following is considered a primary merit of utilizing the institutional approach to studying politics|It accurately predicts revolutionary movements before they occur|It thoroughly exposes hidden corruption networks within the bureaucracy|It clearly clarifies constitutional rights and institutional jurisdictional limits|It measures the exact psychological impact of media propaganda on citizens|Option C|A key strength of the legalistic framework is its ability to map out clear legal rights, formal duties, and the jurisdictional boundaries of government bodies.
3.1|A major limitation of the legalistic institutional approach is that it tends to be static and what else|Overly reliant on unpredictable revolutionary uprisings|Too focused on descriptive formal rules while ignoring informal power dynamics|Excessively reliant on micro-level psychological testing|Incapable of understanding basic constitutional text definitions|Option B|The approach is frequently criticized for being overly descriptive and static because it overlooks informal political behavior, pressure groups, and hidden power dynamics.
3.1|When political scientists critique the legalistic approach for ignoring socio-economic forces what do they mean|It fails to analyze how economic inequalities and social classes influence political outcomes|It does not account for the exact wording of parliamentary bylaws|It refuses to read historical documents written before the industrial era|It places too much emphasis on Marxist economic theory|Option A|Critics argue that focusing solely on legal texts blinds researchers to how wealth, class, and broader economic conditions actively shape political life.
3.1|Which political actors or groups are typically neglected or heavily under-analyzed by a strict legalistic institutional framework|Elected members of the national parliament and supreme court justices|Official cabinet ministers and state governors|Informal pressure groups and grassroots lobbying organizations|Formally appointed legislative committee chairpersons|Option C|Because the legalistic approach prioritizes official state institutions, it routinely overlooks non-governmental actors like interest groups and social movements that heavily influence policy.
3.1|How does the legalistic institutional approach view the study of constitutions and legal codes|As secondary documents useful only for historical context|As the core foundation and primary framework for understanding political life|As completely irrelevant illusions masking true economic power|As subjective guidelines that can be rewritten by any citizen at will|Option B|This approach treats constitutional texts and official laws as the central architecture that defines and limits state authority.
3.1|Which of the following research topics would best fit within a traditional legalistic institutional study|Examining the structural division of powers between the judiciary and the legislature according to constitutional amendments|Tracing how underground bribery influences municipal zoning decisions|Analyzing the psychological traits of voters who support populist candidates|Measuring how social media algorithms alter political polarization among teenagers|Option A|Analyzing constitutional divisions of power directly aligns with the legalistic focus on formal rules, official institutions, and legal boundaries.
3.1|What criticism is most commonly leveled against the institutional approach regarding political reality|It is too dynamic and changes its theoretical focus too rapidly|It paints an overly idealistic picture that does not match how politics actually functions on the ground|It relies too heavily on quantitative statistical modeling of voter behavior|It completely ignores the existence of courts and parliaments|Option B|By focusing exclusively on formal rules on paper, the approach often misses the messy reality of how politics is actually practiced through informal bargaining and corruption.
3.1|Why might a strict institutionalist fail to understand a major policy shift driven by widespread public protests|Protests are illegal activities that fall completely outside the scope of political science|Public protests represent formal constitutional amendments rather than policy shifts|Street-level activism and mass protests operate outside official institutional channels and formal rules|Protests only occur in nations that lack written constitutions|Option C|Since institutionalists focus primarily on official government structures, spontaneous mass movements and protests fall outside their standard analytical lens.
3.1|Which pair best represents the contrast between merits and limitations in the legalistic institutional approach|Clarity of jurisdictional limits versus blindness to informal power dynamics|Ability to predict revolutions versus inability to read legal texts|Focus on economic classes versus disregard for written laws|Excellence in analyzing corruption versus failure to recognize parliaments|Option A|The legalistic approach excels at defining formal legal boundaries and rights, but it fails precisely because it ignores informal forces and corruption operating outside those rules.
4.1|Which academic institution and intellectual tradition are primarily credited with laying the foundational roots of the behavioural approach in political science during the 1950s?|The Chicago school emphasizing empirical and quantitative measurement|The Oxford school focusing exclusively on classical normative political philosophy|The Frankfurt school specializing in critical theory and historical sociology|The Paris school concentrating on institutional legalism and constitutional frameworks|Option A|The behavioural revolution emerged heavily from the Chicago school in the 1950s, championed by scholars like David Easton and Harold Lasswell who emphasized empirical and quantitative observation.
4.1|Which of the following is considered a core tenet of the credo of behaviouralism as outlined by David Easton?|Pursuit of unverified philosophical assertions and normative speculations|Value-free inquiry and the systematic organization of empirical knowledge|Exclusive focus on legal statutory texts and historical narrative analysis|Rejection of data quantification in favour of intuitive political interpretation|Option B|Behaviouralism mandates value-free inquiry and the systematic organization of empirical data to build scientific theories of politics rather than relying on pure normative speculation.
4.1|How does the behavioural approach fundamentally differ from traditional approaches in political science?|It completely ignores individual human behavior to focus only on abstract state sovereignty|It relies exclusively on moral philosophy and theological interpretations of justice|It prioritizes empirical observation, quantification, and scientific verification of political actions|It rejects all forms of systemic data collection in preference of unverified ideological opinions|Option C|Unlike traditional approaches that focus heavily on legal texts and formal institutions, behaviouralism focuses on measurable human political behavior using empirical data and verification.
4.1|What primary methodological shift did the behavioural movement introduce into the study of politics?|A shift toward strict quantification, measurement techniques, and systematic verification|A complete abandonment of scientific methods in favour of artistic prose|A strict limitation of research to ancient philosophical texts without modern data|An insistence that political science should never use statistical instruments|Option A|Behaviouralism revolutionized political science by introducing rigorous quantification, advanced measurement techniques, and a commitment to empirical verification.
4.1|Which intellectual figure is most famously associated with the development and formalization of the behavioural approach in political science alongside the Chicago school?|David Easton|Plato|Karl Marx|Thomas Hobbes|Option A|David Easton is a central figure of the 1950s behavioural movement, notable for defining its core credos and advancing systems analysis in political science.
4.1|What was the major driving critique that led to the emergence of post-behaviouralism in political science?|Behaviouralism became too obsessed with pure technocratic data while ignoring pressing real-world crises|Behaviouralism relied too much on classical philosophical debates rather than statistical surveys|Post-behaviouralists wanted to completely eliminate the use of numbers and statistics in all academic research|Post-behaviouralists argued that political scientists should remain completely detached from human suffering|Option A|Post-behaviouralism arose because critics felt behaviouralism was overly focused on methodology and value-free neutrality while neglecting urgent societal crises like poverty and war.
4.1|According to the tenets of post-behaviouralism, what should be the primary moral and practical obligation of political science?|To remain strictly neutral and indifferent to real-world human suffering and political crises|To maintain academic detachment and never address contemporary societal problems|To actively remain socially relevant and address critical human challenges like war and inequality|To abandon all empirical research and return exclusively to ancient institutional descriptions|Option C|Post-behaviouralism insists that political science must remain socially relevant and actively address pressing human challenges such as poverty, inequality, and war.
4.1|Which of the following best describes the principle of value-free inquiry within the behavioural credo?|Deriving political values exclusively from religious scripture and dogma|Suspending personal ideological biases to ensure objective empirical observation of political phenomena|Imposing the researcher's personal moral opinions directly onto the data analysis|Avoiding any form of systematic data gathering to prevent objective conclusions|Option B|Value-free inquiry requires researchers to separate their personal political biases and normative values from empirical observations to maintain scientific objectivity.
4.1|In the context of behaviouralism, what does the principle of verification entail?|Accepting theoretical claims solely based on the authority of classical philosophers|Subjecting hypotheses to rigorous empirical testing and validation using observable data|Relying purely on intuitive judgments without any need for data or evidence|Dismissing all forms of data collection in favour of unexamined assumptions|Option B|Verification in behaviouralism requires that political claims and hypotheses be rigorously tested, measured, and validated against observable empirical evidence.

8.1|Which scenario best illustrates the use of prestige and persuasion in politics?|A dictator outlawing opposition parties to secure a monopoly on power|A respected civic leader convincing legislators to adopt a new environmental policy through expert testimony|A police department arresting protesters for violating a curfew ordinance|A court system sentencing a convicted felon to a prison term|Option B|Using expertise, prestige, and persuasion to shape legislative outcomes is a clear application of political influence.
8.1|Why is the rule of law considered a foundational source of political legitimacy?|It guarantees that the ruling elite remain entirely immune from prosecution|It ensures that governance follows predictable, accepted legal frameworks that citizens perceive as fair|It eliminates the need for any form of public participation or elections|It concentrates absolute authority in the hands of the executive branch|Option C|The rule of law provides predictability and fairness, which strengthens the public conviction that the legal and political system is morally valid.
8.1|In the context of political science, how is political influence best categorized?|As an absolute monopoly held exclusively by the head of state|As a non-coercive method of shaping political decisions and policy outcomes|As a formal legal instrument found only in written constitutions|As an illegal practice utilized solely by fringe political organizations|Option B|Political influence describes non-coercive processes such as lobbying, persuasion, and prestige used to affect decisions.
8.1|Which factor most directly links government performance to political legitimacy?|The ability of the state to win foreign military conflicts consistently|The delivery of essential public services and maintenance of economic stability that satisfy citizen expectations|The complete elimination of political opposition parties from the legislature|The reduction of government transparency to protect administrative secrets|Option B|Effective performance, such as delivering services and maintaining stability, validates a government's right to rule in the eyes of the public.
9.1|Which of the following best defines an ideology within the context of political science?|A random collection of short-term policy reactions to economic crises|A coherent set of normative beliefs that explains political reality and offers a blueprint for organization|A strict economic doctrine focusing exclusively on industrial production methods|A legal framework used solely by the judiciary to interpret constitutional law|Option B|An ideology provides a structured system of normative beliefs that both interpret social reality and propose a blueprint for political structures.
9.1|What core principle distinguishes classical liberalism from other major ideologies regarding the role of government?|Totalitarian state supremacy over all public and private institutions|Advocacy for a limited state focused on individual liberty and free markets|Collective ownership of all major industries and means of production|Preservation of feudal hierarchies and absolute monarchy at all costs|Option B|Liberalism prioritizes individual liberty and free markets while advocating for a limited state to protect those freedoms.
9.1|Which ideology emphasizes collective ownership of resources and a fundamental commitment to social equality?|Fascism|Conservatism|Socialism|Anarchism|Option C|Socialism centers on collective ownership and socioeconomic equality as the primary goals of political and economic organization.
9.1|Which prominent theorist is most commonly associated with traditional conservatism and the defense of gradual change and established order?|Karl Marx|Edmund Burke|Benito Mussolini|Mikhail Bakunin|Option B|Edmund Burke is widely recognized as the intellectual founder of traditional conservatism, emphasizing organic social order and gradual reform.
9.1|How does fascism fundamentally view the relationship between the individual and the state?|The individual possesses inalienable natural rights that the state can never infringe upon|The individual is completely subordinate to the supreme authority of the totalitarian state|The individual and the state exist in a temporary contractual arrangement based on consent|The state should be immediately dismantled to allow individuals total self-governance|Option B|Fascism and Nazism champion totalitarian state supremacy, where individual identity and rights are fully subordinated to the collective state.
9.1|Which ideological perspective calls for the complete rejection and abolition of all forms of state authority?|Liberalism|Socialism|Conservatism|Anarchism|Option D|Anarchism is defined by its core rejection of state authority, viewing governments as oppressive and unnecessary.
9.1|In the context of major political ideologies, what is a primary focus of the socialist critique of capitalist markets?|Markets inherently produce fair outcomes without the need for state intervention|Markets generate socioeconomic inequalities that require collective remedies|Markets destroy traditional religious institutions and cultural heritage|Markets lead directly to the establishment of direct democratic city-states|Option B|Socialism critiques capitalism primarily for generating systemic inequality, arguing instead for collective ownership and economic fairness.
9.1|Which of the following sets of characteristics best aligns with the ideology of liberalism?|Absolute monarchy, state planning, and religious orthodoxy|State supremacy, militarism, and aggressive nationalism|Individual liberty, limited government, and free-market capitalism|Abolition of private property and total worker control of production|Option C|Liberalism is built upon the foundational pillars of individual liberty, limited government intervention, and free-market economic systems.
9.1|What is the primary stance of conservatism regarding rapid or radical political and social change?|It is encouraged to modernize archaic economic structures quickly|It is viewed with skepticism, favoring instead traditional order and gradual evolution|It is necessary to overthrow oppressive capitalist hierarchies immediately|It is the only legitimate method to achieve a classless and stateless society|Option B|Conservatism values institutional continuity and traditional order, viewing abrupt, radical changes as destructive to social stability.
9.1|Which of the following ideologies is characterized by totalitarian control, extreme nationalism, and the denial of individual pluralism?|Fascism|Liberalism|Anarchism|Democratic Socialism|Option A|Fascism and Nazism are distinguished by totalitarianism, aggressive nationalism, and the absolute suppression of political pluralism and individual liberties.
12.1|Which form of political change is characterized by a peaceful, gradual, and institutional process rather than a sudden systemic overthrow?|Revolutionary change|Evolutionary or reformist change|Coup d'état|Military intervention|Option B|Evolutionary or reformist change involves gradual, peaceful, and institutional adjustments to the political system rather than sudden or violent transformation.
12.1|How does a coup d'état fundamentally differ structurally from a social revolution?|A coup is a top-level illegal seizure of state power without necessarily changing the underlying social structure whereas a revolution transforms the entire socioeconomic and political system|A coup relies entirely on mass civilian uprisings while a revolution is executed solely by professional soldiers|A coup is a slow constitutional reform while a revolution happens instantly through legislative voting|A coup always results in democratic governance while a revolution always leads to military rule|Option A|A coup d'état is typically an elite-driven, illegal overthrow of existing executive authorities, whereas a revolution fundamentally restructures society and political institutions.
12.1|A country experiences a rapid and total violent collapse of its economic system followed by widespread riots and the complete replacement of its ruling class and foundational ideology. What concept best describes this event?|Reformist policy adjustment|Coup d'état|Systemic revolution|Bureaucratic reshuffling|Option C|This scenario describes a revolutionary change, which involves a violent, systemic overturn of both the government and the underlying social and economic structures.
12.1|Which of the following is considered a primary institutional or internal motive for military intervention in politics?|The desire to implement nationwide free-market capitalism immediately|The protection of corporate perks and institutional military privileges from civilian budget cuts|A constitutional mandate requiring military officers to manage civil service elections|The mandatory retirement age of civilian judges and bureaucrats|Option B|Military organizations frequently intervene in politics to protect their institutional autonomy, corporate perks, and budgetary allocations when they feel threatened by civilian governments.
12.1|Deep-seated corruption, chronic economic mismanagement, and systemic failure of civilian politicians to maintain order are typically categorized as what in the study of military rule?|Structural causes or preconditions for military intervention|Triggers for evolutionary reform|Legal mechanisms for constitutional succession|Direct symptoms of a successful socialist revolution|Option A|Pervasive corruption and economic collapse create the political vacuum and loss of civilian legitimacy that act as foundational causes for military interventions.
12.1|If a group of high-ranking military generals suddenly deposes the sitting president and suspends the constitution overnight without altering the broader capitalist economic framework, this is best classified as a|Social revolution|Reformist transition|Coup d'état|Democratic consolidation|Option C|A sudden, illegal seizure of top-level state power by military elites without a complete restructuring of the socioeconomic system is a classic coup d'état.
12.1|Which factor frequently exacerbates political instability and increases the vulnerability of a developing state to military intervention?|Ethnic polarization and deep societal divisions among different regional groups|An excess of financial resources in the national treasury|Complete consensus among political parties regarding economic policy|A surplus of independent judicial oversight bodies|Option A|Ethnic polarization weakens national cohesion and creates severe friction that civilian governments often fail to manage, inviting military intervention under the guise of restoring unity.
12.1|What distinguishes a revolutionary change from a coup d'état regarding mass participation?|Revolutions require deep and widespread mobilization of the masses whereas coups are typically executed by small elite military factions|Coups always involve the entire working class whereas revolutions are restricted exclusively to palace guards|Revolutions are planned secretly by three officers whereas coups involve nationwide referendums|There is no difference in mass participation between the two phenomena|Option A|Revolutions inherently involve broad-based popular uprisings and systemic mass mobilization, whereas coups are generally narrow, top-down elite actions.
12.1|When civilian authorities repeatedly rig elections and manipulate democratic institutions for partisan survival, what secondary political consequence frequently follows?|The immediate strengthening of civil society organizations|The complete elimination of military budgets|A loss of government legitimacy that invites military intervention to restore order|The spontaneous establishment of a socialist economy|Option C|Rigged elections erode public trust and civil legitimacy, giving military officers a convenient pretext to step in and claim they are rescuing the nation from political decay.
12.1|Which term describes a political transformation that occurs through slow, legal, and institutional adjustments rather than sudden disruption?|Coup d'état|Revolutionary upheaval|Evolutionary change|Military dictatorship|Option C|Evolutionary change relies on continuous, legal, and reform-oriented processes within existing institutional frameworks instead of abrupt or violent overthrows.
10.1|What is the defining structural characteristic of a rigid constitution compared to a flexible one?|It can only be amended through a special, more demanding legislative or referendum process than ordinary laws|It is always codified in a single, comprehensive formal document ratified by international observers|It completely prohibits any form of legislative amendment or structural revision over time|It is exclusively found in unitary states with centralized parliamentary sovereignty|Option A|A rigid constitution requires a special, complex amendment procedure to safeguard fundamental laws against casual legislative changes.
10.1|Which country's constitutional system is traditionally cited as the primary example of an unwritten constitution?|United Kingdom|United States of America|Federal Republic of Nigeria|French Republic|Option A|The United Kingdom lacks a single codified constitutional document, relying instead on unwritten conventions, statutes, and common law.
10.1|What core political principle is best captured by the concept of constitutionalism?|The limitation of governmental power through a fundamental law to protect individual civil liberties|The absolute supremacy of the legislative branch over judicial review and executive actions|The systematic elimination of written statutes in favor of flexible executive decrees|The concentration of all sovereign authority within a single centralized unitary tier of government|Option A|Constitutionalism ensures that rulers exercise power within legal boundaries designed to prevent tyranny and protect citizen rights.
10.1|In the context of the 1979 Nigerian constitutional development, who led the famous Constitution Drafting Committee (CDC) popularly known as the 49 Wise Men?|Chief Rotimi Williams|Alhaji Shehu Shagari|General Murtala Mohammed|Dr. Nnamdi Azikiwe|Option A|Chief Rotimi Williams served as the chairman of the CDC, which was tasked with laying the preliminary groundwork for Nigeria's transition.
10.1|What major institutional change did the 1979 Nigerian Constitution introduce to replace the parliamentary system of the First Republic?|An Executive Presidential system combining the roles of head of state and head of government|A direct monarchical council appointed by traditional regional rulers|A collegiate presidency shared rotationally among regional governors|A unicameral legislature with supreme judicial appointment powers|Option A|The 1979 Constitution marked Nigeria's formal transition from a Westminster parliamentary model to an American-style Executive Presidential system.
10.1|How does a unitary constitution structurally distribute political power within a state?|Concentrating supreme legal authority in a single central government with subordinate regional units|Dividing power equally and constitutionally between autonomous regional governments and a central authority|Delegating all primary law-making powers exclusively to localized municipal councils|Dissolving national governance entirely in favor of confederated independent states|Option A|A unitary system vests ultimate sovereignty in a central national government, which may delegate administrative duties to lower tiers.
10.1|Which body was primarily responsible for debating and enacting the transitional framework that culminated in the 1979 Constitution after the CDC submitted its report?|The Constituent Assembly|The Supreme Military Council|The Federal Electoral Commission|The Judicial Service Commission|Option A|Following the CDC, a Constituent Assembly was established to review, debate, and finalize the constitutional blueprint for civilian rule.
10.1|What is a primary functional advantage of a flexible constitution?|It allows the legal framework to adapt swiftly to changing societal conditions through ordinary legislative processes|It prevents any political party from altering fundamental governance structures without a national referendum|It permanently locks in executive powers to shield them from short-term legislative manipulation|It mandates dual-chamber ratification for every routine administrative policy change|Option A|Because flexible constitutions can be amended like ordinary laws, they offer high adaptability to political and social evolution.
10.1|What distinguishes a federal constitution from a unitary constitution regarding governmental authority?|A federal constitution constitutionally divides power between a central government and coordinate regional units|A federal constitution allows the central government to abolish regional boundaries at will|A federal constitution eliminates the need for any written framework or judicial oversight|A federal constitution concentrates all fiscal and legislative authority within the federal capital|Option A|Federalism establishes a constitutional division of powers where both central and regional governments have independent spheres of authority.
10.1|Which of the following best describes a written or codified constitution?|A fundamental body of laws consolidated and formally articulated in a single comprehensive document|A collection of uncodified judicial precedents and historical political conventions|A series of unwritten royal proclamations that bypass the legislature entirely|A temporary legislative decree that expires automatically at the end of an electoral cycle|Option A|A written constitution organizes the foundational rules of a state into a single authoritative document for clarity and protection.
